en: The Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land (First Series), compiled by the Pure Land disciple of Tongyi, Zhuang Guanghuan.
Illustration of the Western Pure Land (also known as the World of Ultimate Bliss, or An-yang, or An-le, or Qing-tai, or Miao-yi; collectively termed the Pure Land).
Appended: A Poem by Master Zhongfeng on Recollecting the Pure Land (for details, see the Chapter on Rebirth, among the excerpts from Venerable Elders).
Seven layers of dense, true pearl nets; Three tiers of level, agate steps.
The Compassionate Guide of An-yang’s vow is profound; He stretches forth his golden arm from afar to receive those who come.
In the lotus ponds, flowers bloom every day; The four-colored radiance reflects upon the jeweled terraces.
His golden arms extend afar as his compassionate thoughts descend; For what reason do sentient beings not contemplate coming?
The shadows of the seven rows of trees interlace; Day and night, white lotuses bloom in full splendor.
The Buddha’s hand comes of its own accord; you cannot block it. Why do sentient beings seek the infinite?
The parrots and kalaviṅkas circle the tree, their voices harmonious and elegant, truly worthy of being heard.
Why is it that their diligent and unceasing [song] serves only to bewilder the spiritual essence of weary worldly beings?
Six times a day, rain falls of heavenly flowers, Their exquisite fragrance and novel flavor—what could surpass them?
At early dawn, they fill their robes and satchels; Returning, they again offer these to the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*.
For what reason is this world called "Ultimate Bliss"? Simply because it cannot be invaded by any of the various sufferings.
If a practitioner of the Way wishes to seek the path home, They need only realize their own mind amidst the dust of the world.
A journey of over a hundred thousand miles is not separated from this dust; Cease regarding delusion and enlightenment as distant or intimate.
When every momentary thought is exhausted, one becomes a Buddha as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, And is truly a person within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
An Appendix: Zen Master Xizhai’s Poem on Recollecting the Pure Land (His name was Fanqi, courtesy name Chushih; for details, see the *Wangsheng ji*).
About to attend the Dharma assembly to pay homage to the Golden Immortal, I gradually follow the fragrant breeze out from the precious lotus.
The light from his red flesh-protuberance flows endlessly, And his purple-golden body reflects boundlessly.
Layer upon layer, smoke-tinted trees hang over the level earth; Each and every flower pedestal reaches the distant heavens.
This rare occurrence within the realms of all Buddhas Is as clear as a bright mirror appearing before me.
Pointing afar toward the setting sun at my hometown, A single path of return stretches straight as a bowstring.
Melodies play in the air as every kind of joy; Lotus flowers bloom upon the water, petal by petal.
The branches and stalks of various trees become a hundred jewels; Their dwellings and sustenance surpass those of the devas.
My Master, may you grant your grace in accordance with your vow, So that my fifty years of diligent devotion are not in vain.
A single lotus holds a sacred embryo; when a lifetime’s merit is perfected, a flower blooms.
Necklaces of jewels appear according to one's heart; vessels of *sudhā* arrive with every thought.
The golden hall possesses a radiance that contains the sun and moon; the jade towers have no place for dust to settle.
The Dharma King has expounded the ultimate truth for me, Causing even the void to break into a full-cheeked smile.
Above the lotus flowers upon the pond stands a man; Buddha-light shines upon his purple-gold body.
Hearing further the wondrous Dharma, he removes the defilements of the mind, Completely rescuing deluded beings from the wheel of suffering.
With every step, he travels through lands as numerous as motes of dust, Fulfilling the causes for nirvana to benefit sentient beings.
In this Sahā world, time and light are short; In Sukhāvatī, how many kalpas of spring have passed?
Relax body and mind before the Buddha’s presence, Where the Dharma sound constantly fills the ears.
The wind in the branches plays only the song of non-arising; The sun-viewing peak forever opens the sky of no-night.
Walking, one follows the jade steps as clouds drift slowly; Sitting, one leans against the pearl trees as the moon shines brightly.
When ordinary beings reach this place, they all become sages; Without passing through kalpas of practice, the great fruit is perfected.
The palace of the jewel-king and the jade gardens, The places for sitting, reclining, and walking are of gold;
From time to time, the śarīra emits wondrous sounds, As kalaviṅka birds clearly play celestial melodies.
By turning the hearing back, one suddenly awakens to the principle of non-birth, Abiding eternally in the all-pervading, unmoving mind.
Everything the eye touches is the Pure Land; From kalpas past until this very day, every inch of time is an inch of gold.
I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and quickly turn your heart back [to the Dharma];
Though one may hold the nobility of the Phoenix Pavilion and Dragon Tower, One cannot escape the encroachment of crow-like skin and crane-like hair.
The incense smoke within the burner has not yet dispersed, And the celestial procession has already arrived from afar in the void.
Though every dust mote and every world-system is pure, Only Amitābha’s power of vow is profoundly deep.
(Return) I have carefully examined the poems of the two masters; though they are many, they do not exceed the two meanings of praise and exhortation. Now, regarding what follows...
Although this collection consists of seven verses, it fully encompasses two essential meanings.
As in Zhongfeng’s first five verses, which praise the excellence of the Pure Land, the sixth verse exhorts people to realize their own minds. How is one to realize one's own mind?

It cannot be accomplished except through the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Therefore, the seventh verse encourages people to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation), as in the preceding verses of the "Western Chamber" [poem].
The first five stanzas likewise praise the excellence of the Pure Land. The sixth stanza exhorts people to realize birthlessness (*anutpāda*).
How can one realize birthlessness? It cannot be done except through the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*buddhānusmṛti*). Therefore, the seventh stanza encourages people to practice *buddhānusmṛti*.
This is a compilation that summarizes the intent of these two poems, intended for practitioners of pure karma to chant and contemplate after their daily devotions.
Lustful dissipation! When the mind is satisfied and the meaning is harmonized, can there be anyone who does not dance with their hands and stamp with their feet?
The provisions for rebirth in the Pure Land begin here.
Preface to the Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land.

The Layman Zhuang compiled the sutras and treatises on the Pure Land from both ancient and modern times, selecting essential passages and arranging them by category, while occasionally appending his own reflections.
Once the volume was completed, he came to my door and informed me, saying: "This is the 'Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land.
Commentators say that works concerning the Pure Land stand shoulder to shoulder like rows of bookshelves; indeed, the chest has more than enough provisions and the sack has more than enough grain."
"What further need is there for this? I replied, "It is not so. Nowadays, when traveling ten thousand *li* abroad, we have never heard of anyone who would grow weary of an abundance of provisions.
Therefore, if one encounters exhaustion on a journey, even a few copper coins, a pint of gold, a grain of rice, or a measure of millet will suffice.
How much more so for a destitute son who has not returned for hundreds of thousands of *kalpas*, arriving at a treasure-land that is difficult to reach across hundreds of billions of worlds!"
Is it that you take offense at the abundance and wealth of the Dharma-treasures of merit? Or is it that you find the journey across the maps of the realm too arduous?
In remote regions and secluded villages, the difficulty of procuring even a single sūtra or śāstra is beyond measure.

If this compilation were to be widely disseminated so that people might read it, they would gain a rough understanding of the general outlines of the temporal teachings of a single era. Nevertheless, without carrying the coins for books...
Carrying a single grain of rice, one may be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the duration of a single thought-moment. Is there truly no such person in this world?

To speak of such matters before such people would indeed be superfluous words. However, if this were not entirely the case, then this work shall circulate alongside the various scriptures on the Pure Land;
who knows that it might not be of some benefit?
On an auspicious day in the first month of spring, in the year of Jiawu during the Great Ming Wanli era, Yunqi Zhuhong (Huan) respectfully records this.
Regarding the teaching that one should not carry a single coin nor possess a grain of rice, some have expressed doubt.
As for the Layman of Wutai, he maintained that both the sudden and gradual gates must rely upon the provisions (*sambhāra*). Now, as for what Master [Zhizhe] Liang said...

[The interlocutor] says: "They are not comparable. Why is that? I reply: "The Master Padmasambhava refers to those of superior intelligence (*adhimātra-prajñā*). The provisions (*sambhāra*) for one of superior intelligence consist of innate knowledge and spontaneous practice (*jāta-jñāna-anābhoga-caryā*).
How could such a person further rely upon this collection? What you now call 'carrying' (*chā*) or 'bearing' (*ji*) implies the force of grasping and the intent of guarding;
these pertain to the practice of those who learn through study and act with effort (*śruta-mayī-prajñā-viśeṣa-caryā*). How can such [terms] be used [to describe the former]?"
This is the mark of superior wisdom. Therefore, it is said that "he does not carry coins of script nor bring a grain of rice," which does not mean he truly lacks the provisions for the journey.
Readers may well refrain from allowing the literal phrasing to obscure the intended meaning.
Preface to the Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land:

The Direct Pointer to the Source of Reversion states: "Those who wish to be born in the Pure Land must prepare the provisions. Indeed, the path of the Pure Land is truly a swift shortcut to transcendence."
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni, through his greatest skillful means, specifically brought this forth and repeatedly instructed and admonished us, no less than three times and five times.
Throughout antiquity, the myriad sages and thousand worthies have praised and offered their teachings with one voice.
For sentient beings of the final age who wish to transcend birth and death, if they set aside the Pure Land, where else could they seek rebirth? Yet, as for the Pure Land...
In traveling, how could a pauper leave empty-handed? Although there are two gates—the sudden and the gradual—both necessarily rely upon provisions (*sambhāra*).
One who gives rise to [the aspiration] all at once in a single thought is like a person of great capacity and stature; a load of ten thousand *hu* can be prepared in an instant.
Those of a gradual disposition are like those of meager strength and resources; they must accumulate by the *dou* and the *sheng*, relying upon years and months. The world...
Those of superior intelligence are rare. It is essential that the provisions (*sambhāra*) be discussed in advance. What are these provisions? They are said to be faith, aspiration, and practice.
These three can be prepared in advance during the twelve periods of the day and night; then, when one sets out, they will be sufficient for whatever use is required.
Even if one traverses as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, there will be no hardships or distress—how much less so for ten trillion [lands].
Regarding the Pure Land: My friend, the Chan Master Lianchi, having received the Buddha’s seal of mind, propagated the Dharma in the southeast.
Among the disciples he guided, regardless of whether their faculties were sharp or dull, he tirelessly spoke of the Pure Land.
His eminent disciple, Layman Zhuang, fearing that those traveling west with empty bellies would find it difficult to advance, personally compiled this book and divided it into three volumes.

I have specially established this great causal Dharma for those of like-minded aspiration who follow the gradual path. Its final volume is titled *The Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land*.
This is intended to elaborate upon the meaning of "Directly Pointing to the Source of Return.
Upon examining its general scope, it does not transcend the three factors of faith, aspiration, and preceptual conduct; yet, it compiles past events and draws extensively from various sources.
This maxim compares [the accumulation of merit] to amassing great wealth, nearly filling a thousand granaries and ten thousand storehouses.
For those who aspire to the Land of Bliss, if they proceed according to this path, how could the attainment of Sukhāvatī not be possible?

Alas, since the principle of the Pure Land as one’s own mind has not been clarified in the world, those who favor the eccentric have often privileged *dhyāna* (meditation) while disparaging rebirth. Master Lianchi...
Since the Master has already guided those lost at the ford of delusion, this record by the Layman further aids their successful crossing.

It is the profound intention of the Western Sage that only after delivering all sentient beings does one ascend to Perfect Enlightenment. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states that the gift of Dharma is greater than the gift of wealth;
the Layman takes the dharma of rebirth in the Pure Land as his provisions and widely bestows it upon the Dharma-realm, employing the three thousand [worlds] for this purpose.
Even the merit of bestowing the seven treasures upon the great trichiliocosm—could it ever surpass this?

It is because he did not merely uphold the will of Master Lianchi, but also deeply repaid the grace of the Compassionate Honored One, Śākyamuni. Those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land should not forget the noble kindness of this layman.
Ah! This layman’s name is Guanghuan and his courtesy name is Fuzhen; he is a man of refined character and spiritual cultivation.
On the tenth day of the third month of spring in the year of Yimwei during the Wanli era, Lu Guangzu, a layman of Wutai at Danghu, respectfully records this.

In this "Autobiographical Preface to the Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land," I have observed that among the affairs of the world, there are matters determined by destiny whose outcomes do not depend on oneself;

these cannot be achieved through mere luck. There are matters that arise from Heaven and whose execution does not depend on man; these cannot be forcibly sought. Recognizing this, I have bestowed [this collection] upon you.
This can be known for a lifetime. That I have obtained a teacher is a rare occurrence indeed. In my youth, I inherited the Confucian tradition;

before long, however, due to my mother’s illness, I took up the study of medicine. I have practiced both of these disciplines for nearly twenty years, yet alas, my fortune has been ill-fated and my efforts unrequited.

For forty years he remained unlearned, like an ordinary man. He eventually abandoned his studies to devote himself to the profound mysteries (*xuan*), yet in the end no oral instructions were transmitted.
On the verge of developing a strange ailment, he sighed deeply and said, "Can I not simply become a man of leisure within this world?
He then constructed a small garden, planted flowers, and piled up stones, spending his days reciting poetry and resting therein.

In the interim, whenever I observed the flowers flourish and wither, suddenly becoming empty once more, I thereby realized the principles of fullness and emptiness, and the ebb and flow of all things;
such is the nature of physical phenomena. Am I alone not a phenomenon? On another day, I too shall surely be like this. Thereupon, I destroyed my garden and closed my door.
I practiced stillness to seek dhyāna and recited the various *Vajra* sūtras. In the year Wanyili (1605), I traveled by boat to Lin’an.
There, I encountered an old man who saw me engaged in Buddhist discourse and suddenly asked, "You study Buddhism; whom do you take as your teacher?
I replied, "Not yet. He then said, "I have heard that at Yunqi there is..."
"Master Lianchi’s reputation has been widespread here for many years; you ought to go and take him as your teacher.
Furthermore, you must read the letter by Liu Zongyuan to Li Muzhou concerning the practice of *qi* (breath cultivation). Having said this, he departed, and no one knew who he was.
I sighed and said, "As for that letter on the practice of *qi*, it is something I read in my youth; now it belongs to Master Kou."

This is recorded in the *Biography of Huo Guang*. His instructions to me were most earnest; how could I bear to fail him? Consequently, I traveled on foot to Yunqi, where I knocked at the gate to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master joyfully received me, instructed me in the practice of Pure Land, conferred upon me the five precepts, and gave me the name Guanghuan. I was filled with gentle warmth.
If they were long-time acquaintances, the Master would invite them to seek further instruction upon their departure, saying:
"The Buddhist scriptures fill the rafters; how can I teach your son? To summarize: seeing one's nature is the essence, while saving sentient beings is the function.
Mañjuśrī said that for practicing cultivation, nothing compares to reciting the Buddha’s name. This is the urgent task of our day."

"You must exert yourself in this. He reverently accepted the instruction and returned home. He set a daily task of reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times, having no leisure even for meals.
Before half a year had passed, his mind became tranquil; he felt as though he had attained something. He then thought that if he maintained this practice, seeing one's nature would not be difficult.
However, he wondered how he could save those still living in the world of birth and death. Suddenly, he recalled a passage from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* which says: "By means of..."
To bestow the seven treasures in alms is not equal to using even a four-line verse to bring liberation to others; the latter brings merit superior to the former.
Thus, it is clear that the gift of Dharma excels the gift of wealth. Yet, failing to examine myself, I proceeded to read the sutras and treatises on the Pure Land.
I have extracted the essential passages and categorized them by topic: first, "Determination of Rebirth" to establish one's destination;
next, "Arousing Faith" to redirect one’s orientation; then, "The Vow" to resolve one’s will; followed by "Fasting and Precepts" to perfect one’s virtue; "Daily Recitation" to develop one’s capacity;
and finally, "Combined Meditation" to reach the ultimate goal. These are divided into six fascicles and titled *Jìngtǔ zīlì* (Provisions for Pure Land).
Once the *Liang* had been published in woodblock form, he further revised and supplemented it, renaming it the *Quanji* (Complete Collection), and submitted it for correction to his Master.

The Master said, "Without this, there is no means to save sentient beings. He then re-examined and edited it once more, and consequently requested a word from [the Master] to serve as a preface for the beginning of the work.
The Master replied, "Yes, yes. He further conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him, after which [the man] returned home. On the way, he lowered his head in thought and sighed upward;
he was suddenly distraught, as if he had lost his very spirit and self-possession. The boatmen marveled at this. One guest among them asked me, "From where do you come? I replied, "From Yunqi.
Thereupon, I related the preceding circumstances in detail. The guest said, "Now that you have received the precepts, your recitation of the Buddha's name will not be in vain."
This is the Way of realizing one's nature. It is the true provision for the Path; it is the means by which the gift of Dharma is perfected and the beginning of saving sentient beings.
These two things are sufficient to bring one self-consolation. Yet, the Master seems to harbor a hidden anxiety. Why is this? I replied:

"When I look back on the past, I began as a Confucian while simultaneously practicing medicine; subsequently I turned to the Mysterious (Daoism), and later still to idleness. In none of these was there any [certainty]."

"And now, my temples are already white with age. He continued, "Had I set aside these few matters at that time and applied myself early to the study of the Buddha’s teachings, the achievements I might have attained today would likely be beyond measure.
Yet, instead of pursuing this, I pursued that; now that I am old and weary, I can only grieve in vain.
The guest laughed and said, "Sir, you are mistaken. There is no way to understand the principles of Buddhism without Confucianism."
Without medicine, one cannot reach the Buddha’s mind; without the profound (xuan), one cannot initiate the Buddha’s stillness; without seclusion, one cannot lay the foundation for the Buddha.
You, Master, seem to rely on these various means to study the Śākya teachings; yet you do not consider this fortunate, but instead regard it as a cause for sorrow.
Why is this? Nevertheless, that is not all. Had Confucianism been employed in the governance of the world, then rank and emolument—

If one is bound by worldly affairs and practices medicine extensively, then wealth and profit will drown one's resolve. If one obtains esoteric oral instructions, then one may become lost in deviant paths.
If one does not engage in introspection during leisure, then one will rot along with the grass and trees.
How could such a person ever obtain the provisions for rebirth in the Pure Land? The Master used these various points to awaken the Buddha-nature in him, yet in the end—
"These various factors constitute obstacles to Buddhahood. Is it perhaps that these are fixed by destiny and cannot be altered by the self;

that they depend on Heaven and do not involve human effort? You, Master, must surely possess the karmic conditions for transcendence, rather than having attained them through forced striving or mere luck.
I rose and thanked him, saying: "What you have said is indeed a sound argument. However, I know..."
One [point] I know; the second remains unknown to me. Throughout my entire life’s experience, it has been destiny and the decree of Heaven.

Now, who is the one whose merit it is that establishes destiny through teaching rather than surrendering to destiny, and who exhausts human potential to harmonize with Heaven rather than resigning to Heaven?
Alas! Is this not the complete assemblage of all necessary provisions? It is no other.
This was the inspiration of Master Padmasambhava. How could it have come about otherwise? Yet, when one investigates the reason for this, it is none other than destiny;
it is Heaven. Were it not so, how could our meeting in a guesthouse in the past have been so filled with earnest instruction, as if someone had been sent specifically to inform me?
It cannot have been without cause. From this, I came to understand that my attainment...

The Master was not my peer. My realization of nature and my vow to deliver sentient beings involve receiving [the Dharma], which is not like the various claims found in texts on the practice of *fuqi* (ingesting pneuma).
Long ago, Wang of Hefen said: "To have attained understanding from the Master is to receive the debt of infinite gratitude. Returning to...
Master Padmasambhava also said this. The guest looked startled and said, "I am but a vulgar man; I am not worthy to reach such heights.
You, sir, may truly be called one who knows the root. I beg you to set down these teachings so that I may record them."
On an auspicious day in the first month of spring in the year of Gengzi during the Great Ming Wanli era, the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple,
the eighty-year-old Fu Zhen Zhuang Guanghuan,
respectfully records this preface for the solicitation of funds to carve the *Complete Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land*.
The Buddha-way is a supramundane dharma; it is sublime indeed. Yet, among all the dharma-gates within the entire Tripitaka, none is as swift and direct as the path of Western Pure Land cultivation.
Thus, from the distant patriarchs of Mount Lu to the renowned masters of successive generations, the source has been vast and the stream deep.
This has persisted for a long time. Reaching the present age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), heterodox teachings run rampant. Some falsely claim to be the patriarchs of the Three Teachings;
some forge books of the Five Sections; some secretly transmit the Sutra of Sixteen Characters; some clandestinely pass down the Buddha of Seven Characters;
some practice internal circulation of qi and mental visualization, calling it "public cases" (*gong'an*); and some claim to hear sounds or see visions in the darkness of night.
They treat material objects as miraculous signs; some, having no genuine realization, falsely claim to teach the Chan school;
others deny cause and effect and slander the True Dharma. These myriad paths and diverse methods cannot be fully recounted—it is truly as Master Lianchi said.
Fearing that the Buddha-Dharma was on the verge of decline, the Master acted as a keystone for those caught in the middle stream.
He established the Pure Land school and founded the Xuyun Monastery; his reputation has resounded throughout this region for more than thirty years.
Yet, although the Master’s teachings have generally spread through major cities and great capitals, they have occasionally been obstructed in remote regions and secluded lands;
and while they have circulated within monastic groves and hermitages, they have sometimes been hindered among the common folk in villages and hamlets.

The Master surely felt an irrepressible compassion. Although I am unskilled, I have the misfortune of being numbered among his disciples; thus, I share in the responsibility for the rise and fall of this Way.
Though I well know that a mere drop cannot supplement the great rivers, I also believe that by borrowing their light, the various dark obscurities may be dispelled.
Therefore, casting aside my own meager learning, I have compiled these provisions, gathering the essential words of the various sutras and synthesizing them.
This definitive treatise by the various masters categorizes the teachings into distinct divisions and arranges them through comparative analysis and literary composition.

Having first rectified it for my teachers and subsequently clarified it for my fellow students, I revised this draft three times before the complete collection was finalized. It is truly a swift method for rebirth in the Pure Land and an essential compendium for transcending the world.
If it were kept hidden away in a chest rather than widely disseminated, it would certainly not serve the purpose of universally delivering all sentient beings.
I think that while one may focus solely on oneself without including others, this is not the mind that excels at being in harmony with others.
Therefore, we have once again undertaken the labor of carving the woodblocks and followed the precedent of soliciting contributions.

Whether the assistance is great or small, all alike plant the supreme cause for rebirth in the Pure Land; whether they are monastics or laypeople, they shall all surely realize the supreme fruit of rebirth therein.
It is because this single set of provisions is where all virtues converge. Above, it can cause the supramundane Buddha-dharma to flourish;
below, it can stem the rampant flow of heterodox teachings. In the long term, it can continue the orthodox transmission of Mount Lu;
in the short term, it can broaden the influence of the teachings of Yunqi. All of these originate from a single wholesome thought. Possessing this—
As for merit, why doubt rebirth? As the ancient saying goes, "Plant a single grain of millet in spring, and reap ten thousand ears in autumn"—how could these words deceive me?
Alas! All you faithful men and women of the four quarters should know that my words are not false;
I urge you to take this to heart.
On an auspicious day in the eighth month of autumn in the year of Jihai during the Great Ming Wanli era, Zhuang Guanghuan respectfully submits this memorial.
(Huan) has carefully examined the claim that Master Lian forged the Five Sections (*Wubu*). Some have doubted this, asserting that the texts of the Five Sections belong to the Luo Teaching.
The founder of the Luo Teaching was styled the Elder Wukong; since he was called "Awakened to the Void" (*Wukong*), it follows that he must have attained the *Vajra-prajñā*.
As for this principle, why do you consider it a fabrication? I say: Have you not heard alone the discourse of Sengzhao?
The discourse states: "The emptiness of nature refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The true mark means neither being nor non-being.
Neither being nor non-being does not mean the 'being' of those with views of existence or permanence, nor the 'non-being' of those with false views of annihilation."
...is non-existent. If one takes existence to be existent, then one takes non-existence to be non-existent. Since existence is not truly existent, then non-existence does not exist either.
One who does not rely on the concept of non-existence to contemplate phenomena may be said to understand the true mark (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.

Now, although the texts of the five schools do not possess the "existence" of those with views of existence or permanence, they nonetheless fail to avoid falling into the nihilistic view of annihilation.
To see [them] as non-existent is to be far removed from the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, whether they be false or correct. Is the meaning of *prajñā* truly like this?
Would it not be called a fabrication? Nowadays, many people take this book as their primary authority; it is likely because they have not yet clarified this point.

General Discourse on Maintaining the Precepts from the "Chapter on Observing the Precepts" in the *Shorter Commentary on the Illustrations* (*Duānzhāi túshuō*) **General Discourse on Maintaining the Precepts** The precepts are the foundation of the path; they are the gate to liberation. Without the precepts, there can be no cultivation of the Way. Therefore, the Buddha taught that one who upholds the precepts well will attain birth in the heavens, while one who violates the precepts will fall into the evil realms. Furthermore, the precepts are the root of all merit and virtue; they are the source of all noble qualities. Just as a tree cannot grow without roots, so too can one not attain the fruits of the Path without the precepts. There are three grades of precepts: the precepts for laypeople, the precepts for those who have left the household life, and the bodhisattva precepts. Although these differ in their specific rules, they all share the same purpose: to restrain the mind and body from transgression and to serve as the basis for cultivating wholesome dharmas. Regarding the maintenance of the precepts, one must first cultivate a sincere heart of reverence and shame. One should regard the precepts as a protective armor against the afflictions and as a vessel for carrying the Dharma across the ocean of suffering. One must not harbor even the slightest thought of violation, for a single breach can cause the entire edifice of virtue to collapse. In practicing the precepts, one should be mindful at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and maintain constant vigilance over one’s thoughts, words, and deeds. One should examine oneself frequently, as if looking for a hair in one’s own eye, to ensure that no subtle transgression remains hidden. Moreover, one should practice the four ways of attracting disciples (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to assist others in maintaining the precepts, and one should never disparage those who uphold them. By thus honoring the precepts, one honors the Buddhas of the three times. In summary, to maintain the precepts is to protect the mind from wandering and to ensure that one’s conduct is pure. This purity is the very essence of the Buddhist path. May all practitioners strive with diligence to uphold the precepts, thereby attaining peace in this life and the ultimate fruit of liberation hereafter.

That Dharma Master is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. Fifth, the *Ninth Sutra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* states:
During the time of the Buddha King of Emptiness (Śūnyatā-rāja), there were four bhikṣus whose afflictions [were heavy].

In the *Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Seal of Immeasurability of the Illusion-like Samādhi*, it is said: "During the time of the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita-Prabhāsa, there was a king named Jayendra who held [the Buddha] in deep reverence. [He] instructed his mind to contemplate the Buddha within emptiness, and thereby attained the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. That third bhikṣu is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. Six.

As stated in the *Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Seal of Immeasurability of the Illusion-like Samādhi*: "At the time of the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita-Prabhāsa, there was a king named Jayendra who revered [him]."
He made offerings to that Buddha and practiced the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That king of that country is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha.
Seventh, the *Ekavyūha-parivarta-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a crown prince who, upon hearing this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate, upheld it with diligent effort.
Furthermore, he taught and transformed eight thousand *koṭis* of people, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression. That...
The Prince was none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. The above is but a brief enumeration of several points;
if one were to consider his many kalpas and manifold causes, they would likewise be immeasurable.
The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara made these great vows.
Thereupon, abiding in true wisdom, he practiced with courageous diligence, cultivating immeasurable merits to adorn his land.
When his merits were perfected and his majestic spiritual power was blazing, he finally accomplished his aspirations and entered the rank of a Buddha."
Examination and Verification: The *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* states: "After Dharmākara had made these vows, he then applied himself with diligence to bring an end to birth and death.
Next, he entered the stages of a Bodhisattva. To 'bring an end to birth and death' means that one is at ease within the cycle of birth and death.
To 'enter the stages of a Bodhisattva' means to cultivate wisdom internally and cultivate merit externally. As for cultivating wisdom..."
One causes the nature of wisdom to expand day by day.
When the time comes to attain Buddhahood, the nature of wisdom will encompass the world of empty space, such that there is nothing unknown and nothing unseen.

As for those who cultivate merit, they take birth among all sentient beings, assuming their same physical forms and their same speech, in order to establish their transformation through teaching. Thus it is.

If one establishes the transformation of sentient beings, there is none who does not obtain merit. Because one obtains merit without personally enjoying it, that merit accumulates more and more and becomes ever greater.
When merit is great, majestic spiritual power is great; thus, with such majestic spiritual power, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Only then can one fulfill one's vows and enter the rank of a Buddha.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
"From here, to the west, passing through a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of buddha-fields, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is currently residing and preaching the Dharma."

The Commentary states: "Traveling ten thousand *li* across a hundred cities to seek out spiritual teachers, climbing mountains and crossing seas to pay homage at sacred sites—how can one remain indifferent and neglectful toward the Tathāgata of Ten Thousand Virtues who is currently preaching the Dharma?
To willingly fall away from this, as if at the eastern city gate, is truly to be pitied."

**Examination and Verification:** The *Chao* (Extracts) states: "Ten thousand li" refers to a monk who asked Dawsui, "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, I wonder whether this [reality] is destroyed or not?
He replied, "It is destroyed. The monk said, "If that is so, then it follows along with it. He replied, "It follows along with it.
The monk remained in doubt and could not resolve it; he traveled ten thousand li back and forth, visiting and studying under various masters (*jñānin*) before finally attaining realization.

"Great Enlightenment. Regarding "a hundred cities": this refers to Sudhana’s southern journey through one hundred and ten cities to visit fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), which is used here as a metaphor for Amitābha Buddha, who is the supreme spiritual friend.
Regarding "crossing mountains and sailing across oceans," such as to places like Mount Wǒméi and Pútuó: this is used as a metaphor for the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
This is the most supreme site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Yet, those who traveled on foot in the past did so to personally bask in the presence of the sages and worthies;
our hurried journeys today are merely for the sake of gazing from afar at their images.

Furthermore, having endured numerous hardships and not shunned toil, how can we now abandon the Compassionate Honored One who is present before us and fail to go? The old woman to the east of the city was with the Buddha.
To be born and yet not see a Buddha—does this not describe our own condition? Buddhas of the past and future are difficult to encounter by their very nature;
that we let the present pass in vain is truly to be pitied.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (The Lotus of Compassion) on the Grounds of Practice of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta states:
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha again addressed the eldest prince Animiṣa (who was formerly the crown prince of the universal monarch):
"I shall now bestow upon you the name Avalokiteśvara. After the parinirvāṇa of Amitāyus Buddha, you shall attain Buddhahood."
He shall attain Buddhahood and be known as the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain King.
He further told the second nun, Prince Ma, "Next you shall become a Buddha, named the Tathāgata Well-Abiding Merit Jewel King; by the power of your vows, you shall take hold of a pure land."
Furthermore, you are also titled Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

According to the *Kaozheng Niepan Zhenguo Ji* (Collection for Examining the Correctness of Errors in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra): "The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* is translated here as 'quiescent extinction' (*jimiè*).

As for 'quiescent extinction,' since both arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one. This refers to that which is without arising and without ceasing. [The text continues: "Without..."
There is no going and no coming; true permanence is revealed alone. Suffering and pleasure both vanish; thus it is said that "nirvana is bliss. The Sixth Patriarch said:

"The unsurpassed Great Nirvana is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating. It is the ultimate state of correct illumination—how can people of the world mistakenly identify it as death?
It is merely that when the conditions for transformation are exhausted, one manifests the same cessation as an ordinary person."
This is to cause them to know that all phenomena are impermanent, so that they do not give rise to greed or attachment.
The *Zhao lun* says: "The Way of Nirvana is silent, vast, and empty; it cannot be grasped through form or name. It is subtle, wondrous, and signless;
it cannot be known by a mind possessed of thought. It transcends all existence to ascend into the profound, and it measures the Great Void in its eternal duration. The Sūtra says:
The Treatise says: Nirvana is neither existent nor non-existent. It is cut off from the path of language and extinguished where mental activity reaches.
Consider the composition of the sutras and treatises—how could they be mere fabrications? Indeed, there is a reason why it is not existent;
therefore, it cannot be apprehended as existent. There is a reason why it is not non-existent; therefore, it cannot be apprehended as non-existent.

Why is this? If one traces them back to the realm of existence, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are eternally extinguished. If one pushes them forward to the direction of non-existence, the profound spirit is never exhausted.
Because the profound spirit is never exhausted, one embraces the One in profound stillness. Because the five aggregates are eternally extinguished, myriad entanglements are largely cast off.
Because myriad entanglements are largely cast off, one penetrates and merges with the Dao. Because one embraces the One in profound stillness, one is divine.
It is without merit. It is divine yet without merit; therefore, its supreme merit ever endures. It is in pervasive communion with the Dao;
therefore, it is profound yet undergoes no change. Being profound and unchanging, it cannot be said to exist. Its supreme merit ever enduring, it cannot be said not to exist.
This is the realm of the rarefied and the silent, the abode of the Great Mystery. How could one wish to discuss it in terms of existence and non-existence?
That divine way is indeed profound and remote. The *Mahā-amitābha Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "When that Buddha reaches the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara shall then become a Buddha.
Grasping the power of transformation, he will teach, transform, and deliver all the devas and people of the worlds of the ten directions."
Even down to the species of wriggling insects and crawling creatures, he causes them all to attain the Way of Nirvāṇa.

They transform and teach one another, delivering and liberating beings just as the Great Master Amitābha Buddha does, without end. He remains for incalculable kalpas before finally entering Parinirvāṇa.
Next, Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall become a Buddha; grasping the power of transformation, he will teach and deliver beings exactly as [Amitābha does].
Amitābha Buddha. Throughout the succession of kalpas, he never has a time of parinirvāṇa.
Examining the evidence in the *Nirvāṇa-zao-lun* (Treatise on the Origins of Nirvāṇa), it says: "Nirvāṇa" and "nieh-p'an"—these two names appeared at different times;
they are merely differences between the dialects of Chu and Hsia. To say "nieh-p'an" is the correct pronunciation. In the Sanskrit language, it is "nirvāṇa."
"Nirvāṇa" (Huán nièpán) means "the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) in the language of Qin; it is also called "extinction and transcendence" (*nirvāṇa*).

"The unconditioned" refers to its emptiness, stillness, and silence, which are wondrously transcendent of all conditioned phenomena. "Extinction and transcendence" signifies that the great afflictions are forever extinguished and one has surpassed the four currents [of existence].
As for why "Nirvāṇa" and "Niyuán" are sometimes written with the character "ban" (般), it is because they are the *Vajra* [Sūtra].
The Sūtra states: "I shall cause all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to extinction. Here, *pan* (般) means "to enter.
Furthermore, the *Śrī-samādhi-sūtra* says: "*Ānāpāna*. In the language of China, this means "exhalation and inhalation. Contemplate this.
Thus, the meaning of "entry" (*praveśa*) can also be understood.
In the *Dà āmítuó jīng* (Great Amitābha Sūtra), the commentary by Chángshì Fǎqǐ states briefly: "In the present assembly, there are two Dharma-princes."
In that buddha-field, his wisdom, spiritual power, and the radiance of his meritorious deeds are preeminent. When he enters [the assembly], he sits in attendance to engage in correct discourse;

when he emerges, he propagates the transformation [of beings] in other directions. Within that land, he does not lose the present [opportunity], and as the successor to the Buddha’s position, he arises in succession.
Upon reaching this state, the former name "Anle" (Peaceful Bliss) is transformed into "Zhongbao Shan" (Excellence of Many Jewels).
It is adorned with all splendors. Regarding its environment and dwelling place, it is situated in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita, within that realm;
however, these matters have not yet been mentioned in this book.
The Vows for Gathering Beings, Section Seven:
The Seven Vows for Gathering Beings (as found in the Forty-eight Vows of the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*).
**First Vow:** When I attain Buddhahood, there shall be no women in my land. [May all beings from the countless worlds of the heavens...]
From human beings down to the smallest crawling insects, all who are born into my land shall be born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures;
until this vow is fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
The twenty-third vow: When I become a Buddha, my name shall be heard throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions.
Each of the Buddhas, amidst their great assemblies, shall proclaim my merits as well as the excellence of my land, and so shall the devas and human beings.
Even those of the crawling and wriggling species who, upon hearing my name, feel compassion and joy—may they all be reborn in my land;
if this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
The twenty-fifth vow: When I become a Buddha, my radiance shall illumine countless worlds;
all places of darkness and gloom shall become brilliantly clear. From the devas and human beings down to the smallest insects that fly and crawl, all shall behold my light.
May there be none who do not cultivate goodness with a compassionate heart, and may all be reborn in my land. If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
The twenty-seventh vow: When I become a Buddha, may the gods and people of the countless worlds throughout the ten directions...
There may be those who resolve to attain Bodhicitta, uphold the fasts and precepts, practice the six *pāramitās*, and cultivate various merits;

with a sincere heart they make a vow, desiring to be born in my land. At the time of their death, I shall appear before them together with my great assembly and lead them to their next life, establishing them as non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
The twenty-eighth vow: When I become a Buddha, may the devas and humans of incalculable worlds,
upon hearing my name, burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang silk banners, provide food for śramaṇas, erect stupas and temples, observe the precepts with purity,
perform various good deeds, and single-mindedly fix their thoughts upon me— even if they do so for no more than a single day and night without interruption.
They shall also necessarily be born in my land. If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
The twenty-ninth vow: When I become a Buddha, may the gods and humans of the countless worlds in the ten directions...
If one believes and rejoices with a sincere heart, desiring to be born in my land, and recites my name ten times, they will certainly succeed in being reborn there.
This vow shall not be fulfilled—nor shall they ever become a Buddha—if they have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.

The thirtieth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all the devas and humans, as well as even the smallest crawling and flying insects, throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions, who have committed evil in previous lives, immediately repent and practice goodness upon hearing my name.
Upholding this sutra and its precepts, they vow to be born in my land. At the end of their lives, none shall pass through the three evil realms; they shall come directly to be reborn there.
Whatever they desire shall be fulfilled without fail. If they do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
The verse he subsequently spoke was summarized as follows:
"When I attain Buddhahood, my fame shall transcend the ten directions; humans and devas, rejoicing to hear it, shall all come to be born in my land.
With the light of my wisdom, I shall widely illumine infinite realms, eliminating the afflictions of greed and hatred from all sentient beings."
Those afflicted by delusion and darkness—those in the hells, among hungry ghosts, and as animals—shall likewise be born within my land.
(I) respectfully examine the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha; they are all intended for the salvation of sentient beings.
These seven vows alone are what serve to gather in and lead those who seek rebirth; therefore, they are specifically set forth here.

From Master Padmasambhava’s Commentary and Sub-commentary: "When sentient beings are submerged in the realms of suffering, the Buddha rescues them, like reaching down a hand from the depths of a deep abyss."
Sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses. The Buddha pities them, like one leaning against a gate and gazing for his child.

Though his efforts to pull them back are earnest and his thoughts of them are profound, they remain deeply submerged and do not rise; they flee far away and do not return. This is to leave the Buddha’s vow alone—how lamentable it is!
Regarding the "birth by transformation within a lotus," the Commentary on the Master [Padmasambhava] states:
"This lotus is the mystic palace for casting off the shell of ordinariness and the divine abode for the life-force of wisdom.
When those who cultivate the Pure Land prostrate to the Buddha, they should imagine themselves within a lotus performing the prostration, while the Buddha receives them within a lotus."
Homage and respect. When recollecting the Buddha, you should imagine yourself seated in the lotus posture within a lotus flower, while the Buddha, amidst the lotuses, extends his hand to guide you.

Only then should you single-mindedly hold the name. In the past, there were two monks who visualized the opening and closing of lotus flowers and thereby attained rebirth in the Pure Land; how much more so for one who adds to this the single-minded holding of the name!
Is there anyone who is not born?
The *Longshu Jingtu Wen* (Text on the Pure Land of Dragon Comfort) states: "The 'quivering and flying' refers to minute flying insects;
the 'crawling and moving' refers to minute maggots. If even such beings as these are still transformed and delivered by the Buddha, how much more so for human beings?"
If a person of former acquaintance takes refuge in a single thought, they will accordingly be reborn in that land; there is no room for doubt. Someone asked:
"How can the Buddha deliver such creatures as insects? The answer is: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a mud-clam in Lake Kālaka.
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, it immediately rose from the lake and hid beneath the roots of a grass plant to listen.
Hearing the Buddha’s Dharma, there was a cowherd who went before the Buddha and stuck his staff in the ground;
he accidentally killed a frog, which was immediately reborn in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Thereupon, it recounted the reason for its birth in heaven.
From this we can see that even a mud-frog could be reborn in a higher realm by relying on the power of the Buddha. Among the wriggling and crawling creatures, [only...]
Can one not rely on the power of the Buddha to attain rebirth there?
The *Dharmadhātu-krama-prathama-mukha* (The First Gate of the Sequential Order of the Dharma-realm of the Six Pāramitās) states: "This is a term from the Western Land [India].
Now, three translations are briefly presented: first, 'the culmination of the task'; second, 'reaching the other shore'; third, 'crossing over to the unconditioned.'"
Chapter One: The Dānapāramitā (Perfection of Giving). *Dāna* means "generosity" in the language of Qin.
When there is internal faith, external fields of merit, and material wealth—when these three factors converge—a mental state of relinquishment arises that is able to destroy stinginess and greed;
this is what constitutes the giving of *dāna*. There are two kinds: first, the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*); second, the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
2. Śīlapāramitā. *Śīla* means, in the language of Qin, "practicing the path of goodness with excellence. To be without self-indulgence is called *śīla*.
Whether one practices goodness by receiving the precepts or practices goodness without receiving the precepts, both are called *śīla*.
3. Kṣāntipāramitā. In the language of Qin, this means "patience" (*rěn'ǔ*). It is the ability of the inner mind to remain tranquil regarding external [afflictions].

It is called "patience" (*kṣānti*) because it endures offensive conditions. There are two types: first, patience toward sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*); second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Patience toward sentient beings has two aspects:
first, being able to endure without attachment when receiving respect and offerings, and not giving rise to arrogance or negligence;
second, being able to endure when subjected to anger, abuse, beating, or harm, and not giving rise to resentment, hatred, or malice. Patience regarding phenomena...
There are two kinds: first, those that are not mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), namely enduring cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, death, and so forth;
second, those that are mental phenomena, namely enduring anger, sorrow, grief, doubt, lust, pride, and various false views.
4. *Vīrya-pāramitā*. *Vīrya* means diligence (*jingjin*) in the language of Qin; it is the diligent practice of what is wholesome.
The Dharma: not being self-indulgent is called diligence (*vīrya*). It is of two kinds:

first, physical diligence, which is the diligent practice of wholesome dharmas—walking the path, performing prostrations, reciting, lecturing, exhorting, assisting, and transforming others; second, mental diligence.

Diligently practicing the path of goodness with a continuous succession of moments of mind. Furthermore, diligently cultivating the wholesome dharmas of giving and ethical discipline constitutes physical diligence;
diligently practicing patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom constitutes mental diligence. (5)
The Dhyāna-pāramitā. "Dhyāna" means "cultivation through contemplation" (siwei xiū) in the language of Qin.
All practices of gathering the mind, binding the mindfulness, and training in various samādhis are termed "cultivation through contemplation. There are three kinds:
first, mundane dhyāna, which is the dhyāna practiced by ordinary worldlings; second, supramundane dhyāna, also called the dhyāna common to the two vehicles; third...
This is the supramundane, most excellent dhyāna; it is also called the "unshared dhyāna" because it is not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
[6] Prajñāpāramitā: *Prajñā* is translated in the Qin language as "wisdom.
It illuminates all phenomena (*dharmas*) as being ultimately ungraspable, yet it is able to penetrate all things without obstruction; this is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is of three kinds: first, the wisdom of the *śrāvaka*; second, the wisdom of the *pratyekabuddha*;
and third, the wisdom of the Buddha. Because a bodhisattva practices the three kinds of giving with a sincere and pure mind, it is called *dāna*.
If one can possess five kinds of mental states within this *dāna*, then at that time, the act of giving is [truly] named *dānapāramitā*.
The Perfection [of Giving]. What are the five? First is knowing the true mark of giving.
At the time of giving, the three things—the giver, the recipient, and the gift—are all empty and unobtainable. One enters the correct contemplation of the true mark;
by means of the dharma of non-renunciation, one is able to give without stinginess whenever others have a need. This is called knowing.
First, the true nature of giving (*dāna-tattva-lakṣaṇa*). Second, the arousal of the mind of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-citta*).

Although a bodhisattva knows that the true nature is non-existent, they give rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion, desiring to bestow all happiness and extract all suffering upon others by means of this giving;
this is called the arousal of the mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Third, the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*). At the time of giving, one makes a vow, wishing that by means of this giving...
To attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, without seeking the fruits of retribution of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles—this is the making of a vow.
Fourth is dedication (*pariṇāmanā*): at whatever time one practices giving, to dedicate the merit of this giving toward *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) and toward all sentient beings—this is dedication.
Fifth is the perfection of skillful means (*upāya*), which refers to being able to...
The single dharma of giving revolves to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas and universally cultivates all practices;

this constitutes the perfection of skillful means. If a bodhisattva possesses these five kinds of mind at the time of giving, then speaking of the fruit within the cause, it is called the "consummation of the deed," it is called "reaching the other shore," and it is called "paramita" (the ultimate transcendence).

The true nature (*dharmatā*) known through each of the remaining five *pāramitās* may be inferred by analogy with these. The other four mental states are to be categorized as in the analysis provided for *dāna*.
Question: What are the names of the six perfections? Answer: *Dāna* (generosity) delivers those in the realm of hungry ghosts; *śīla* (ethical discipline) saves those in hell;

*kṣānti* (patience) rescues animals; *vīrya* (diligence) uproots the *asuras*; *dhyāna* (meditation) brings tranquility to humans; and *prajñā* (wisdom) illuminates the hosts of devas. Thus they are brought forth.
Yin said: "The *dāna* [perfection] belongs to the hungry ghosts because they are stingy and greedy, eating alone and refusing to practice giving.

The *śīla* [perfection] belongs to those in hell because they commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes and do not maintain the precepts. The *kṣānti* [perfection] belongs to animals because they devour one another according to strength and weakness and are unable to endure.
The *vīrya* [perfection] belongs to the asuras because they are arrogant and self-important, and do not cultivate diligence."
"Up to the point that humans practice by clinging to objects of perception, they lose their concentrated mind; the devas are deluded by sensual pleasures, and thus they lose their wisdom-mind.
For these reasons, the Bodhisattva separately classifies them into six perfections. Therefore, it is said: 'The Six Perfections.

*Jieshu Fayin* (The Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Question: Regarding the characteristics of fulfilling the Six Perfections, one practices what is difficult to practice. If the merit is such as this, why..."
What belongs to the Lesser Vehicle? It refers to what is called the "partial Bodhisattva. The answer is: this concerns the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as practiced and fulfilled gradually;

because they have limits, they are categorized as such. For instance, when Śibi cut his own flesh to feed the hawk, his giving reached the point where he offered his own body’s flesh and blood—this was the ultimate limit of giving.
Pūrmamati regarded death as returning home in order to preserve his integrity; he sacrificed his body but did not abandon the precepts.
His observance of the precepts reached the ultimate. The Rishi Kṣānti endured having his limbs severed, yet his mind remained unmoved; his forbearance reached the ultimate.
Prince Mahādāna, because he had lost a pearl, sought to drain the ocean until it was dry, yet his heart never faltered or grew weary; his diligence reached the ultimate.
Śāṇakavāsin entered meditative absorption while a magpie built its nest upon the crown of his head; only upon emerging from concentration did he become aware of it. His dhyāna [reached the ultimate].
This is the ultimate [of their achievement]. They diligently divided the cities, towns, mountains, and rivers of Jambudvīpa into seven parts so that the various kingdoms would cease their strife;
they reached this state through wisdom and skillful means. Such is the ultimate limit of their insight.
Nevertheless, it does not transcend the dharmas of cause and effect, arising and ceasing; therefore, it remains partial and belongs to the Lesser Vehicle.

If one were to say that the *Amitābha Sūtra* states that those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) can still be reborn [in the Pure Land], and that it excludes only these five crimes, then the merit of its salvation would be narrow indeed.
This is because one fails to recognize that following the phrase "excluding only the five heinous crimes," there are the four characters "slandering the True Dharma.

It is one who commits the five heinous crimes while simultaneously slandering the Dharma who is excluded. Even if one has committed all five heinous crimes, if they do not slander the Dharma, they are not excluded.
As for the Dharma, it is not necessarily that it does not arise. It is simply because one slanders it that one does not believe; because one does not believe, it does not arise.
This is what is meant by the saying: "If there is doubt, the flower will not open. The *Contemplation Sūtra* does not explicitly mention the slander of the Dharma;

however, if one also slanders [the sūtra], then [the lotus] likewise will not arise. Regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*): they are patricide, matricide, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

The shedding of the Buddha’s blood pertains entirely to the karma of the body. The schism of the *saṃgha* regarding the performance of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and the turning of the wheel of Dharma pertains to the karma of speech.
As for the inquiry concerning insects and crawling creatures: how can they perform repentance and aspire for rebirth?
Master Padmasambhava said: "The Buddha-nature resides within all sentient beings; it is inconceivable. It is not to be assumed that animal species are forever devoid of an awakened mind.

For instance, there was the frog who was reborn in heaven, the *garuḍa* who revered the Vinaya, the tiger who lowered its ears to avoid the earth, the python who shed tears and transformed its heart, the sea fish who, in a subsequent life, promoted the Dharma-gate, and the flying bird who..."
Having been reborn, they again became disciples. Of such a kind, how could one ever finish enumerating them?
Viewed from this perspective, how can one know that even the classes of wriggling and crawling creatures are incapable of repenting and aspiring for rebirth?
Chapter on All Sages Converging (found in the *Lian-shi wangsheng ji*).
Selection of Rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss:
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: At that time, Vaidehī wept aloud and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray..."
"Please explain to me in detail the place free from sorrow and affliction; I shall be reborn there. I take no pleasure in this turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted a light from between his eyebrows, which illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
The lands of all Buddhas appeared therein. When Vaidehī had seen this, she addressed the Buddha, saying: "Although these Buddha-lands are indeed pure, they are all..."
There is radiance. I now only wish to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.
(This is verified by the commentary on the "Sixteenth Meditation on Visualizing" in the fifth fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* [Wei-ti-hsi jing]).

The *Sutra on the Rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life of Innumerable Bodhisattvas* states: Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, "In this world, how many bodhisattvas will be reborn in Sukhāvatī?
The Buddha told Maitreya, "In this world, there are sixty-two billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas."
Bodhisattvas of minor practice who will be reborn in that land are beyond measure and calculation.

Not only from this land, but from the Buddha-fields of other directions as well—such as the Buddha-field of Dūraprabhāsa, where eight billion bodhisattvas shall all be reborn—and even throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, those who will be reborn are exceedingly numerous and incalculable.
If I were to describe them in detail, even an entire eon would not suffice to finish.
Master Padmasambhava’s Praise (the same applies hereafter) says: "If beings from this world and other realms are reborn in infinite numbers, how can the Pure Land contain them?
Alas! The vast ocean still receives the hundred rivers, and space still encompasses the myriad phenomena.
Yet, the ocean of boundless lands does not emerge from outside a single pore of Samantabhadra. Thus, even a needle-point-sized area of the Pure Land can contain the inexhaustible."
Is their rebirth there not truly vast and more than sufficient? Examination and Proof: The *Commentary* states:
"In the world-system of the Buddha Prathama-prabhā-dūra-avabhāsa (First Light Shining Afar), there are eight billion bodhisattvas who shall all attain rebirth there.
In the world-system of the Buddha Ratnagarbha (Treasure Store), there are nine billion."
At the abode of the third Buddha, Immeasurable Sound (Amitaghoṣa), there were twenty-two billion [beings].
Passing on in succession through fourteen buddha-fields, as well as immeasurable buddha-fields, those who attained rebirth there could no longer be calculated.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The chamber of Vimalakīrti accommodates eighty-four thousand lion thrones. Now, this purity...
Sentient beings from the ten directions who attain rebirth are as numerous as raindrops; they are all born within the ponds of the seven treasures, yet there is never any crowding or constraint.
This is precisely the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"to behold Amitābha face-to-face."
In the *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra*, the Buddha prophesied that Mañjuśrī would be born in Sukhāvatī. Mañjuśrī’s verse of aspiration says:
"When my life comes to an end, May all obstacles be extinguished; May I behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face And be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Having been born in that Buddha-land, May my great vows be fulfilled; May the Tathāgata Amitābha Appear before me and grant me his prophecy."

The Ten Vows for Rebirth from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describe how Samantabhadra Bodhisattva made ten kinds of great vows, universally seeking rebirth in the Pure Land for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.
A verse therein says: "May I, when my life is about to end, completely eliminate all obstacles and behold [the Buddha] face-to-face."
That Buddha is Amitābha; one shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. It is further said: "The assembly of that Buddha is entirely pure;
at that time, I was born from a supreme lotus flower. I personally beheld the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light, who bestowed upon me the prophecy of Bodhi before my very eyes."
The commentary states: Mañjuśrī is the patriarch of the seven Buddhas, and Samantabhadra is the sovereign of the myriad practices;

yet, regarding rebirth in the Pure Land, they speak with one voice in their earnest exhortations. The worthy ministers of this Sahā world are themselves the close retainers of Sukhāvatī—how profoundly clear this is!
To refuse to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Lands outside this world is a grave error.
Examining the *Saptabuddha Dharmaratna Sūtra* and the *Platform Sūtra*, it is stated:

During the past *Kṛta-yuga* (Adorned Kalpa), there were the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū; in the present *Bhadrakalpa* (Worthy Kalpa), there are Krakucchanda and Kanakamuni... [and so forth].
Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha—these are the seven Buddhas.
The "Ten Vows" refers to the ten vows from the *Pratimokṣa-saṃvara-vinaya* (or the *Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta*).
The verses discuss the Pure Land.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was a native of India who extensively composed various treatises. He ascended to the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven to pay homage and visit Maitreya.
Furthermore, he authored the *Treatise on Amitāyus*, the *Verses on the Pure Land*, and the *Five-Gate Method of Practice*, universally exhorting others to be reborn there.
Requesting an Image of the Buddha (from the *Gantong zhuan*):
A Bodhisattva with the five supernatural powers from the Kukkutapāda Monastery in India used his spiritual power to travel to the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

There he beheld Amitābha Buddha and presented this request: "The sentient beings of the Sahā world aspire to be reborn in the Pure Land, yet they lack an image of the Buddha’s form. I pray that you will deign to grant one."

The Buddha granted his permission, saying, "You should go first; he will soon appear before you. Having returned with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the sacred image had already arrived.
One Buddha and fifty bodhisattvas were each seated upon lotus flowers atop the leaves of trees. He then took the leaves and transcribed them for circulation.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, the twelfth patriarch of India, composed the *Awakening of Faith*. Later,
he clarified that seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the most essential practice.
Verification: The twenty-eight patriarchs of Western India, from the first patriarch Mahākāśyapa down to the twenty-eighth patriarch Bodhidharma.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*,
as prophesied by Nāgārjuna, states: "O Mahāmati, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there will be in a future age one who upholds my Dharma—
a bhikṣu of great name and virtue known by the title Nāgārjuna— who will be able to destroy the tenets of existence and non-existence."
In the interim, he manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma, attained the first stage of joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), and was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss;
this is an examination and verification of the fifth of the ten epithets of the Sugata Tathāgata.
The Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*) is the first of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃgraha-parivarta* (or *Mahākaruṇā-saṃyukta-sūtra*) states: The Buddha said, "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu in the country of Northern India named Gopa."
Kāśyapa, having cultivated immeasurable and various most excellent roots of merit for enlightenment, he will pass away and be reborn in the Western Quarter,
in the Land of Immeasurable Life beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds. There, in the presence of that Buddha,
he will plant all manner of roots of merit and shall later become a Buddha named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light).

The *Bodhisattva Cih Dizhi Jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Holding the Ground) states: The Buddha said, "At that time, Makhadeva attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Five hundred laymen and twenty-five laywomen all attained the stage of non-retrogression. At the end of their lives, they were all reborn together in the Immeasurable [Life]."
The Pure Land of the Buddha of Longevity.

The commentary states: To seek rebirth in the Western Land is to desire the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and to ascend to the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
Having already attained such patience and already attained non-retrogression, to further seek rebirth therein—such is the joy of a Bodhisattva in drawing near to the Tathāgata.

Now, ordinary beings who are still bound by all fetters lack the full power of patience and face infinite conditions for regression; yet they do not resolutely direct their minds toward the Pure Land.
What can be said of such people? They are truly to be pitied.

An examination and verification of the five types of patience (*kṣānti*) in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing): 1. Patience of Subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*): This corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

2. Patience of Faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*): This corresponds to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). 3. Patience of Accordance (*anuloma-kṣānti*): This corresponds to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). 4. Patience of Non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*): This corresponds to the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*). 5.
Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*): This corresponds to wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Wang Longshu said: "Those who are reborn in the Pure Land..."

One will certainly realize the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is the thorough understanding of birth and death.
To thoroughly understand birth and death means that even while entering the realm of birth and death, this single nature (*eka-svabhāva*) remains unobscured.
Since this single nature is not obscured, by what means could one commit evil? In principle, there is certainly no possibility of falling away; how much more so when one relies upon the Buddha.
By the power [of this vow], falling into [the lower realms] shall certainly never occur. Therefore, those born in the Pure Land do not merely achieve longevity and freedom from aging;
they also attain mastery over birth and death.
This is the second great vow.
The *Bodhisattva-nei-jie jing* (Sutra on the Inner Precepts of Bodhisattvas) states: "A bodhisattva has three vows. The second vow is:
'May I, at the end of my life, be reborn before Amitābha Buddha.'"

Regarding the extinction of sins through the recitation of the Buddha's name, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There were certain bodhisattvas who claimed they had slandered the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and consequently fell into the evil realms.

For immeasurable kalpas, although they cultivated other practices, they were unable to extinguish their sins. Later, they encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instructed them to recite the name of Amitābha."
Only by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha can one eliminate obstacles and transcend rebirth into the Pure Land.
The commentary states: "To recite the name of the Buddha with a sincere mind even once extinguishes the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas;
this is a clear proof. Why is this so? It is because of the sincerity of the mind. If it is not a sincere mind, the sins will not be extinguished. Do not say..."
How unfounded are these sacred instructions! The record of the Lotus Assembly names Chan Master Ze of Changlu as its founder.
Following the legacy of his distant ancestors, he established the Lotus Assembly to universally exhort others to practice nianfo.
One night, he dreamed of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, whose appearance was refined and elegant. The man bowed and said, "I wish to enter your Lotus Assembly of Excellence;
I beg you to write down my name. Zhe asked what his name was, and he replied, "Puhui.

After Zhe had written it, the man said again, "My elder brother Puxian also begs that you write his name as well. Upon waking, Zhe consulted the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
There were two bodhisattvas by name; they were subsequently appointed as the leaders of the assembly.
The eulogy states: "Whenever monks form a religious society, the names of the ancient sages are inscribed therein. How profound it is that the Pure Land is no small matter!"
It is truly because when an affair arises from sincerity, it communicates with the unseen and elicits spiritual response;

yet if there is even a trace of falsehood, those among the world who value goodness will not deign to regard it, let alone the ancient sages. As for what is nowadays called a "Buddhist assembly," Master Ze has seen it.
One must sigh deeply at this.

To cite briefly some venerable masters (this section combines the "Chapter on Cultivating Practice for the Western Pure Land" from *Xingyunqi* with other materials, and thus contains more entries than the *Wangsheng ji*):
Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu profoundly realized the deep purport of Prajñā and was hailed as a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma in the East. And...
Reciting the Buddha’s name during the six periods of the day, beholding sacred images three times, and being reborn in the Pure Land—
these were the practices of the Tiantai Master Zhizhe, the patriarchal ancestor of ten thousand generations who attained wondrous realization of the Lotus Sūtra’s teachings and contemplations;
yet even he was born facing west, resolving ten kinds of doubts and annotating the *Sixteen Contemplations* to discourse extensively on the Pure Land.
Chan Master Baizhang Hai was the direct heir to the transmission of the Way from Mazu and the great patriarch of the monastic communities for ten thousand generations.
His established regulations stipulated that when praying for ill monks or performing the funeral rites for deceased monks, all were to be sent to the Pure Land.
National Teacher Qingliang succeeded to the ancestral seat of the Avataṃsaka school and was hailed as an emanation of Mañjuśrī;
he pointed out that Amitābha is none other than Vairocana, and he also commented upon the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, widely propagating the Pure Land teachings.
Chan Master Huanglong Xin studied under Old Master Jue and attained his realization. He succeeded him on the seat of Huanglong, where his school’s influence flourished greatly.

Yet he was deeply devoted to the practice of pure karma; a "Text for Encouraging Nianfo" (Buddha-recitation) composed by him circulated in the world, moving people to lament their own lot and inspire faith.
Chan Master Yongming Shou possessed unimpeded eloquence and served as a pillar for the Zen school.

He composed the "Fourfold Discrimination" (Sì Lì Jiǎn), which specifically extols rebirth in the Western Paradise in the highest grade of the highest class, extending his reverence even to the realm of the underworld.
Chan Master Zhenxie Le succeeded Master Danxia Chun. This lineage of the Dongshan school reached its greatest manifestation through this master.
