while the flames burn sentient beings, one cannot help but avoid this and hasten toward that. To deliver sentient beings through skillful means, the Dharma naturally requires this.
Once born in that land, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and only then realizes that this mind is originally equal.
The *Jingtu zhigui* (Guide to the Pure Land) states: "To rejoice in the pure and loathe the defiled is to not yet have forgotten grasping and rejecting.
How could it be that the Sages transform people through a path of dualistic views? It replies: Does the Scripture not say:

"Though one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land to teach and transform all classes of beings"? This is indeed a fervent state of rejoicing in the pure and loathing the defiled.
Yet, one does not perceive any signs of longing or aversion; this is what constitutes attainment.

In the *Sūtra of the Great Amitābha*, in the section on the City of Doubt and Womb-Birth, the Buddha addressed Maitreya:
"Do you see that land as having womb-birth? He replied: "I see those who have womb-birth. [The Buddha asked:
"For what causes and conditions does womb-birth exist in that land? The Buddha said: "If there are sentient beings who cultivate various merits and vow to be born [there]..."
Regarding that buddha-field, they later feel regret and are further filled with doubt;

they do not believe in the existence of that buddha-field, nor do they believe in those who are reborn there, nor do they believe in giving alms or performing good deeds to obtain merit in future lives.

Although such a person is thus, they continue to maintain a mindful heart, occasionally believing and occasionally disbelieving, their will wavering and having no fixed reliance. At the time of their death, the Buddha then—
He manifested his body so that they might see him with their own eyes; though they were unable to speak, their hearts were immediately filled with joy and they felt remorse.

Thus, they could not help but perform various good deeds to repent for their transgressions, whereby their faults became few. They were also reborn in that land, yet they were unable to proceed directly to the presence of the Buddha.
Instead, upon entering the peripheral region of that land, they saw a city made of the seven treasures and entered it, arriving at a lotus flower.
He was born there, and his body grew naturally large; food and drink were likewise provided spontaneously. His happiness was like that of the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
However, within that city, for five hundred years he was unable to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or behold the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
Having no means to make offerings to the Buddha or to cultivate the merits of a Bodhisattva, because of this—
It is suffering. To demonstrate this, a minor reprimand is shown; therefore, that land is called "womb-birth. One should know that those who give rise to doubt and suspicion lose great benefit.
If there are sentient beings who believe and accept the teachings of the sutras, observe the precepts of fasting and purity, and perform various meritorious deeds, [they shall not suffer thus].
With a sincere heart, they dedicate their merit. At the end of their lives, they are immediately reborn sitting cross-legged within lotus flowers in a pond of the seven treasures.
In a mere moment, their physical forms, radiance, wisdom, and majestic spiritual power become equal to those of the various bodhisattvas. How could they be called "womb-born"?
When great bodhisattvas from other directions resolve to see Amitābha Buddha and the various bodhisattvas...

Having heard [the Dharma], they pay respectful homage and offerings; at the end of their lives, they go to the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and are born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures.
There, they spontaneously and immediately behold the Buddha. How could this be called "womb-birth" (*jarāyu-ja*)?

(Reply: I have carefully examined those who practice the Pure Land path. Although from ancient times there have been those who momentarily believed and momentarily doubted, such instances seem to be even more prevalent in this age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*).

how could he have done nothing at all, yet directly engaged in such talk that slanders the sutras and opposes the Sage, thereby giving rise to doubts for ten thousand generations?

Regarding this eulogy, it is said that its profound reserves are not slight; indeed, there are those who perceive its depths alone.
Why do people today fail to follow its underlying intent and instead merely cling to its literal words, thereby concluding that it disparages the Pure Land? Could this truly be so?
Nevertheless, as for the Sixth Patriarch and the three masters—whether they are to be trusted or doubted—I shall set them aside for now and discuss only Yong...
An Essay Clarifying the Pure Land: Following the example of former sages, I respectfully receive the Buddha’s command to establish words that are certainly free from error.
How profound these words are! They suffice as a definitive treatise; there is nothing further to be doubted.
Should you still not find full resolution, I shall face the West with palms joined and say: "The establishment of the City of Doubt was precisely for such a person as this."
The *Kaozheng taisheng lian chi shu* (Commentary on the Verification of Womb-Born Lotus Pools) states: Question: Apart from the lower grade [of rebirth], there is also mention of womb-birth.
Does this actually exist? Answer: It is used to symbolize that the power of one's faith is not firm; in reality, there is no womb-birth.
For example, when a son of the Kṣatriya caste commits a crime, he is secluded within the inner palace and provided with magnificent pavilions and rare, exquisite treasures for his amusement.
Their clothing and provisions are abundant, yet their two feet are bound so that they cannot move freely; this is the analogy for birth from a womb.
If one deeply repents and reproaches oneself, seeking to leave that original place, one will immediately be able to go to the abode of Amitāyus Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva Garbha-vāsa Sūtra* states: "To the west of here, at a distance, lies the realm of *Kṣānti-māndya* (Laxity).
Its land is composed of the seven treasures, and its bliss is incomparable. Yet, though one resolves to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, one remains stained by attachment to this world."
They are unable to advance. This is also similar to being suspicious of the outskirts of a city. All such cases arise because their faith is not earnest.
The sutras and śāstras are clear on this point; as the commentary states: "Among the sutras that exclusively discuss the Pure Land, such as the *Amitābha-vyūha-sūtra*..."

These include the *Sūtra on the Buddha of Longevity*, the *Sūtra of King Drum-Sound*, the *Sūtra of the Verses on Amitābha Spoken Later*, and the various *Amitābha Sūtras* in both their large and small versions.
Furthermore, there are other sūtras that, while not exclusively discussing the Pure Land, nevertheless exhort and praise rebirth therein;
such as the "Chapter on the Vows of Practice" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which leads one back to Sukhāvatī by means of these ten vows. This is it.
As it says in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Those who recite this sūtra shall be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. This is an example.

Furthermore, in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana-sūtra*, and other such scriptures, the Pure Land is mentioned alongside [the path] in multiple layers and not just once.

This is another example. As for the remaining works that praise and extol the Pure Land, they are treatises (*śāstra*), such as the *Ten Doubts* (*Daśasaṃdeha*) and the *Jewel King* (*Ratnarāja*). These are...

As for prose compositions, such as those by Wulongshu and Wujin, they are compiled as anthologies; works such as *Jueyi zhigui* (Resolving Doubts and Pointing to the Goal) are recorded as collections;

works such as *Jingtu zixin* (Self-Confidence in the Pure Land) are transmitted as biographies; works such as *Jingtu lüe zhuan* (Brief Biographies of the Pure Land) are rendered in verse; works such as *Jinglu xingxiu* (The Direct Path of Practice) are composed as rhapsodies;
works such as *Shenqi anyang* (The Spirit Dwells in Peaceful Nurturing) are written as poems; and there are those like the various families’ expressions of longing for the Pure Land.
The words concerning the lands and so forth are too numerous to record in full. Judging from this, how could one not believe in the Pure Land?
The *Record of the Sixth Patriarch* states:
"The *Platform Sutra* says: 'If people in the East commit evil deeds, they should recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the West.'"
Furthermore, people of the West commit evil deeds; yet they recite the Buddha’s name and pray to be reborn in some land. It is also said that fools wish for the east or the west.
Later generations clung to this [misconception] and consequently doubted that the Sixth Patriarch taught there is no Western Land. Therefore, I have composed these Four Clarifications.
The first point concerns the diversity of gateways. Since the Jin and Song dynasties, practitioners have vied with one another to exalt the practice of *dhyāna* and contemplation;

consequently, the meaning of the direct pointing and single transmission was nearly obscured. At that time, Bodhidharma first proclaimed it, and the various patriarchs subsequently arose, desiring solely to bring this Way into great clarity.
This Way is without Buddha and without sentient beings. Now, in the West...
This [present path] correctly instructs sentient beings on how to proceed toward Buddhahood; yet in this path, the moment the mind is raised it errs, and the moment a thought stirs it deviates.
Now, the Western Path (Pure Land) correctly teaches people to give rise to the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha;
in this path, both mind and object are tranquil. Now, the Western Path takes the Buddha-land as its object, causing one to resolve to seek rebirth there. This is why...
Although the principle is without dual aspects, the pedagogical methods (mencement) employed differ; according to the time and the capacity of the individual, such is the natural way of the Dharma.
Had the Sixth Patriarch merely propagated the "Direct Pointing" while simultaneously praising the Western Paradise, the intent of that Direct Pointing would never have been made clear.
Thus, were the Sixth Patriarch and the various masters of the Pure Land tradition to exchange places, the result for each would have been the same.

The second point is: "It appears to be a denunciation, but it is actually a praise. Regarding the so-called theory of the Sixth Patriarch traveling east and west, this was merely an exhortation that people must practice goodness with a sincere heart;
empty vows are of no benefit. How could he have ever said there is no Western Pure Land?
In the authentic scriptures, it is consistently stated that one attains rebirth in that land by means of many roots of goodness. How, then, could this be called a denunciation? The third point is:
This was not intended for beginners; as the Sixth Patriarch himself said, "My [teachings on] precepts, concentration, and wisdom are for those of the highest vehicle.
Now, those of initial resolve and lowly station look down upon the West with the worldly wisdom of a mere autumn hair, recklessly claiming to expound Prajñāpāramitā.

"It is not merely that it is of no benefit, but rather that it harms them. Therefore, regarding the *Dànyán Jīng* (Platform Sūtra), one must be careful never to show it to those at the beginning stage of practice.
If it is cast upon those who are not suitable vessels, they will immediately fall into the ranks of mad demons; this is truly to be lamented. Fourth: "There are errors in the recorded text."
The *Platform Sūtra* further states that the Western Land is one hundred and eight thousand li from here;
this is an error that takes the Five Indias to be Sukhāvatī. Both the Five Indias and China are equally part of this defiled Sahā world;
why then should one distinguish between vowing for the East and vowing for the West? Sukhāvatī is, in fact, ten trillion lands away from this Sahā world.

The *Platform Sūtra* was recorded by various students; how can we guarantee it is free from error? This is what the ancients meant when they said, "To trust a book entirely is not as good as having no book at all.
Moreover, this work is that which has been praised by the thousand Buddhas of the West;

yet now you doubt the words of those thousand Buddhas while placing your faith in the speech of a single patriarch. If even the Buddha is not to be trusted, how much less so the patriarch? Thus, [your] wisdom...
One who shall resolve the doubts of worldly people and inspire faith in them, widely praising and circulating [this teaching], thereby repays the profound kindness of the Buddha.
Were one to contravene the sacred words, it would be the teaching of Māra; how could the gravity of such a transgression even be described?
The *Huangbo Xinyao* (Essentials of the Heart of Huangbo) by Chan Master Huangbo Duanjie states: "All that the Tathāgata has spoken is for the purpose of transforming people;
it is like using yellow leaves as gold to stop a small child's crying—it is certainly not real. It further says:
If all the Buddha-activities of the Pure Land were merely the completion of karmic deeds, they would be called "Buddha-obstructions," for they would obstruct your mind.
This is because the direct pointing transmitted by the Master shares the same approach as the Sixth Patriarch; it is precisely what Master Huiyuan meant by "the gates being different.
This is identical in meaning to the aforementioned *Platform Sūtra*. How, then, can there be any cause for doubt?
Master Tianyi Huai said to his disciples: "To be born is indeed to be born; to depart is truly not to depart.
Do you not contemplate the various Pure Lands? Or have you perhaps asked about the verse in praise of the Buddha? The mind encompasses the vast void."
Its measure encompasses the entire realm of sand-grains. This is because the empty space of the ten directions is immeasurable and boundless, yet it is entirely encompassed by the measure of my mind.
When one observes that ten trillion lands exist within my mind, the mind itself has no boundaries.
Where does it go? Its appearance is such that it seems to be easily defiled yet pure, as if it were going somewhere;
how could one say it goes from here to there, like the worldly passage through cities and villages described in the sutras? Therefore it is said: "To go is, in reality, not to go."
When Master Yang Cigong was about to pass away, he composed a verse which said: "Taking error for error, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This was because [he taught] that the Pure Land is but one's own mind and Amitābha is one's own self-nature.

He did so fearing that those who practice the path of purity might know only that there is a Pure Land and Amitābha in the West, while remaining unaware of the Pure Land within their own minds and the Amitābha of their own self-nature.
"A-mi. Thus he spoke this to warn him; it was not meant to suggest that his cultivation of the Pure Land was erroneous.

Therefore, when Master Lien (Nianfo) said to Mr. Ci that he had attained realization through Chan meditation and yet returned to the Pure Land, there was no small amount of profound significance in his words "taking what is mistaken as correct."
*The Treatise on the Ultimate Goal of the Pure Land:

Ten Kinds of Faith* If one wishes to understand birth and death and cultivate pure karma, one must give rise to ten kinds of faith, maintaining them in mind without forgetfulness, so as to be certain of rebirth in the Pure Land.
First, one must have faith that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is the sincere word of his golden mouth—true and not false. Second, one must have faith...
Ordinary beings remain in delusion; their consciousnesses do not cease, and they circulate through the six realms of existence without rest.

Those who possess the three kinds of faith practice in this land, yet as long as they have not attained the fruits of the Way, they cannot escape saṃsāra. Those who possess the fourth kind of faith have not yet emerged from saṃsāra; even if they are born in the heavens, they remain within it.
One cannot avoid falling [into lower realms]. Fifth, those who believe that beings born in the world of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) never again undergo retrogression.

Sixth, those who believe that sentient beings who make a vow to be born in the Pure Land will certainly attain rebirth there. Seventh, those who believe that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name [is sufficient for rebirth].
It can extinguish the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty-one kalpas.
Ninth, those who believe and recite the Buddha’s name are gathered in and never forsaken by the supernatural radiance of Amitābha Buddha.

Tenth, those who believe and recite the Buddha’s name are constantly protected and mindful of by the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, through their shared spiritual power. Once this faith is born, one attains longevity in the Pure Land.
One's lifespan is immeasurable; in a single lifetime, one shall attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Regarding these ten points, those who cannot have deep faith and instead give rise to doubt and uncertainty will not attain rebirth there, even though they practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The *Kǎozhèng jué shēng jìngtǔ guīyuán zhízhǐ* states: "In the past, there was Mingchen, who could paint snakes;
he depicted the 'posture of the Changshan snake' and composed a 'Treatise on the Snake,' whereupon his living body transformed into a snake. Li Bashi painted horses;
he depicted the 'posture of the rolling horse,' and the form of the horse appeared vividly. By examining these two instances, the principle is clearly demonstrated."
If one practices the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will surely attain Buddhahood; if one single-mindedly believes in the Pure Land, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
Longshu’s *Essay on Arousing Faith in the Pure Land* states:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings sinking in the sea of suffering with no means of escape, have themselves [taken action]..."
Through the power of their vows, they invite and lead people to be born in the Pure Land; it is only that people fear not believing them.
If one has faith and is willing to go, then even if one possesses evil karma, there is no reason one cannot be reborn there. For if one lacks great compassion, one is insufficient to be a Buddha;
if one does not deliver sentient beings, one is insufficient to be a Buddha; and if one does not possess great majestic power, one is insufficient to be a Buddha. It is for this reason that...
Because of his compassion, he beholds sentient beings sinking in the ocean of suffering and desires to deliver them.
Because he possesses great majestic power, he is able to fulfill his resolve to deliver them and achieve the merit of their salvation; this is why he is called a Buddha.
The Sūtra says: "The Great King of Physicians can cure all diseases, yet he cannot cure one whose life has reached its end.
The Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith. Faith is but a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).
If a person is alive, when the mind intends to go, the body follows; when the mind intends to stay, the body follows.
While dwelling here, one constantly maintains mindfulness of this body; yet, even as there is still the thought of wishing to depart, the body remains bound and constrained.
At the moment the body perishes, there is only a single thought. Wherever that single thought reaches, there is nowhere it does not arrive.

Therefore, if a single thought arises directed toward the Pure Land, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land. How much more so when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves invite and lead people to be reborn there!
Regarding those who do not believe, the *Zongjing lu* states: "Those who do not believe cannot be saved even by a thousand Buddhas.
As it is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, faith is like a hand; just as a person with hands can reach [whatever they need], so too is it with faith.
It is a treasury of jewels; one may take them as one pleases. Yet, if one has no hands, one will obtain nothing at all.
Likewise, those who enter the path of the Buddha possess the hand of faith, by which they may take the jewels of the Dharma as they please; but if they lack faith, they shall have nothing.
Emptiness is non-attainment.
The *Xizicao* (Draft on Requisites for the Western Land) states:

"To attain birth in the Pure Land is to rely upon the power of others—the embrace of Amitābha’s vows, the encouragement and praise of Śākyamuni, and the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. It is like that great ocean; once one has obtained a [great] ship..."
The boat is there, and there is still a skilled guide; moreover, with favorable winds, one will surely reach the other shore swiftly.
If, however, one lacks faith and refuses to board the boat, lingering instead in this wretched land—who is to blame?
Furthermore, when people suddenly hear descriptions of the Pure Land’s scenery, many do not believe them; this is not to be wondered at.
For they are constrained by what they perceive before their eyes, and thus conclude that even what is not seen before their eyes must be exactly like this. Therefore, regarding...
In this turbid world of Sahā, people do not believe that there exists a pure buddha-field;
thus they are born from a womb, unaware that there is the transformation-birth within lotuses.
Their lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, unaware that there is a lifespan as vast as the sands of the Ganges. They must rely on labor for food and clothing, unaware that there is spontaneity.
Regarding food and clothing, pleasure is always intermingled with sorrow and affliction; one does not realize that there exists a singular, pure happiness.
Thus, one should not disbelieve the words of the Buddha simply because they are not perceived by the senses at present.

Moreover, since the Buddha strictly admonishes people against false speech, he would certainly not himself speak falsely to deceive others. Those among the world who speak falsely are not [the Buddha].
One seeks profit to avoid harm. The Buddha has no desires for the world; how could he seek profit?
The Buddha regards birth and death as a sword cutting through empty space; how could he avoid harm? Thus, there is no occasion for the Buddha to employ false speech.
Even those among the worldly who are superior to the average person would refuse to speak falsely so as to ruin their conduct.
How much more so for the Buddha! Thus, the former sages said: "If the words of the Buddha are not believed, what words can be believed?

In the past, there was one who branded a loyal minister as a member of a treacherous faction and engraved this upon stone; yet a heavenly thunderbolt struck it down. Now, [the Buddha's image] is adorned with gold, jewels, and vibrant colors.

It was carved, bound, and illustrated to form a *dharmacakra* (wheel treasury), wherein the words of the Buddha were enshrined; it was offered with incense and flowers and adorned with divine dragons.

Had its words been false, they would have been even more egregious than the inscriptions of traitorous factions—why, then, has heaven’s thunder not struck it down throughout the passing of thousands and hundreds of years? It is because its words are sincere. This is the teaching of the Pure Land.
There is nothing further to doubt. Moreover, from antiquity to the present day, those who have practiced this have experienced many instances of spiritual response;
it is therefore utterly impossible not to believe in it.
Regarding the examination of the stone stele struck by lightning during the reign of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty: at that time, Cai Jing [purged] the Yuanyou Party...
More than twenty people, including Ren Sima Guang and others, were carved onto a stone stele for being wicked and depraved and were imprisoned;
it was erected at the End Gate (Duamen), whereupon a thunderbolt from heaven struck it down.
Furthermore, within this world, human life is entirely like a bubble; its arising and ceasing are not constant. It has been rare since antiquity for anyone to reach the age of seventy.
People see only the elderly before their eyes, yet they fail to reflect upon those who have already departed without waiting [for old age].
It is many. Furthermore, there is nothing in this world that is not suffering; it is only because one does not reflect upon it that one fails to perceive it.

When things do not accord with one's wishes, they are certainly suffering. Even when they do accord with one's wishes, such a time lasts but briefly; or else, it may be the end of one’s own allotted span of life.
It arrives suddenly. The evils committed throughout one’s life do not stop at eating meat or wearing silk;

yet, if one does not reflect upon them, it remains so, but once reflected upon, they are truly terrifying. From youth to old age, from birth until death, these accumulations have become so vast that they entangle and solidify the soul, leaving no way for liberation.
After closing one's eyes, one cannot avoid following the conditions of one’s karma into the profound and dark realms of the afterlife.
In darkness, one knows not where one will be: perhaps falling into hell to undergo various extreme sufferings; perhaps becoming an animal, slaughtered for human consumption;
perhaps born as a hungry ghost, with the fires of hunger burning the body; or entering the realm of the asuras, oppressed by anger and resentment.
Even if one possesses wholesome karma and attains birth in the heavens or among humans to exhaust their store of merit, one continues to revolve in saṃsāra, drifting and wandering on.
Sunk in the depths, there is no time of emergence. Only the Western Pure Land serves as the swift path for transcending the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
A physical body is difficult to obtain; while one is still in good health, one should prepare for this great matter. One should constantly maintain this thought:
Since beginningless time, I have wandered through the six realms of rebirth, yet I was never aware of this Dharma-gate;

therefore, I could not attain liberation. Having known it today, how could I fail to apply myself immediately? Those who are advanced in years should certainly exert themselves, and the young likewise must not be remiss.
Upon the end of life, one shall be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. [Return...]
To contemplate death and enter the underworld, seeing King Yama and undergoing such terrors, is something that cannot be compared to [ordinary life] in the same breath.
Regarding the verification of departing according to karmic conditions, Master Wang said: "The spirit is the self; the form is..."
This is what I have relinquished. Because I have coming and going, that which is relinquished undergoes formation and destruction.
Now, as for the arrival of the spirit (*śen*): from where does it come? It comes following the conditions of karma (*karmapratyaya*). As for the departure of the spirit: to where does it go?
It goes following the conditions of karma. What are these conditions of karma? They are the things one has done. A person...
If one performs the karma of the human realm, the spirit follows it and is born among humans.
If one performs the karma of the heavens, the spirit follows it and is born in the heavens. If one performs the karma of an asura, the spirit follows it and is born as an asura.
If one performs the karma of the three evil realms, the spirit follows it and...
Following this, one is born into the three evil realms; thus, one wanders through the six destinies of saṃsāra with no time of escape.
Now, as for the spirit (ātman), since beginningless time, it has entered various wombs and changed its shells, unable to remain long in a single place.
Why is this so? It is because the karma created by me is not exhausted until after a long duration.
Therefore, the spirit dwells within karma. When karma is exhausted, the form perishes; when the form perishes, the spirit has no place to dwell.
Furthermore, it proceeds according to the karma created by oneself in this present life.
It is like a person who builds a house and must reside within it, or a person who prepares food and drink and must enjoy its flavor. Thus, one creates such [karma].
Karma inevitably brings about such retribution; this is indeed the natural law. Thus, how could one not be cautious regarding what one does in this present life?
For those who wish to directly escape saṃsāra and forever leave behind suffering and affliction, nothing compares to the Pure Land of the West;
therefore, it must be cultivated. *Jingtu zhizhi* says:
The two wheels of good and evil, and the two retributions of suffering and joy, are all created by the three karmas and produced by the four conditions.

If for even a single thought-moment one harbors anger or engages in sexual misconduct, this is the karma of hell. If one is stingy and greedy and does not practice giving, this is the karma of the hungry ghosts.
If one is obscured by the darkness of ignorance, this is the karma of animals. If one is arrogant and conceited, this is the karma of asuras. Firmly...
Observing the five precepts is the karma of humans. Diligently cultivating the ten wholesome paths is the karma of devas. Realizing the emptiness of persons is the karma of śrāvakas.
Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached is the karma of pratyekabuddhas. Practicing the six perfections in equal measure is the karma of bodhisattvas.
True compassion that is impartial is the karma of Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is like a person entering a great city who must first seek a place to stay before going out to attend to business;
when evening falls and it grows dark, they will have a place to lodge. Seeking a place to stay is what is meant by practicing for the Pure Land.
"Arriving at dusk when it is dark" refers to the arrival of one's great destiny (the time of death).
"Having a place to lodge for the night" refers to being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms. It is also like traveling far during the spring months:
one must first prepare rain gear; if a sudden downpour arrives, one will be free from the distress of being drenched and disheveled. Those who have prepared their rain gear in advance—
This refers to the cultivation of the Pure Land. "Sudden torrential rain arriving" refers to the imminent end of one's great life.
"Being free from the distress of soaking and disarray" refers to not falling into the evil realms to undergo various sufferings.
Furthermore, "first seeking a place to settle" means that it does not hinder the completion of one's task; "first preparing for the rain" means that [it does not hinder the completion of one's task].
This will hinder one's distant journey. Those who cultivate the Pure Land do not obstruct any worldly affairs;
why, then, would people not practice it?
Furthermore,
In this world, there are those who specialize exclusively in Chan meditation (*chan-dian*). They claim that the Pure Land is solely within the mind;
how could there be any further Pure Land? That Amitābha is one's own nature; there is no need to go on to see Amitābha. These words seem plausible but are actually erroneous. Why is this?
The Western Pure Land possesses both principle (*li*) and manifestation (*ji*). If one discusses its principle, it is because one can purify one’s own mind; therefore, all things are...
It is indeed true that the Pure Land is the land of the mind-only. Yet, regarding its actual manifestation, there truly exists the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Since the Buddha spoke of it with such earnestness and detail, how could he have spoken falsely?

Furthermore, some may believe in the existence of the Pure Land while adhering rigidly to the doctrine of "mind-only," thereby claiming that the Western Paradise is not a place where one should seek rebirth, and asserting instead that the realization of one's nature through Zen meditation transcends the Buddha.
The Patriarch said: "Those who find Amitābha difficult to perceive have all missed the mark. Why is this? This [Amitābha] is spoken of as being so sublime that I fear it is not easily reached.
Yet in that Western Pure Land, there is no greed and no attachment; no anger and no delusion. Can my own mind be free from greed and attachment?
Can it be free from anger and delusion? In that Western Pure Land, when one thinks of clothing, one obtains clothing..."
He eats when he obtains food; if he wishes to remain still, he remains still; if he wishes to go, he goes. When he thinks of clothing but has no clothing, cold distresses his mind;
when he thinks of food but has no food, hunger distresses his mind; and when he wishes to remain still, he cannot remain still.
Then the various movements of the world disturb his mind; he wishes to depart but cannot do so. Furthermore, the shackles of worldly entanglements vex his mind.

This is what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," which is truly not easy to attain. That Amitābha Buddha possesses blessings as vast as mountains and seas, and power that encompasses heaven and earth;
he could transform a hell into a lotus garden as easily as turning over his palm. Behold this inexhaustible [merit].
That world appears as if before one's eyes. Yet even by my own power of merit, I am unable to act for myself;
I constantly fear that my past karma is so deep and heavy that I might fall into hell, let alone transform myself into a lotus flower.
I cannot even perceive what occurs on the other side of a wall, much less see the infinite worlds. This is what is called the Amitābha of self-nature.
Truly, it is not easy to reach. Nevertheless, my own mind can be the Pure Land, yet I cannot suddenly become the Pure Land;
my nature can be Amitābha, yet I cannot suddenly become Amitābha.
How could one neglect the Pure Land without cultivation, or abandon Amitābha without desiring to see him? Therefore, one cultivates the Western Paradise in order to behold the Buddha.

Yet, attaining the Way is exceedingly easy. If one remains only within this world, wishing to practice Chan and awaken the nature in order to transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs is extremely difficult.
How much more so for those who cultivate the Pure Land; they are not hindered by practicing Chan. Why is this? Because those who practice Chan...
One will surely disregard the Pure Land and fail to practice it.

Judging from this, those who claim that the "Pure Land is Mind-only" and "Amitābha is one's own nature" speak of something vast yet unnecessary, lofty yet irrelevant; they have misled many whose cultivation has not reached its goal.
It would be better to tread upon solid ground through recitation and practice; then every person will surely be born in the Pure Land and directly escape the cycle of birth and death.
To turn back [from this] and associate with those whose words are empty and devoid of substance is as far apart from the Way as heaven is from earth.
Furthermore, it is said: "To attain great enlightenment through Zen meditation and thereby escape the cycle of birth and death is certainly the superior path;

however, among a hundred people, not two or three reach such a state. If one cultivates the Western Paradise, however, one will directly exit the cycle of birth and death and attain mastery over life and death."
If not one out of ten thousand is free from leakage, and if you do not cultivate the Western Paradise, you will inevitably be carried away by the conditions of your karma.

Although there were those such as the Chan Master Qingcaotang, Zhenru Zhe, and Huigu—who were all like [the masters of] the past—they were nonetheless submerged in the cycle of saṃsāra; this is truly to be feared.
The *Jingtu zhizhi* (Pointing to the Destination of the Pure Land) states:

"To reach the Pure Land of Mind-Only, one must first understand that all phenomena are mutually interfused. People of the world do not understand this, and consequently cling to the mind within the chest as the Pure Land.
They fail to realize that the descriptions of the adornments of the Buddha-lands spoken of by the Buddha in the sutras are entirely symbolic expressions and lack any substantial reality."
The Dharma. One will inevitably incur the fault of slandering the Dharma. One must realize that there is no phenomenon outside of the mind; therefore, it is called "Mind-Only. As a sutra says:
"It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room; their light fills the space entirely, without being destroyed or mixed.

Thus, from the Buddhas of the ten directions and the sentient beings of the nine realms, including all matter and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, down to a single speck of dust or a single hair, [all arise] accordingly with...
To take one dharma: it is but one lamp among hundreds of thousands of lamps.
For the practitioner, a single thought-moment is like being at the eastern lamp, while Amitābha’s Pure Land is like the western lamp; this is because their light pervades everywhere.
One is all; all is one. Outside the mind there is no land; outside the land there is no mind.
This is the principle within phenomena: it is the Pure Land of Mind-Only. Because it is neither destroyed nor mixed, this lamp and that lamp [are one].
They are not confused with one another: the mind is simply the mind; the Buddha is simply the Buddha; the Pure Land is simply the Pure Land.
Thus, the sentient beings of this land contemplate the Buddha of that land and seek rebirth there. This is precisely the principle within the phenomenon—the Western Pure Land.
Although phenomenon and principle are distinguished, they are in reality not two separate paths. If one is restricted to the west...

If one adheres strictly to [the literal] method without realizing that all is mind-only, one attains the phenomenon but loses the principle; thus, although one has not yet conformed to the principle, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, one still attains rebirth there.
Although one may dwell in the lowest grade, there is nonetheless no retrogression. If, however, one restricts oneself to one's own mind alone...
If one does not seek the Western [Pure Land], then both the phenomenal and the noumenal are lost. Because one does not seek rebirth, one fails to attain birth there;

this is the loss regarding the phenomenal. Because one does not know that there are no phenomena outside the mind, one dogmatically clings to this very square inch as being the mind, thereby obscuring the principle of the perfect interfusion of mind and dharmas; this is the loss regarding the noumenal.
The *Pure Land Text of Longshu* by Qingcaotang states: During the Song dynasty, there was a man named Qingcaotang who was over ninety years old.
A woman from the Zeng family regularly provided him with vegetarian offerings and gave him clothing and other gifts.
Moved by her kindness, the monk said, "I, this old monk, shall become a son to you, Madam. One day, this woman gave birth to a child.
He sent someone to look at Qingcaotang; [the master] had already passed away while sitting in meditation (zuòhuà). His biological son was none other than Prime Minister Zeng.
Because he had been a monk in a previous life and had cultivated merit and wisdom, he attained high honors in the civil service at a young age and later served as Chancellor.
Nevertheless, even so, he was mistaken; he was not reborn in the Western Pure Land to see the Buddha and bring an end to birth and death.
He then reflected: "To be preoccupied with such trivial favors and to act as a son for others means one does not escape craving and remains forever in saṃsāra;
how utterly mistaken this calculation is!
Furthermore, Master Jie of the Five Patriarchs said: "Master Jie of the Five Patriarchs was the previous incarnation of Dongpo. This too—
This is a great error. If one was previously a monk who practiced Chan meditation while concurrently cultivating the Western Pure Land, they would certainly have been reborn in that pure land;

how could they have ended up being born in this world to undergo so much suffering? When it was heard that东坡 (Sōngp'o) was traveling south, he carried with him nothing but a single scroll of Amitābha Buddha.
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied: "This is for the sake of Śì’s rebirth in the Western Land."
This is the public record. It was only when东坡 (Sōngpó) reached this point that he truly achieved his purpose;
it was also because of his long-cultivated roots of merit and his extraordinary clarity of insight that he finally realized this principle.
Zhentuozhe further said: "There was an elder named Zhe who sat in meditation for forty years without sleeping.

His asceticism was so profound that had he cultivated the Western Pure Land, he would surely have become a Bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression, and thus would have been at ease within the cycle of birth and death.
Not knowing to cultivate this, he was instead reborn in a place of great wealth and status, where he suffered much throughout his life."
How distressing! How pitiable! Someone asked: "The Venerable Zhe was so diligent in his cultivation; why is it that he experiences so much sorrow and suffering in this life?
The answer was: "The Buddha said: 'Even if a hundred thousand kalpas were to pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten.
When causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself. Master Yongjia also said: 'If one realizes it, karmic obstacles..."
Originally empty; not having realized this, one must still repay past debts. If Elder Zhe were to be reborn in the Western Paradise, then he would have no need to repay those past debts.
Huigu also said: "There was an elder named Huigu, also known as the Venerable Master Xing. After his death..."
To be born into the family of a high minister and later to pass the highest civil service examinations is indeed considered a source of honor by the world;
yet, it is also a profound miscalculation. Why is this so? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that those who practice in the world are like turbid water:
though it may be made clear by settling, the dregs have not been removed, and if stirred, it becomes turbid once more. This is what the ancients have said.
Just as one who is born in the Western Land sees the Buddha and attains the Way, yet returns to be born again in this world, they then wash away their turbid feet so that they become pure water;

even if it is stirred, it will no longer be turbid. To be born now into a wealthy and noble family, and later to succeed in the highest civil service examinations, is like a great elephant entering the mud: with every step, it becomes deeper by that same measure. What can be done about this?
Why is this? Therefore, even those renowned as venerable elders must not fail to cultivate the Western Land; the ancients were sufficient to serve as a mirror for this.
*Gulmo* (The Submerged) states:
"He enters together with the gulma and emerges together with the gulma. [Note: *Zai* (齎) refers to the navel of the water.]
Furthermore, "submerging" (*mò*) refers to water bubbles entering from above and sinking below; "gushing forth" (*gǔ*) refers to bubbles rising from below and emerging above;
hence the term "gushing and submerging" (*gǔmò*).
Moreover—

According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*), all of whom live for a thousand million years. Yet when their lifespan is exhausted, they re-enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Because they have never realized the true nature (*tathatā*), they are categorized as part of the "seven realms" (*sapta-gati*) alongside the sentient beings of the six paths.

Thus, they are all individuals within the cycle of birth and death. Among the people of the world who study the arts of immortality, not one in ten thousand succeeds; and even if they should succeed, [they remain within this cycle].
One still cannot escape saṃsāra because one is attached to form and spirit and is unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are merely delusive thoughts manifested within true nature; they are not reality. Thus, Hanshan’s poem says:

Even if you were to attain the state of an immortal (*ṛṣi*), you would be no different from a corpse-guarding spirit (*śavaga*). This is not like the Buddhist approach to birth and death, which is spontaneous and free from all constraints.
In recent centuries alone, those who have studied the arts of immortality have numbered in the millions, yet they have all ultimately died and been buried beneath the earth.
If you wish to seek long life, nothing compares to the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*). Those who are born in the Pure Land...
The lifespan therein is immeasurable; how great indeed is its longevity! To fail to know that one should cultivate this Dharma-gate and instead study the arts of immortals—is this not delusion?
Some may say: "Pure Land is a matter for after closing one's eyes [in death]; what proof or verification is there?"
The reply states: "The *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) fully records such spiritual responses; how could there not be verified evidence?

Furthermore, those who are immortals (*shenxian*) keep what they have attained secret and do not transmit it. In the Dharma-gate of the Buddha, one only fears that the transmission will not be widespread.
This is because its compassion is vast and great, difficult to fathom, and is not comparable to that of the immortals."

(Reply: I have carefully consulted the *Wangsheng ji* (Collection on Rebirth), which states that during the Later Wei dynasty, Tanluan received from Tao Hongjing the ten fascicles of the *Candraprabha-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
He was filled with joy and felt he had attained his goal, believing that the state of a transcendent immortal (*xiān*) could certainly be realized.
Later, he encountered the monk Bodhiruci, who asked him: "In the Way of the Buddha, is there eternal life? Can one ward off old age and attain immortality?"
Zhi said, "Longevity and immortality—this is my Buddhist Way. He then gave him the *Sutra on the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "You should recite this.
Then you shall no longer be born within the three realms, nor wander again through the six paths. You will understand the cycles of fullness and emptiness, and the processes of arising and ceasing."
As for calamity and fortune, success and failure, none can reach him. His longevity is such that there are kalpa-stones and grains of sand in the Ganges River;
while the number of these sands and stones is finite, the measure of his lifespan is infinite. This is the "long life" of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha).
Wăn Xìn believed this deeply, whereupon he burned the immortals' scriptures and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Despite the changes of cold and heat and the onset of illness, he did not slacken in his practice. One day, he instructed his disciples to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in a loud voice;

facing west and prostrating himself, he passed away. At that time, both monastics and laypeople alike heard the sound of pipes, strings, and flutes coming from the west, which ceased only after a long while.

Master Lián praised him, saying: [The original Chinese text follows: 雖寒暑之變。疾病之來。亦不懈怠。一日令弟子高聲念阿彌陀佛。西向叩頭而亡。是時僧俗同聞管絃絲竹之聲。從西而來。良久乃止。蓮師贊曰： (Note: As the instruction specifies to provide only the translation and no additional information, the final output is the English rendering above.)
It was said: "The yellow-capped practitioners always claim that those of the Śākya school die, while the immortals (xian) achieve eternal life.
Now, Master Zhi [Daolin] asserts that the Buddha possesses eternal life, whereas the immortals do not. This argument is incisive, concise, and appropriate; it stands preeminent throughout the ages.
That Dharma Master Luan abandoned the false to return to the true—discarding them like worn-out sandals—is it not because he possessed the correct cause from past lives?"

How extraordinary! It does not end there. Furthermore, according to the *Mingzong ji* (Collection on Clarifying the Source), when Lü Dongbin first visited Huanglong, he attained immediate realization upon hearing the Master’s words.
He then composed a verse, saying: "I have cast away my gourd and bag and smashed my zither;
Now I no longer crave gold within the mercury. Since the moment I first beheld Huanglong, I have finally realized that all I did before was a mistake."

Heart! Alas! If even Lü Dongbin, who had already attained the Way of the Immortals, spoke in such a manner, then it can be known all the more clearly that the Way of the Immortals is inferior to the Way of the Buddha.
Yet people today still cannot abandon the quest for immortality to seek the Buddha, as did Master Luan.
How can this be called anything other than lamentable?

In the *Kaozheng Jinxianshi Huiwen* (Examination and Verification of Questions Regarding the Golden Immortal), the *Shijiafo Chengdao Ji* (Record of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Attainment of Enlightenment) states:

"The Golden Wheel [King] acts as a sovereign. The commentary notes: "The Golden Wheel King rules over the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*). From there, he ascends into the void and travels throughout the four heavens.
In all lands, upon seeing the golden wheel fly toward them, they all submit of their own accord. By this means, he attains [sovereignty]."
"He is named the Golden Immortal (Suvarṇa-ṛṣi). Is this so? Or is it not? Answer: "I fear that the significance does not lie merely in this.

It is because his *dharmakāya* is adamantine and indestructible that he is named the Golden Immortal. Nevertheless, since all Buddhas are adamantine and indestructible, why is the title 'Golden Immortal' applied exclusively to Śākyamuni Buddha?
Perhaps there is something to be derived from the 'Golden Wheel' (Cakravartin) as well; yet this remains uncertain."
This may be understood.

Regarding the three realms and six paths: from the Great Avīci Hell up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, all are called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), because sentient beings possess desire therein.
Above this is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), which possesses only form.
The body has neither male nor female form. Furthermore, above this is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is likewise no physical body;
there exists only the soul-consciousness (*vijñāna*), like that of ghosts or spirits. These together are collectively termed the Three Realms (*tridhātu*).

On the four sides of Mount Sumeru are what are called the Heavens of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*). Above those is the Heaven of Śakra Devendra. Above that again are the four layers of clouds.
The heavens are collectively termed the Realm of Desire (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, the eighteen layers of heavens above the clouds are collectively termed the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
Moreover, the four layers of heavens in the space above are collectively termed the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The details regarding these various heavens will follow later.
○ The Layman of Longshu said: To clearly understand the six realms of existence, one must first understand the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The first gate of the twelvefold dependent origination states: "A single thought-moment arising is already complete with the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. It further states: "Dependent origination refers to the twelve factors that, through their mutual interaction, are capable of producing fruits."

Therefore, they are called causes. That which exists through mutual dependence is termed a condition (*pratyaya*). When causes and conditions continue in succession, the cycle of birth and death proceeds without end.

If one understands ignorance and does not give rise to grasping for existence, then the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms, as well as birth and death themselves, will both cease. This is the essential method for transcending the world.
The diagram of the twelve links of dependent origination:
it is because of emotion (*qing*) that these twelve links arise, creating the karma for the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and six paths, which cannot be severed.
By proceeding toward the West, emotion is extinguished and the true nature (*xing*) manifests; therefore, there shall be no further cycle of rebirth throughout eternal kalpas.
The first gate: First, when ignorance causes the arising of craving for forms seen by the eye, this is precisely ignorance.
Second, when volitional formations (saṃskāra) create karma through craving, these are termed formations.
The three consciousnesses reach the mind and focus their attention; therefore, they are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Fourth, when name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) cognize their respective objects, this is called "name-and-form.
Fifth and sixth, when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) give rise to craving, these are called the "six sense bases."
Sixth, seeking craving through the sense bases caused by contact is called *sparśa* (contact).
Seventh, the mind of greedy attachment is called *vedanā* (feeling).
Eighth, being entangled in craving and unable to let go is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
The ninth is that these dharmas, such as seeking, are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
The tenth is that when such dharmas arise, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).
The eleventh is that when birth occurs in uninterrupted succession, it is called "birth" (*jāti*).
Because the twelve links of old age and death are successively severed, it is called "death.
Layman Longshu said: "Ignorance" refers to the obscuration of true nature. "Volitional formations" refer to mental activity. "Consciousness" refers to the soul-consciousness.
"Name-and-form" refers to sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness. "Form" refers to the physical body. "The six sense bases" refer to the six faculties. "Contact" refers to...

This refers to that which contacts the six sense organs. Because it fails to realize the true nature due to its obscurity, it cannot remain quiescent and unmoving, and thus the *ālaya*-consciousness arises.
From this, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) comes into being; from name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); from the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*);
from contact, sensation (*vedanā*); from sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); from craving, grasping (*upādāna*); and from grasping, there is constant becoming (*bhava*). From [becoming]...

This undergoes rebirth again; because there is birth, there is old age and death. These factors pull one another along without interruption, and are therefore called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is the diagram of the three realms and six paths of existence.
There is the karma of the twelve links of dependent origination, which creates the retribution of the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and six paths; thus, one cannot attain liberation.
By being born in the Western Land, karma is severed and retribution becomes empty; therefore, there is forever no falling back into saṃsāra.
The six realms are also called the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). "Destiny" (*gati*) means "to arrive. It signifies that the karma one has created carries one to those respective places.
First is the realm of hell; the *Fourfold Teaching Ritual* (*Sishijiaoyi*) states: it is also called *niraya*. As for the term "hell" (*diyu*), [it is explained as follows].
This place lies beneath the earth, consisting of the eight cold and eight hot great hells, each with its own retinue.
Among these, the most painful experiences vary in degree according to one's karma, lasting for kalpas or other durations.
The most severe cases involve eighty-four thousand births and deaths within a single day, continuing for immeasurable kalpas. Thus it is said: "Having committed [karma], one undergoes [retribution]."
Regarding those who commit the ten grave evils and the five heinous crimes of the highest grade, they receive this body of the path (the hellish realm).
The *Fozu Tongji* states: "As for the hells of the four continents: Jambudvīpa has both the primary and peripheral [hells]; Pūrvavideha and Aparagodānīya have the peripheral but not the primary;
Uttarakuru has neither the primary nor the peripheral. The primary hells are located twenty thousand *yojanas* beneath the earth; the peripheral ones are on the ground."

Above the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), those from the three continents who have created karma all come to the primary hells of Jambudvīpa, as well as the peripheral hells of the eastern, western, and southern continents, to undergo their retributive suffering.
Furthermore, it is said that there are three types of hells: the eight hot hells, where one undergoes the suffering of burning affliction;
the eight cold hells, where one undergoes the suffering of freezing cold; and the three peripheral hells, where one undergoes the retribution for individual karma.
The retribution is called the "Light Bondage" (Mṛdu-bandhana) and is also named "Solitary" (Ekākī).
The fifth is the Avīci Hell (the Hell of No Interval), which is the eighth among the hot hells. Those who commit the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes fall into this hell.

It is called "No Interval" because suffering follows immediately upon the transition from death to rebirth; because there is no interval of pleasure between the sufferings; and because the duration is fixed at one kalpa.
Therefore, there is no interval in terms of life, because it is uninterrupted; there is no interval in terms of form, because whether one person or many, they fill [the space].
Second, regarding the animal realm, the *Sìjiàoyí* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings) states: "This realm pervades all places; [its inhabitants] have fur and wear horns."
Scaly and armored, feathered and furred; four-footed, many-footed; with feet or without feet; moving through water, on land, or in the air—they devour one another, suffering without end.
Those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes of the middle grade receive this body of the animal realm.
Master Sengzhao said: "Because delusion and arrogance are pervasive and heavy, many fall into the realm of animals."
The *Sijiao yi* (Outline of the Four Teachings) regarding the third, the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), states:
This realm also pervades all places. Those with merit become spirits of mountains, forests, tombs, or temples;

those without merit dwell in impure places where they obtain neither food nor drink, constantly suffering flogging, filling up rivers, and damming up seas, undergoing immeasurable suffering. This occurs when one commits the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) of the lowest grade.
The ten evil deeds induce rebirth in this realm of hungry ghosts. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* states that there are three grades:

the severe suffer the flames of hunger that parch and rot their joints, such that they do not even hear the names of water or grain; the middling seek out and consume pus, blood, excrement, and filth;
the minor occasionally obtain a meager meal to satisfy their hunger. Sengzhao says: "Those who are stingy and greedy lack merit, and thus frequently fall into the realm of hungry ghosts."
Regarding the four paths of the asuras, the *Sijiao yi* states: This is translated as "those without wine.

They reside either on seashores or at the bottom of the ocean, where their palaces are magnificently adorned; they constantly delight in combat. During their causal stage, they harbored a mind of suspicion and jealousy.

Although one practices the five constant virtues, because of the desire to surpass others, one performs the ten wholesome actions of the lowest grade (*adhamā*), which results in this body of the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the categories of beings, the *Dharmasaṃkhyā* states there are four types: ghosts (*preta*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), humans (*manuṣya*), and devas (*deva*). As for ghosts: they dwell on the shores of the great ocean and are born from a womb (*jarāyuja*);

they are included within the human realm as those whose merit has declined and who have fallen from among the devas. As for animals: they dwell on the shores of the great ocean and are born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*).

Those who protect the Dharma-vehicle and travel through emptiness are categorized among the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Those who are human are characterized by arrogant pride and a lack of virtue;
they are moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*) and are categorized among the inferior births from the waters of the ocean. Those who are celestial beings dwell in rock caves on the slopes of Mount Sumeru;
they are transformation-born (*upapāduka*) and are categorized among the realm of gods (*deva*), possessing the power and fearlessness of attaining mastery over the world.
The *Wǔmén Dào Sìjiàoyí* states: "The four continents differ. In Pūrvavideha in the east, the life span is two hundred and fifty years.
In Jambudvīpa in the south, the life span is one hundred years. In Aparagoyānī in the west, the life span is five hundred years.
In Uttarakuru in the north, the life span is one thousand years. There is no premature death, and sages are not born there."

Within this realm, suffering and pleasure alternate. During the causal stage, by practicing the Five Constant Virtues and the Five Precepts, and performing the intermediate grade of the Ten Wholesome Actions, one receives retribution as this body of the [Asura] Path.
*Changshui* says: Regarding the four modes of birth for humans:
those born from eggs are the thirty-two sons of the mother Viśākhā; those born from the womb are ordinary people; and those born from moisture are the daughter Nanda.
They were born from the moisture of the *āmra* tree; they were beings of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). These were the humans at the beginning of the eon.
When their merit from the second dhyāna was about to be exhausted, they descended to Jambudvīpa—these are they. As for animals possessing all four modes of birth:

those that move on the ground, such as *rākṣasas*, and the Mother of Ghosts (*Hārītī*), are all born from the womb (*jarāyuja*). Thus we know there are ghosts born from the womb. All others are of miraculous birth.

Regarding birth, the six heavens of the deva realm and the twenty-eight heavens differ. These consist of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the eighteen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
First, as for the six heavens of the desire realm: the first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), which resides—
At the waist of Mount Sumeru dwell the two [lower] Trāyastriṃśa heavens; at the summit of Mount Sumeru dwell the Trāyastriṃśa heavens themselves.
There are thirty-three heavens in total, as there are eight heavens on each of the four sides—four times eight makes thirty-two—and the heaven of Śakra’s Sudharmā Hall.
Śakra, as the supreme commander of the thirty-two heavens, together with them constitutes the thirty-three heavens, which are collectively named the Trāyastriṃśa heavens.
The two heavens mentioned above are attained by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) of the highest grade alone.
Third is the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. These four heavens above dwell in the void.

One attains rebirth therein by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action of the highest grade while concurrently cultivating the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory concentration) through seated meditation.
Next, regarding the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are divided into four dhyānas. The first dhyāna has three heavens:

the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*), the Brahma-ministers (*brahmapurohita*), and the Great Brahma (*mahābrahmāṇa*). The second dhyāna has three heavens: Limited Light (*parīttābha*), Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇābha*), and Light-Sound (*ābhāsvara*). The third dhyāna has three heavens:

Limited Purity (*parīttaśubha*), Immeasurable Purity (*apramāṇaśubha*), and Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*). The fourth dhyāna has nine heavens: Cloudless (*anabhraka*), Merit-born (*puṇyaprasava*), and so forth.

The Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala). The three heavens above these are dwelling places for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); those who practice the ten superior wholesome deeds and cultivate meditation are reborn therein.
The Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva) is the abode of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*).

The Five Pure Abodes—Free from Affliction (Avṛha), Free from Heat (Atapa), Good Vision (Sudṛśa), Good Appearance (Sudarśana), and Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha)—are the dwelling places for those who abide in the third fruit [of the path]. These nine heavens above are free from...

When desire first begins to disperse, yet one has not yet emerged from the "cage of form," it is therefore called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Because one sits and attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it receives the name "dhyāna.

Regarding the four heavens of the Three Formless Realms (*ārūpyadhātu*): they are the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
These four heavens above possess only the four aggregates (*skandha*) and lack the aggregate of form; thus they receive their names.

The explanation provided above, from the hells up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, shows that although suffering and pleasure differ, one cannot escape being born again after dying, and dying again after being born; therefore, it is called "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the "Kalpa Stone" (Jieshi), the *Fozu Tongji* states: "In Tuṣita, a six-liang garment brushes a blue stone.
[Note: The stone is one yojana wide and half a yojana thick.

When a celestial being of Tuṣita brushes it once every hundred years until the stone is completely worn away, that constitutes one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), not a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*) such as a revolving wheel.
As for "river-sands" and "Ganges sands": *Gaṅgā* is also called the *Kīṅga* River. From Lake Anavatapta, four rivers flow out from each of its four sides.
From the Silver Ox Mouth in the east flows the *Kīṅga* River; from the south, north, and west, each likewise flows out [a river].
Rivers flow into the ocean; only the sands of the Ganges are so extremely fine and numerous. Therefore, this is used as a metaphor for the vastness of the number of years in one's lifespan.
This is from Yongming Shou Chan Master’s *Text on Admonishing Others Not to Despise the Pure Land*.

A question is posed: "If merely seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way allows one to transcend birth and death, what need is there to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
The answer is: A true practitioner should examine themselves. It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves.
Herein I shall provide a mirror of reflection to dispel many delusions. You, virtuous ones, should observe your own conduct and understanding.
Have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way? Have you received the prediction of a Tathāgata and succeeded to the position of the Patriarchs?
Can you be like Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna? Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*? Can you be like the Tiantai Master Zhiyi?

Are you proficient in both the doctrine and its exposition, and do you cultivate both practice and understanding? Can you be like National Teacher Huizhong? All these great beings clearly manifested...

The verbal teachings offer profound exhortations for rebirth in the Pure Land. This is truly for the benefit of both oneself and others; how could one be willing to mislead others and bring harm upon oneself?

Moreover, the Great Hero (the Buddha) has offered his praise, and his golden mouth has issued these earnest instructions. One should follow the examples of past sages and reverently obey the Buddha’s decree; it is certainly not erroneous.

Furthermore, the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth) records numerous well-documented accounts of the deeds of eminent figures from both ancient and modern times. It is fitting that [one should follow them].

One should observe and reflect upon this to illuminate one's own understanding. Furthermore, one must examine for oneself: at the time of death, will one certainly attain mastery over the departure from and abiding in birth-and-death?
Will the heavy obstacles of evil karma accumulated since beginningless time certainly not manifest before one?

Will this single retribution-body certainly be liberated from saṃsāra? Will one certainly have the freedom to appear and disappear while wandering among the various classes of beings within the three miserable realms and evil paths?

Are you free from suffering and affliction? In the heavens above and the human realm below, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, can you entrust yourself wherever you wish without any obstruction?
If you have attained clear understanding and can have confidence in this, what could be more auspicious?

If you have not yet reached this state, do not be arrogant for a moment, lest you cause yourself to sink into the depths for eternal kalpas and lose the benefit of the good; whom else would you blame then?
Alas, how lamentable! What can be done now?

Examining the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it says: "To those whose minds are arrogant, he manifests as a great strongman to subdue all who are conceited, causing them to abide in the Unsurpassed Way. Sengzhao says: "The mind of arrogance..."

Those who are self-exalting are like mountain peaks that do not retain water. A Bodhisattva manifests as a strongman to subdue their arrogant mind, and only then moistens them with the water of the Dharma.
— *The Preface for Encouraging the Cultivation of Pure Land by Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi*

Everyone says that practicing the Pure Land is not as good as the methods of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya. I alone say that among the dharma-gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, none compare to practicing the Pure Land.
Indeed, true purity, clarity, and wondrousness—empty, penetrating, and spiritually responsive—is this very nature possessed by all, whether wise or foolish.
Yet, with the sense organs and their objects forming illusory realms, we are swept away together; the cycle of birth and death continues through kalpas without end.
Therefore, the Śākyas employ Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya as provisional skillful means to lead practitioners through various gates so that they may all attain transcendent awakening.
Only Amitābha Buddha provides a single gate, known as the cultivation of the Pure Land. Like a singular remedy for curing disease, it is concise, direct, and straightforward;
with single-minded devotion in a single thought-moment, one reaches the other shore. Regardless of whether one is ordained or a layperson, all—
"You may practice this. However, know that these are shallow and mundane teachings intended to transform the ignorant and the common folk;

in reality, they are the swift path to attaining the Way of the Buddha. Among those who study Buddhism today, there are none who go beyond Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya. As for the ultimate, sudden, and perfect [teaching], nothing surpasses Chan.

Unless one possesses sharp faculties and is of superior capacity, capable of intuitively grasping and understanding through the spirit and mind, one cannot avoid falling into the error of 'stolid emptiness' (頑空)."

To lose oneself in study is to fail; there is nothing like the Teachings for investigating the Three Vehicles. Yet, unless one has "forgotten the trap upon catching the fish" or "seen the moon by following the pointing finger," one cannot avoid the malady of poring over old paper.
There is nothing like the Vinaya for protecting the good and warding off evil; yet, unless one’s body and mind are pure, it will not suffice.

If one treats the internal and external as identical, one cannot avoid the suffering of self-entanglement. Viewing them collectively, if one discusses the means of entry, there are Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;
yet if one considers their ultimate destination, they are Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom.

Is it not the single gate of Pure Land alone that attains Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom without relying on Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya? At the very moment of reciting the Buddha’s name, one chants with the mouth...
Reflect in your mind: "To refrain from all evil—this is not the precepts? To bind one's mindfulness to the pure realm so that illusory objects and dust alike perish—this is not concentration?
To contemplate that there is truly no thought, and the lotus of the mind becomes serene—this is not wisdom?

If a person can set aside myriad concerns and direct their single-mindedness toward the Western Pure Land, then without the striking of staffs or shouts, they will awaken to the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; and without reading the Great Tripitaka, they will [attain realization].
One attains the Eye of the True Dharma. Without relying on the four modes of deportment, one attains great mastery.
Neither defiled nor pure, neither bound nor liberated—at this very moment, what constitutes precept, concentration, and wisdom? What constitutes dhyāna, teaching, and discipline?
My own mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction; this is the ultimate consummation of the cultivation of the Pure Land. It is the water of eight virtues.
The golden lotus pedestal—why then should one harbor doubts?
Examining the evidence regarding Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, it is no less than Master Yuan of the Pure Land who stated in his commentary:

"Among the three schools of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, there are none that do not seek rebirth in the Pure Land. As for Chan, this is exemplified by Yongming, who was a pillar of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen).
Yet he was born into the highest of the high grades. Yuanzhao alone upheld the single transmission, thereby establishing his name in the realm of the Lotus;
his teaching was like that of Sengrui, who assisted Master Kumārajīva, and thus the lotus flower emerged from beneath the lectern. Zhili revived the Tiantai teachings in the region of Siming.

Yet he passed away while seated facing west. Vinaya is like a divine *lingzhi* fungus; one serves it in life through the *vinaya*, and at death one is born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
Qingzhao extensively propagated the study of the *vinaya*, yet he recited a verse to return to the West. If one were to cite such examples at length, they would be beyond counting.
From this perspective, it is clear that the three schools [of Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan] are not equal to the practice of Pure Land.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another.

That person should look at the moon; if instead they gaze at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, this person not only loses sight of the lunar disk, but will eventually forget the finger as well. Why? Because they have taken the pointing finger to be the bright moon."
Not only do they forget the finger, but they also fail to distinguish between light and darkness. Why is this?
Because they take the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon’s radiance; thus, they have no comprehension of the two natures of light and darkness.
Chan Master Shen Zan of Zuanguzi was one day reading a sutra by a window when a bee flew into the paper screen, seeking an exit.
The Master composed a verse, saying: "Refusing to leave the gate of emptiness, To fly into the window is truly foolish."
For a hundred years you have pored over old paper; when will you emerge?
"To catch the fish, one forgets the trap"—the trap is the bamboo device used for catching fish.
*The Collection Clarifying the Source* states: Master Ciming addressed the assembly, using his staff.
He struck the meditation seat once and said, "Does the assembly understand? Have you not heard it said: 'With one strike, all that is known is forgotten;
there is no longer any need for cultivation or maintenance. Those who have attained the Way in all quarters say this is the highest capacity.
But tell me, what excellence does the Zen of the Patriarchs possess? If you seek the principle within words, you will mislead future generations. Straight away—
To attempt to take responsibility under a blow of the staff is to betray the former sages. The myriad dharmas are fundamentally at rest;
it is only people who create their own clamor. Shanhua asked various Chan practitioners: "I have heard that a single shout of the Chan school can transform the ordinary into the sacred.
Now, if a single shout can enter the five teachings of our school, it shall be considered the true tradition. If it cannot, [it is not]."
"This is a heterodox teaching. Master Jicheng then raised his voice and let out a shout. He asked Shan, "Did you hear it? Shan replied, "I heard it.
The Master said, "Since you heard this one shout, you possess something; you can enter the teachings of the Hinayana.
A moment later, he asked again, "Did you hear it? Shan replied, "I did not hear it. The Master said, "Since you did not hear it, as for that previous one..."

"Ho! This is non-existence. One can thus enter the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching). Then [the Master] looked at Shan and said: "When I first uttered 'Ho!', you said it existed. Now that the sound of 'Ho!
has long since faded away, you say it does not exist. To say it does not exist implies that it originally truly existed; to say it exists..."
Thus, at this very moment, it truly neither exists nor does it not exist; one is thereby able to enter the Final Teaching (Jiǒngjiào).
When I let out a single shout, that existence is not a mere existence, for existence arises because of non-existence. When there is no single shout, that non-existence is not a mere non-existence.
Because there is existence, there is non-existence; existence and non-existence are simultaneous. One can thus enter the Sudden Teaching.
You must know that this single shout of mine does not function as a mere shout; it transcends both existence and non-existence, and all intellectual interpretations are forgotten.
