When the Way is present, not even a speck of dust can stand; when the Way is absent, it pervades the void horizontally. Through this very shout, one enters hundreds of thousands [of gates].
Ten billion shouts, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of shouts—all enter into this single shout. This is called being able to enter the Perfect Teaching.
By examining these two matters, the staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji can both be understood by analogy.
The *Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra of the Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom* states:

The Sixth Patriarch asked Zhicheng, "How does your teacher describe the characteristics of the practice of precepts, concentration, and wisdom? Zhicheng replied, "Master Xiu says that 'refraining from all evil' is called precepts;
'practicing all good' is called wisdom; and 'calming one's own mind' is called concentration. The Patriarch said:
Your teacher’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom receive those of the Mahāyāna; my precepts, concentration, and wisdom receive those of the Most Supreme Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
The Dharma I teach does not depart from self-nature (*svabhāva*). To teach the Dharma apart from its essence is called the Dharma of marks (*lakṣaṇadharma*);
therein, self-nature remains perpetually deluded. You must know that all phenomena arise as the functional manifestation of self-nature; this is true precept, concentration, and wisdom.
The Dharma of Wisdom. The verse says: When the mind-ground is free from transgression, it is the self-nature precept; when the mind-ground is free from delusion, it is self-nature wisdom;
when the mind-ground is free from distraction, it is self-nature concentration. Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the original vajra;
the coming and going of the body is fundamentally samādhi. The *Yongjia ji* states: Within the precepts there are three that must be fully possessed: first, the restraint of conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*).
The first is the precept of restraining from evil, which means cutting off all unwholesome deeds. The second is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, which means cultivating all wholesome deeds.

The third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings, which means vowing to deliver all living beings. Regarding the three types within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they must be distinguished separately:
the first is the concentration of abiding, which refers to the wondrous nature that is innate and fundamentally unmoving; the second is the concentration of induction, which refers to clarity...

The mind becomes tranquil and still; its clarity is enhanced and its brilliance increases. Third is the concentration on the accomplishment of tasks, which is like water becoming clear and still so that all images are reflected therein.

Within wisdom, there are three types that must be distinguished: first, the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, which means realizing that the aggregates are not the self—that within the aggregates there is no self—just as there is no hair on a tortoise or horns on a rabbit.
Second, the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, which means realizing that the aggregates and all other phenomena [are empty].

Conditions are provisional and not real, like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water. The "emptiness of emptiness" refers to the wisdom that realizes both the object and the cognition are empty;
this emptiness itself is also empty. This teaching accords with Master Xiu’s intention; however, people are not of superior intelligence.
One should take these two accounts as the starting point.
The *Zhengfayan Mingzong Ji* states: "The World-Honored One held up a flower; Kāśyapa smiled. The World-Honored One said:
'I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa; I entrust it to Kāśyapa. [End of quote] Or, someone asked:
Why is it called the "Eye of the True Dharma"? The *Mingzong ji* states: "The human eye cannot contain even a single object;
though gold dust is precious, once it enters, it becomes a source of harm. The mind of the practitioner is likewise like the eye—it must not have even the slightest attachment.
If one follows the Supreme Vehicle, then the mind has no attachments. Therefore, it is so called."
This is the True Dharma Eye.
Regarding Master Lianchi’s *Discourse on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*:
it is likely that the discourse on the Pure Land merely expresses the underlying principle (*dharmatā*). Wise people ought to directly awaken to the Zen school; yet now...
"If you merely praise and speak of the Pure Land, would this not be an attachment to phenomenal forms (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) while failing to understand the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)?

Answer: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; the skillful means (*upāya*) have many gates. If one understands this principle, the Chan school and the Pure Land school follow different paths yet reach the same destination.
Your doubts will be instantly dissolved like melting ice. In the past, people have alternately expounded upon these two, not as something distinct."
This is sufficient. As the Great Master Zhongfeng said: "Chan is the Pure Land; the Pure Land is Chan.
Those who practice must value entering deeply into one gate. These few words are an immutable thesis for ten thousand generations.
Thus, when Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, he said: [with this...]
The mind of mindfulness of the Buddha enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the inconceivable liberation of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Yet he says, "May I, at the end of my life, be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. These two Great Beings—one attends the Teacher of the Sahā world, and the other attends the Guide of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
While it would seem appropriate for each to establish their own distinct approach, they are here brought together in harmonious and perfect integration.
The two do not obstruct one another; these are all things people have frequently heard and are well-acquainted with. How can you still cling to such biased views?
Furthermore, when you say that the Pure Land symbolizes the Dharma, is it not because the pure mind itself is the Pure Land?
If so, would you then claim that a virtuous mind is itself heaven, and that there is no longer any further world of the seven treasures? If that were the case, then...
The Suyāma and Trāyastriṃśa heavens are nothing more than an evil mind; what need is there for further swords, blades, or boiling cauldrons?
Ignorance is itself the animal realm; what need is there for further things such as shaggy fur or horns?

Furthermore, you take delight in discussing the principle (li) while loathing the discussion of phenomena (shi). This is entirely because you wish to manifest yourself as a high-ranking monk and fear that others might say you are not.

Regarding the principle of pervasive penetration: Alas! If you have truly and clearly realized this principle, you will know that there is no principle apart from phenomena and no nature apart from appearances;
they have been mutually interpenetrating from the very beginning. Why, then, must you insist on abandoning phenomena to seek principle, or leaving appearances to search for nature?

Furthermore, the Buddha-lands are divided into four types. You claim that there is only the True Land of Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhāsvara-bhūmi*), and that there are no others, such as the Land of Actual Reward and Adornment (*vipāka-saṃbhoga-bhūmi*).

Is it not so? If one seeks loftiness and subtlety by speaking exclusively of the signless (animitta), then the teaching that "the mind is the pure land" is something that even beginners and latecomers can speak of after merely reading two or three sutras and treatises; how could this be considered difficult?
Moreover, since your mind is pure and your land is pure, you dwell in a pure land wherever you go. Let me ask you this:
would you be willing to share a trough for food and drink with dogs, pigs, horses, and oxen? Would you be willing to enter burial mounds and sleep among putrid corpses?
Would you be willing to wash, massage, feed, and nurse those afflicted by *gamalā* disease, or those covered in pus, blood, excrement, and urine?
A person with a malignant disease has suffered for many months and years; yet toward these various things, they remain joyful and at ease, hardly giving them a thought.
You have granted that mountains and plains alike are all the Western Land.

Yet, if one outwardly exerts patience while inwardly harboring doubt and resentment, it means the distinction between the pure and the defiled has not been emptied and feelings of hatred and love still persist. How then can you...?
With your mouth, you speak loftily of the transmundane realms of the Great Sage, yet you deny the existence of Buddha-lands and hold in contempt those who aspire to rebirth there.
This may be called deceiving Heaven and deluding men; you have willingly chosen self-delusion. How bitter, how bitter!

Furthermore, if you possess great capacity and strength, and harbor great vows, you should instead plunge headlong into the sea of birth and death, time and again, to practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva.
If you are free from fear and cowardice, then rebirth in the Pure Land is not something I am forcing upon you.

However, should you harbor concerns that the winds of this world are so vast that you cannot act as their master; or that the appearance of a Buddha in this world is so difficult to encounter that there would be no way to practice and study;
or that your power of patience is not yet firm enough to deliver sentient beings from the perilous places of the triple world; or that once this retribution-body has perished—
If one has not yet permanently severed birth and death and cannot endure future existence— fearing that since future existence still lies ahead, one will cast off this body only to receive another,
with the path before them vast and desolate, and their destination unknown— then to abandon the Pure Land and fail to be reborn therein is no small loss.
This Dharma-gate of the Pure Land appears shallow yet is profound; it appears near yet is distant; it appears difficult yet is easy;
it appears easy yet is difficult. You shall know this for yourself in the future; for now, simply believe with earnest conviction. You should quickly exercise restraint over your speech;
do not indulge in the karma of the mouth, which brings calamity upon oneself and others, resulting in suffering and retribution that is endless.
An Examination of the Fourfold Classification of Pure Lands. Someone may ask:
A former sage once said that this single mind alone possesses four kinds of lands: first, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages; second, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder.
The third is the Land of True Reward Without Obstruction; the fourth is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
First, regarding the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, it is divided into two categories: first, the Impure Land of Common Abode; second, the Pure Land of Common Abode.
Regarding the first, the Impure Land of Common Abode, this refers to places such as Sahā. Those who dwell therein include both ordinary beings and sages. And...
There are two categories each for both ordinary beings and sages. Regarding the two categories of ordinary beings: first are evil sentient beings, which refers to the four realms of existence;
second are virtuous sentient beings, which refers to humans and devas. Regarding the two categories of sages: first are the true sages, which refers to those of the four fruits and pratyekabuddhas.

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the sixth stage corresponds to the ten abodes (shizhu). In the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), it corresponds to the final mind of the ten faiths (shixin). Although the delusions common to all three teachings have been exhausted, the retributive body (baoshen) still remains;

these are all termed "real" (shi). Second are the provisional sages (quan sheng), who are said to dwell within the lands of expedient means (fangbian), true retribution (shibao), and tranquil light (jiguang).
Dharma-body Bodhisattvas and Buddhas of Wondrous Enlightenment who manifest birth in the Land of Common Residence due to karmic conditions are all expedient manifestations (*upāya*).

Because these beings dwell together with ordinary people, it is called the "Common Residence of Ordinary Beings and Sages. Because the four realms of rebirth dwell together there, it is called a "defiled land.
Next is the "Pure Land of Common Residence," such as the Land of Ultimate Bliss; although its retributive rewards are exceptionally sublime, [it is still considered a common residence].
It cannot be compared to anything else; nevertheless, ordinary beings and sages dwell together there. Why is this?
Although the four evil realms do not exist, there are humans and devas, for those born in that land are not necessarily all individuals who have attained the Way. As a sutra says:

"Even those who have committed grave offenses can be reborn there by recollecting the Buddha at the moment of death. Thus we know that even those possessed of afflictions and defilements may [be reborn there].

This refers to the place where [the Buddhas] dwell. The nature of the dwelling of the Sages can be understood from the preceding description; however, because it is free from the four evil destinies, it is called "Pure.

Second, regarding the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*): this is the dwelling place for those of the two vehicles and the three types of bodhisattvas who have realized the path of skillful means.
Why is this so? If they cultivate the two contemplations and exhaust the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [they attain this stage].

Regarding the distinct delusions: when ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been severed, one abandons the body of segmented birth (*prātibaddha-śarīra*) and is born outside the triple world (*tridhātu*), receiving the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
This is precisely the state of transformation and change (*pariṇāma*). The land inhabited therein is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*), because ignorance has not yet been severed.
It is called "expedient" (*upāya*), for it is the dwelling place of those who practice through expedient means. Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "They have emerged from the triple world."
Externally there is the Pure Land, wherein Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born; they receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), which is not a birth through the stages of segmentation.
Regarding the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction: there are no followers of the Two Vehicles here;
it is the dwelling place solely for Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body. Having shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) and manifested the Dharma-nature, they attain the true fruit, yet [there is no...]
Wisdom is not yet exhausted; it moistens untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) and receives the Dharma-nature Reward Body (*dharmatā-nirmāṇa-kāya*), which is also called the Land of Fruitional Reward.

As the *Renwang jing* says: "The three levels of Worthies and the ten stages of Sages dwell in the Land of Fruitional Reward. This is precisely that. Because one contemplates the true aspect of reality, the Dharma is truly untainted;
thus, what is obtained as a fruitional reward is termed "real. Since the cultivation of causes is not fixed, form and mind are without obstruction.
Therefore, it is called the Land of True Reward Free from Obstructions; it is the same as what is called the Indra’s Net World in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Fourth, regarding the Land of Constant Quiescent Light: the principle of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma-realm, which is illuminated by the ultimate wisdom of wondrous enlightenment, is designated as a "land.
It is also called the Dharma-nature Land. However, true suchness and Buddha-nature are not a physical body.
It is not a land, yet it is spoken of as body and land; apart from the body there is no land, and apart from the land there is no body.
That which is called "land" has both a single phenomenon and two meanings: it is the place where Samantabhadra manifests and resides within Vairocana, named the Constantly Quiescent Light.
Of these, the first two lands are *nirmāṇakāya* (response-bodies), being the abodes of the *nirmāṇabuddhas*; the third is both *nirmāṇa* and *saṃbhoga* (recompense), being the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The Buddha’s dwelling is the fourth [dhyāna], which is purely pure and not a realm of response. Prajñā is called the Secret Treasury;
it is the place where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and dwell. It is eternally real and ultimate, the most supreme Pure Land.
Viewed from this perspective, what are called the lands of motes of dust are nothing other than the lands within my own mind.

Appendix: On Cause and Effect (Wang Longshu said: "There are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land; therefore, this appendix is attached to inspire faith.

General Discussion on Cause and Effect: The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states: "Within heaven and earth, the five paths are clearly manifest. Karmic retributions arise one after another and transform into one another."
One must endure it. Whether beautiful or foul, whether bitter or cruel, all is experienced by oneself. Who causes this? It is the natural order of things.

When good people perform good deeds, they proceed from joy to joy, and from light to light. When evil people perform evil deeds, they proceed from suffering to suffering, and from darkness to darkness.
The people of the world are ignorant of this; thus the evil paths are never-ending. Corpses revolve within them, life after life through accumulated kalpas, with no way out.
Renunciation is a great affliction; its pain is beyond words. One can only attain transcendence by practicing the Pure Land.
The *Zongjing lu* states: "When a single thought of discernment arises, one follows it toward good or evil, proceeding along the ten paths. First.
1. The path smeared with fire; 2. the path smeared with blood; 3. the path smeared with knives; 4. the path of the asuras;
5. the path of humans; 6. the path of devas; 7. the path of Māra; 8. the path of the Nirgranthas; 9. the path of the form and formless realms; 10. the path of the two vehicles.
The first nine types of mind constitute saṃsāra, like a silkworm binding itself; the tenth type of mind is nirvāṇa.
It is like a roe deer leaping alone: though it may escape for itself, it has not yet attained the Buddha-dharma. All this is due to the deluded mind being confused about this true realm.
Examining the five destinies and six paths of rebirth, excluding the asuras, they constitute the five destinies.
The *Zongnao lu* states: "The five destinies arise from the mind. The essence of the mind is eternally pure; although it pervades the five destinies, it does not receive their forms.
Thus, one may pass through the five realms of rebirth without falling."

The *Jiudao Zongjing Lu* states: First, if one’s mind is moment by moment exclusively devoted to greed, anger, and delusion—such that it cannot be restrained from returning nor extracted—it increases day by day and month by month, giving rise to the ten grave evils (*daśākuśala*) of the highest grade.
One who is like a *pañcāśtika* (a five-fold transgressor) has given rise to a hell-bound mind and is practicing the path of fire and brimstone. Second, if one’s mind...
In every thought-moment, one desires a vast retinue, like the ocean swallowing rivers or fire consuming fuel;

thus one gives rise to the ten unwholesome deeds of medium grade, such as Devadatta’s enticement of the multitude—this is the arousal of an animal-like mind that walks upon a path smeared with blood. Third:
if one’s mind, in every thought-moment, desires to gain fame and renown throughout the four quarters and the eight directions, being praised and extolled, yet lacks [inner virtue]...
In reality, though they possess virtue, they falsely compare themselves to sages and worthies.
To give rise to the ten minor evil deeds—as in the case of Mākaṇḍika—is to harbor a demonic mind and practice the path of the "knife-and-ointment" (the path of violence).

Fourth, if their minds constantly desire to surpass others at every thought, being unable to tolerate those beneath them, looking down on others while esteeming themselves—like a hawk soaring high and looking down below, yet outwardly proclaiming benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.
With wisdom and faith, one gives rise to a lower grade of wholesome mind and practices the path of the asuras. Five:
if one’s mind, in every thought-moment, delights in worldly pleasures, comforts this foul body, and gratifies this deluded mind, this gives rise to a middle grade of wholesome mind.

6. If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, recognizes that the sufferings of the three evil realms are many, while human life consists of a mixture of suffering and pleasure, and the heavens consist of pure bliss, and thus seeks the bliss of the heavens to subdue the coarse mind—this is the superior grade of wholesome mind that leads to rebirth in the heavenly realm.
7. If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, desires great majesty and power through body and speech...
8. As soon as the mind forms an intention, everything follows accordingly; this is the arousal of the mind of a lord of the desire realm, proceeding along the path of Māra.

9. If the mind, in every thought-moment, desires to attain sharp wisdom, eloquence, and sagacity, possessing high talent, courage, and discernment, such that one penetrates the six directions and is looked up to by all in the ten quarters;
this is the arousal of the mind of knowledge, proceeding along the path of the Nirgranthas. 10. If its...

The mind’s every thought is occupied with the five sensory objects and the six desires; external pleasures are but slight. The bliss of the third dhyāna is like a spring in a rock—its joy is profound within.
This gives rise to the Brahma-mind, practicing the paths of the form and formless realms. Ten:

If one’s mind, in every thought, knows that good and evil revolve in a cycle, that the ordinary person is addicted and immersed therein while the sages and worthies rebuke it, then one may destroy evil as if...
Pure wisdom arises from pure meditation; pure meditation arises from pure precepts. One should cherish these three dharmas as one would hunger or thirst.
This gives rise to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and leads to the practice of the paths of the Two Vehicles.

[Regarding] the Pañcālīyas and the Māgandikas, these are all followers of external paths. The path of Māra and the path of the Nirgranthas are both names for non-Buddhist (external) paths. External...
The Way has nine masters and ninety-five schools; is this not of that category?
Devadatta was one who enticed Prince Ajātaśatru to imprison his father, the King, with the intent to commit usurpation and rebellion.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "One creates the ten causes of habitual practice and undergoes the sixfold retributive responses.

As for the ten causes of habitual practice: first, the habit of lust; second, the habit of greed; third, the habit of pride; fourth, the habit of anger; fifth, the habit of deceit; sixth, the habit of guile..."
Seventh is the habit-energy of enmity; eighth is the habit-energy of views; ninth is the habit-energy of injustice; tenth is the habit-energy of litigation.

As for the sixfold reciprocal retribution: first is the retribution of sight; second is the retribution of hearing; third is the retribution of smelling; fourth is the retribution of taste; fifth is the retribution of touch; [and sixth is the retribution of mental cognition].
Sixth is the retribution of thought. The karma created by these six consciousnesses invites evil retribution that emerges from the six sense organs; each individually draws forth its own evil fruit.

At the moment of death, the spirit-consciousness falls into the Avīci Hell, where it perceives the two aspects of suffering regarding light and darkness, hears the two aspects of suffering regarding opening and closing, smells the two aspects of suffering regarding penetration and obstruction, tastes the two aspects of suffering regarding inhalation and exhalation, and touches...

One experiences the two aspects of suffering associated with union and separation; one contemplates the two aspects of suffering associated with non-awareness and awareness of sensation. The suffering experienced in each instance is immeasurable.
The *Zongjing lu* states: "Once the ten causes of habitual practice have been committed, how can the sixfold mutual retribution be avoided? All are but a single thought of evil."

The awakened mind gives rise to inverted perceptions, initiating a continuous stream of mind that functions according to worldly sentiment, taking objects as causes and forming provisional constructs.
Failing to observe with the eye of wisdom, one consequently falls into the karmic paths of ordinary beings;
though one may indulge one's desires for a single lifetime, one fails to consider how one’s body will sink for ten thousand kalpas.
Examination and Verification, Part Ten: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct by the common name 'fire of desire.
When Bodhisattvas encounter desire, they avoid it as they would a pit of fire. They designate excessive seeking by the common name 'water of greed.
When Bodhisattvas encounter greed, they avoid it as they would a sea of miasma. They designate arrogance by the name 'drinking the water of delusion.'"
The Bodhisattva views pride as he would avoid the vast ocean; he regards anger as a sharp sword. When the Bodhisattva sees anger, he avoids it as he would an execution.
He regards deceit and hypocrisy by the same name as slanderous thieves. When the Bodhisattva sees fraud, [he avoids it].
Just as one fears wolves and tigers, so do they regard deception as being synonymous with robbery and murder; when a bodhisattva encounters deception, they avoid it as they would a venomous snake.
They regard an enemy as being synonymous with a malevolent ghost that causes harm; when a bodhisattva encounters an enemy, they view them as drinking poisoned wine.
Holding wrong views is termed a "pit of views"; when a Bodhisattva sees various false and biased attachments, it is like entering a valley of poison.
Slander and calumny are termed "tigers of slander"; when a Bodhisattva encounters them, it is like being struck by a thunderbolt.
The habit of litigation leads to mutual clamor, which arises from concealment; these are equally termed "hidden thieves.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates concealment, it is as if bearing a high mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.

In the *Wanjie chenshen fayin*, it is said: When the Buddha passed through a melon field, he looked at Ānanda and asked, "Between the soil on my fingernail and the soil of the great earth, which is more? Ānanda replied, "The soil on the fingernail is exceedingly minute."
The great earth is inexhaustible. The Buddha said that those who obtain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail, while those who lose their human body are like the soil of the great earth.
Furthermore, when Sudatta was constructing a vihāra for the Buddha, there were ants upon the ground.
The Buddha told Sudatta, "These ants have already been on this ground since the time of Vipaśyin Buddha; now they have passed through..."
The seven Buddhas constantly took the form of ants and were still unable to escape it. Judging from this, how difficult it is to obtain a human body—like a speck of dust on a fingernail!
How could one not believe this to be so? Why is that? As the sutra says: "If the five precepts are firmly maintained..."

Only then does one obtain a human body. If one does not observe the five precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas is cut off. It is clear that since observing the precepts is difficult, obtaining a human body is not easy.
This is especially true when one commits the ten habitual causes, which are even more severe than the failure to observe the five precepts;
at the end of life, one falls into the Avīci Hell and undergoes the sixfold reciprocal retribution, which is far more than merely the difficulty of obtaining a human body.
...and that is all. That one’s body should sink for ten thousand kalpas—is this not indeed fitting?
(Returning to the text: I have carefully examined how the Ten Paths expand upon what was incomplete in the Five Paths, and how the Ten Habits supplement what was not exhaustive in the Ten Karmas.
Thus, as the causes become more numerous, the fruits become more dense; as the karma becomes more weighty, [the retribution becomes more severe].

The retribution becomes ever more profound. Thus, practitioners of pure karma must not hastily consider themselves satisfied simply because they have no one to rely upon in the five realms of existence or because they have not transgressed the ten courses of action.
Only by being able to contemplate the true mark of the mind can all manifold conditions be simultaneously stilled.
When all phenomena are forgotten, there is neither the Way nor karma; what precepts are there to observe, and what transgressions to commit?
It is precisely here that the so-called inconceivable merit resides. Alas, it is a pity that ordinary beings are greedily attached to these matters;
this is why the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have repeatedly issued earnest admonitions. Oh! How can one afford to neglect this?
The *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) states: "There are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land.
Now, how can one fail to believe in cause and effect? A sutra says: 'If you wish to know the causes of your previous life, look at what you are experiencing in this life;
if you wish to know the effects of your future life, look at what you are creating in this life. If you do not believe these words, why not..."

Observing the affairs of the present moment, we see that in human life there are the distinctions of wealth and poverty, nobility and lowliness, suffering and joy, toil and ease, honor and disgrace, longevity and premature death;
thus, the various forms of fortune and misfortune differ. Although these are said to be the decrees of Heaven, how could Heaven act with partiality toward individuals?
It is simply because the actions performed by people in their previous lives were different, and therefore they receive different retributions in this life.
They are also not the same; Heaven simply presides over them. For this reason, this body is called the "retribution body" (pāpa-śarīra).
A retribution body is so named because it arises as a recompense for what one did in previous lives. What room is there for Heaven to harbor personal intent?
Even in the worldly government, rewards and punishments are not meted out to people without cause; how much less could such be the case in the creative transformation of Heaven and Earth?

Is it not because calamity and fortune are bestowed upon people without cause? One knows that there were good and evil deeds performed in previous lives, and thus they are recompensed with calamity and fortune accordingly.
Because one cannot be purely virtuous, one cannot receive purely fortunate retribution;
hence there are those who are wealthy and noble yet suffer from misery and premature death, while there are those who are poor and lowly yet enjoy happiness and longevity. There are...
As for those who experience honor and prosperity or distress and disgrace, their retributions follow exactly what they have done, without the slightest deviation.

Thus it is said: "Planting peach trees yields peaches; planting apricot trees yields apricots. There has never been one who planted hemp and obtained beans, or planted millet and obtained panicled millet.
It is only that the time of sowing is brief while the time of harvest is long; therefore, the acts of doing good or evil at the time of sowing are very small [in duration].
The retribution for receiving fortune or calamity is exceedingly great. Thus it is said: "In spring one sows a single grain of millet; in autumn one harvests ten thousand seeds.
In human life, whether one performs good or evil, the resulting retribution is just like this. This is indeed the natural principle of the creative transformation (*zaohua*).
Furthermore, it is said: when people see good or evil deeds before them that have not yet yielded retribution, they consequently conclude that the law of cause and effect is not worth believing.
This is likely because they do not realize that the fact that good or evil has not yet yielded retribution does not mean there is no retribution;
it merely means it is delayed rather than immediate. The Buddha once said to Ānanda: "Why is it that some people who practice goodness in this life fall into hell after death?"
The good deeds of this life have not yet ripened, while the evil deeds of past lives have already ripened. Why is it that one who commits evil in this life is born in heaven after death?
It is because the evil of this life has not yet ripened, while the good of past lives has already ripened. Where that which has ripened is located, there one first receives retribution;
it is like a debt, where what is most urgent is repaid first. The Master of the Left (Zuo Shi) spoke of Lü Wuzi (whose name was Shu), who possessed—
Virtue can protect one’s children; thus, although his son Yan committed evil, he was able to escape calamity.
Yet Yan’s son Ying practiced goodness, yet Yan’s evil accrued to him. Consequently, despite being virtuous, Ying met with disaster.
To speak of what is visible before our eyes in this world, such is the retribution for good and evil.

How much more so across lifetimes! How can one, because the retribution of cause and effect has not yet manifested before one's eyes, come to disbelieve in causality, and by extension, disbelieve in the Pure Land?
(Reply: I have carefully examined this text. The preceding section discusses the constancy of cause and effect, while the subsequent section discusses the variability of cause and effect.
Yet, people today disregard and fail to believe in its constancy, while they rely upon its variability as a pretext for their own conduct.
Thus, it is no wonder they act wantonly in the ten evil deeds without a second thought. How lamentable!
Verification: *The Scripture of the Great Canon* states:
"In the past, King Cūḍāmaṇi was touring a forest park when he saw a golden cat enter the ground to the southwest. He dispatched men to excavate the site, where they recovered a bronze basin."
He filled it with gold coins. As he gradually traveled five *li*, the entire way was covered with gold coins. When the King saw this extraordinary occurrence, he thought he ought to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha then replied: "This is the karmic reward for the merit accumulated by the King in previous lives.
Long ago, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who placed his alms bowl at a major crossroads and spoke these words: 'If there should be anyone who...'"
"Those who give away wealth and jewels by placing them into this bowl shall become great wealthy men in the future.
A woodcutter, having received three coins, heard these words and gave rise to a heart of joy. With sincere devotion, he made a vow and offered them into the bowl.
Five *li* from his home, his joy increased all the more. The woodcutter of that time is the present King; it was because of the gift of those three coins [that he attained this status].
Through the retribution of merit, one obtains five *li* of gold coins and attains the rank of a king, receiving inexhaustible blessings.
The *Zongjing Lu* states: "For example, Aniruddha offered a single meal to a *pratyekabuddha*; later, when he covered an empty vessel, it was filled with a hundred flavors.
He obtained golden men that were regenerated even as they were spent. It is also like King Kanakavarna."

By giving a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha, one will later cause the entire Jambudvīpa to rain down the seven treasures for seven days, whereby the poverty of all the people will be forever eliminated.
Judging by these three matters, other cases may be inferred accordingly.
Is it not true, as the saying goes, that by sowing a single seed, one reaps ten thousand grains?
The *Zuozhuan* on the House of Lüan of Jin: When Lüan Ying of Jin was accused and fled into exile, he passed through Zhou. He took leave of the Minister of Ceremonies (*xingren*), saying:

"In the past, your humble servant Shu was able to exert his strength for the Royal House, and the King bestowed his favor upon him. His son Yan, however, has been unable to maintain the credit of his father’s labors. If Your Majesty does not cast aside the merit of Shu’s service...

[He then recounted how he had once saved the King from a fire, and that the King had granted him a fief, which his son had failed to protect. "I am now fleeing; I beg the Great Lord to grant me passage."
"I still have something to flee from. If I were to cast aside the power of my office and contemplate the crimes of Siyan, I am already a man deserving of execution.
I shall return to die at Weishi. Ying fled to Qi. The people of Qi received him at Quwo.
Its Grand Minister Xu Wu laid an ambush and feigned a banquet for the people of Quwo. Wu addressed them, saying, "Today we have captured Lü..."
"What do you think of this child? [The other] replied, "To obtain him and die for him is as good as not dying at all.
All sighed, and some wept. From this we can see, in general, the virtue of Wuzi and the wickedness of Ying.
As for Ying’s arrogance, extravagance, and addiction to wine, what more need be said? This extends even to [his son] Ying.
That virtue is sufficient to move others can be further evidenced by those who wept or sighed [at his death].

Thus, it is clear that while the virtue of Wuzi was sufficient to shield [his son] Ying, the evil of Ying was such that it accumulated until it became full; it is evident that he did not follow his father’s example.
The *Xiaoyinguo shuo* (Discourse on Minor Causes and Effects) states: "There are those who repair bridges and those who destroy bridges;
these are minor causes for [rebirth in] heaven or hell. There are those who ride in sedan chairs and those who carry them; these are minor effects of heaven or hell.
One may extend this principle to all similar categories, and it will be evident to all. Constantly maintain such a mindset while practicing the cultivation of the Pure Land. Above.
One is reborn in the higher realms; how could there be any further doubt? The *Zongjing Lu* states:
"Fine food and brocade robes versus tattered clothes and coarse herbs; the humble mat-door and the golden palace;

a thousand horses and a single gourd-bowl—all are created by the very first thought. As soon as the traces of the mind appear, the retribution is difficult to escape. Thus, because of transgression...
Past good and evil serve as the cause; present suffering and pleasure are the fruit. There is not the slightest degree of confusion between them—whom can they escape?

It is an inevitable principle, like an echo following a sound or a shadow following a form. Only by awakening to the Way and being dispelled by the power of meditative concentration can one transcend them.
If one dwells amidst the illusions of the world, how could there be anyone able to escape? As a verse in a sutra says: "Provisional..."
"Even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created will not be forgotten; when the causes and conditions meet, one must personally undergo the retribution.
Thus, it is said in the *Caimitun* (Treatise on Talent and Fate): "The poor have no land even for the point of a cone, while Diaoyi possessed fields exceeding a thousand qing."
The starving man has no store of even a dan or a shi of grain, yet Li Heng’s trees were called his "thousand slaves. If one lacks propriety, they must perish;
why then did Jie Zhitui alone live so long? If one practices goodness, they shall be auspicious; why then did Tu Shao meet an early end?
An Examination of the "Treatise on Talent and Fate" (*Caimit lun*): The *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) states: "Sun Shu'ao served his state with total loyalty;

yet after his death, his son had no land even large enough for the point of a cone. The *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*) states: "Diao Yi held the office of Shangshu Lang (Director of the Imperial Secretariat), yet he did not cultivate virtuous conduct;
he possessed ten thousand *qing* of fields and a thousand male and female slaves. The *History of Wei* (*Weizhi*) states: "Hua... [text truncated]
Xin served as an official with such integrity and poverty that his family possessed no store of grain even sufficient for a single *dan* or a *shi*. The *Book of Jin* states:
"Li Heng planted a thousand *ju* trees, which he called 'a thousand wooden slaves' (*mù nú qiān tóu*). The *Zhuangzi* states: "The follower of the robber Di was nine thousand strong;
they roamed across the world at will, plundering and oppressing the feudal lords, yet [Di] enjoyed longevity. The *Commentary on the Analects* (*Lunyu Shū*) states: [as cited above].
Xiang Tuo became the teacher of Confucius at the age of seven, yet he died young.
The *Record of the Merit of Compassionate Heart* states: The Buddha said that there are two kinds of retribution for good and evil: the first is karmic fruit (vipāka).
First is the retribution of maturation: performing good or evil deeds in this life and receiving the resulting suffering or happiness in a future life. Second is the retribution of flowers:
performing good or evil deeds in this life and receiving the resulting suffering or happiness in this very life.
(Thus,) I have reverently examined the matter of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). That which people find difficult to know remains obscure and unnoticed;
yet as for the "flower-retribution" (*puṣpa-vipāka*), which people behold with their own eyes, they nevertheless remain stubbornly indifferent. What can one say of this? Alas!
How truly lamentable it is!

Regarding the ten wholesome karmas and their pure retribution, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The ten wholesome paths are the bodhisattva’s pure land. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, [beings there] do not meet with untimely death;

they possess great wealth; they maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); their words are truthful; they always speak with gentle speech; their retinues do not separate from them; and they skillfully reconcile disputes."
Their speech is invariably beneficial; they are free from envy and anger; and they perceive sentient beings with right view—such people will be reborn in that land.

Sengzhao said: "That their lives do not end prematurely is the retribution for abstaining from killing. That they possess great wealth is the retribution for abstaining from stealing. That they practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) [is the retribution for abstaining from sexual misconduct]."

Celibacy is the retribution for [the cause of] non-lust. Speaking with sincerity and truthfulness is the retribution for non-lying. Constantly using gentle speech is the retribution for non-abusive language.
Having a retinue that does not disperse is the retribution for not engaging in divisive speech. Skillfully reconciling disputes is the retribution for non-slanderous speech.

Ensuring one’s words are invariably beneficial is the retribution for non-frivolous speech. Because anger, envy, and false views are the most grievous afflictions of the mind, three [additional precepts] are established separately.

"Good. (Returning to the text,) I have carefully examined the terms "anger," "envy," and "false views. [The statement that these] "lose non-greed" must be a textual omission. Zhaoluo says that three distinct virtues were established separately;
the meaning of this is not yet clear. Some say that when the three karmas are not performed, they transform into the opposites of the three virtues. This has not [yet been verified].
To know whether or not [this is so]:
regarding the ten karmic evil retributions, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said that when one’s mind is bound by attachment to female form and does not let go, there is lustful desire; thus, all...
In the world, parents and children are born in succession without end; these are rooted in the greed for desire.

Craving the taste of blood and flesh, their minds nourish this craving without ceasing; thus there is the eating of meat. Furthermore, among all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, transformed, from moisture, or from a womb—they devour one another according to their strength and weakness;
these are rooted in the greed for killing. For instance, when a person eats a sheep, the sheep dies.
When one is a human, upon death one becomes a sheep; eating other sentient beings is likewise the same. Death after death and birth after birth, they come to devour one another.
Evil karma arises together with them, persisting until the end of the future. If it is thus, then greed for theft is the root. "You owe me my life; I shall repay you with your debt.
Because of these causes and conditions, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one remains constantly bound in fetters. This is killing.

Theft, sexual misconduct, and the three [other non-virtues] constitute their fundamental roots. By these causes and conditions, the retributive fruits of evil karma continue in succession without end.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "The sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. Even if they are born among humans,"
One receives two kinds of retribution: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness. The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
The sin of sexual misconduct also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born...
Among human beings, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, a wife who is not chaste and virtuous; second, being unable to have companions according to one’s wishes.
The *Record of the Merit of a Compassionate Heart* states: the *Record of Cause and Effect* says that there are three kinds of evil retributions for killing. First:
First is the direct retribution: receiving a body within the three miserable realms. Second is the residual retribution: if born among humans, one suffers from many illnesses and untimely death.
Third is the retribution of enmity: if the sentient being one killed is among venomous insects, one will inevitably be stung by them; if among humans, [one will suffer their vengeance].
"He will certainly meet his death.
It further says: A question was asked: "In the past, there were sentient beings who constantly dwelt atop mountains of blades and trees of swords;

their limbs and joints were severed and shattered, suffering bitter and acrid agony. By what offense was this brought about? The Buddha said: "Because in previous lives they made the slaughter of living beings their profession, they obtained [this retribution]."
This is the retribution. In the past, there was a sentient being who was once impaled with an iron fork by a cow-headed demon and thrust into a cauldron to be boiled until he was烂 (làn—putrefied).
He was then immediately blown upon to restore life, only to be boiled again. For what offense did this occur? The Buddha said:
"In a previous life, he slaughtered sentient beings, pouring boiling water over them to scald off their fur; therefore, he has received this retribution."
The *Pure Land Text* by the Layman of Longshu states: During the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Zhang Zhongkui who made his living by slaughtering chickens.
One day, he suddenly saw a person dressed in crimson driving a flock of chickens toward him to peck at his eyes from all sides. His two eyes bled profusely, and he suffered great agony.
Furthermore, Zhang Shanhe of the Tang dynasty made his living by slaughtering oxen. At the moment of his death, he saw several oxen speaking in human voices, saying, "You have killed us.
Greatly terrified, Shanhe told his wife, "I am now entering hell.

(Although there was a monk who urged him to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha so that he might immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land, this was due to the power of past wholesome karma; it should not be regarded as a standard rule.)

The *Water Repentance* (*Shuishan*) states: "Regarding the second precept against stealing, there were sentient beings who acted as thieves and constantly dwelt in the Snowy Mountains; they were blown by cold winds until their skin and flesh were torn and split.
The *Brief Essentials of the Vinaya* (*Lüyī yāoyuè*) states: "A sūtra records that one śrāmaṇera stole seven pieces of fruit belonging to the Sangha, while another śrāmaṇera..."
A certain śrāmaṇera stole the cakes of sentient beings several times, while another stole a small amount of rock honey from sentient beings; both fell into hell.
Therefore, a sutra says: "It would be better to have one's hand cut off than to take what is not rightfully one's own. Alas! How can one not be cautious?

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* records the case of the bhikṣuṇī Bāoliánxiāng, who secretly engaged in sexual misconduct. She claimed that sexual desire was neither killing nor stealing, and thus carried no karmic retribution;
consequently, her body emitted fierce flames and she fell alive into hell. Therefore, the sutra says:
To live through lustful desire is not as good as to die in chastity. Alas! Should one not be cautious? (The evil retribution for the three karmas of the upper body). The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The sin of speaking falsely also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans,"
One receives two kinds of retribution: first, being frequently slandered; second, being deceived by others.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their retinue will be estranged; second, their kinsmen will be base and wicked. The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three [evil realms].
The evil paths. If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, one constantly hears unpleasant sounds;
second, one's speech is frequently met with contention and litigation. The sin of frivolous speech likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil paths.
If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, no one accepts what one says; second, one’s speech is not clear and distinct.
A poem on the karmic retribution of verbal actions from the *Huashu* (*Book of Transformations*) says: "The retribution for the human mouth’s karma is no light matter;

Do not take perverse speech as your daily practice. To speak falsely is to treat the void as reality; Flowery words multiply a hundred names into a thousand. Blood flows incessantly from the lancet-stone;
Sins accumulated in the underworld offices have already filled their tally. One need not seek hell by plowing one's own tongue— It lies right before one's eyes."
The public case is quite clear.
Examination of the records states: Among the people of Kŭich’ŏng was Chuk Kisaeng, who possessed a ready tongue.
If anyone committed even the slightest fault or evil deed, he would broadcast it far and wide and further embellish it, turning non-existence into existence and making one appear as ten.
There are ten [reasons]. Taking what is suspicious as definitive; taking what is accidental as a deliberate offense; taking what is unavoidable as a superior achievement;
and taking what is an error as the actual truth. As for confronting them face-to-face and subjecting them to public humiliation—having practiced this for so long, they do not recognize it as wrong.
In middle age, he contracted the disease of a yellowed tongue, which compelled him to have others perform bloodletting on it.
He bled. Within a single year, he suffered from this ailment five or seven times; each time it occurred, he lost one or two *sheng* of blood, which became his constant state.
One day, while conversing with his disciples about the matters of offerings and libations to spirits and ghosts, he reviled them all.
Suddenly, he reached out with his hand and pulled out his tongue, scratching it with his fingernails until saliva and blood flowed profusely, like a butcher at work.
He was transformed into a pig-dog. Hundreds and thousands watched as he himself proclaimed his transgression, saying, "The karmic act of the mouth must not be committed.
After remaining in this state for over a month, his tongue withered; he was unable to eat and subsequently died.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: The sūtras record that a śrāmaṇera once mocked an elderly bhikṣu, saying his recitation of the scriptures sounded like the barking of a dog.
This elderly bhikṣu was, in fact, an arhat. Because he instructed the śrāmaṇera to perform an urgent confession, the latter narrowly escaped hell;
yet he still fell into the body of a dog. A single word of evil speech can bring such harm as this. Therefore, the sūtra says: "As for a man..."
Living in this world, the axe is in one’s own mouth; it is by means of evil speech that one cuts oneself down.

Alas! Should one not be cautious? The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* says: The Buddha said, "There was a foolish man who heard that the Way of the Buddha is maintained through great benevolence and compassion:
'When evil comes, respond with goodness. Thus, he came to revile the Buddha. The Buddha remained silent and did not answer, out of pity for his mad folly. He reviled him.
He stopped. [The other] asked, "When you follow someone with courtesy and that person does not accept it, what do you do with that courtesy? He replied, "I take it back.
[The other continued,] "Now you insult me, and I likewise do not accept it; you must take it back yourself, and it will bring calamity upon your own person."
(Reply: I have carefully examined the affairs of śrāmaṇeras; how could the words of the sūtras not be true? Alas!

If one inflicts harsh speech upon others, the calamity resulting is such as this. If one inflicts false speech, frivolous talk, and double-tongued speech upon others, what can be said of the transgression?
Harsh speech inflicted upon others is something clearly known by all people, and they still know how to avoid it; yet [to inflict] false...
Regarding frivolous speech and double-tongued speech directed at others, the person targeted may not even realize it; yet the harm inflicted upon them will surely be profound.
From this, it can be known that the calamities resulting from these [four karmas of the mouth] do not diminish in their severity. (The evil retribution of the four karmas of the mouth.)
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The sin of covetousness causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their minds know no contentment; second, they have many desires and are never satisfied.
The sin of anger also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first..."
They are constantly sought out by others for their faults; secondly, they are perpetually afflicted and harmed by others.
The sin of wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are born into a family of wrong views; second, their minds are deceitful and crooked.
The *Longshu Jingtu Wen* states: There were two officials who sought a dream at the temple of the Two Ministers (Erxiang) to inquire about their future careers.
That night, one of them dreamed that he saw a person holding a single volume of registers. Opening the cover, the person said:

"This is the future career of you, the official who came here with us. Look at it. It was a sequence of appointments starting from a minor official and ascending to the rank of Prime Minister (*zhāngxīn*).
Furthermore, there were "hooks" attached to certain positions. When asked what these hooks signified, he replied: "This official loves wealth;

for every single item of wealth he takes unrighteously in the world, there is a corresponding hook here. If he were to repent and reform his ways urgently, he could still become a provincial governor (*jiānsī*)."
Upon hearing this, the man did not dare to take property improperly again. Later, he indeed attained the rank of Surveillance Commissioner (*jian si*).

Furthermore, during the time of Immortal Lady He, there was the home of a District Magistrate (*zhubù*) where a "Celestial Scripture" suddenly descended; as its characters and strokes were illegible, they went to consult the Immortal Lady.
The immortal said, "The District Magistrate accepted ten taels of gold; this shall reduce his stipend by five years.
Judging from this, ill-gotten wealth is truly to be feared."
It is further said: Formerly, there were two monks practicing together. One performed meritorious deeds but was prone to much anger;

the other monk constantly admonished him, but he would not follow this advice. Later, the one who was prone to anger died. The one who had admonished him boarded a passenger boat and arrived at Gongting on the river.
The deity of that temple was extremely powerful and could converse with people. He spoke to the one who had admonished him, saying, "I am your companion..."
A practicing monk, because of his excessive anger, fell into this state as a deity. Someone offered him ten rolls of silk, saying, "Please perform a memorial service for me;
afterwards, you shall see me on Mount Xi in Hongzhou.
The monk followed these instructions and indeed saw a dead python on Mount Xi, one or two li in length. Such is the retribution for hatred and anger.
The *Lüshi ji* states: Once, there was a man who visited a monk together with Master Lü. At that time, the monk was lying on his bed.
[The visitor] saw a small snake emerge from the crown of the monk’s head; after a short while, it re-entered the crown of his head. He asked:
"Why is there this snake? Lü Gong replied, "This person must have been poisonous by nature and full of resentment;

its toxic energy has already transformed into this snake. After his death, it will undoubtedly become a snake. (This refers to the retribution for the evil karma of the three actions of the upper realm.)
(Reply: I have carefully examined the practice of the superior man (*śreṣṭha-puruṣa*). There is no good he does not perform, and no evil he does not eliminate.

Although he is not ignorant of cause and effect, what room is there for his own mind regarding cause and effect? Now, the virtuous retribution in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* is intended as a teaching for those who seek blessings;
the evil retribution in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is intended as a teaching for those who fear calamity.
Are they not all merely believers of the middle or lower capacities?

As for the common people, they harbor a heart of disbelief within and indulge in unrestrained conduct without any sense of shame or dread without; they deny cause and effect and reject both sin and merit.
The reward for good deeds cannot encourage them; the retribution for evil deeds cannot deter them.
I am at my wits' end regarding such people; alas, how lamentable it is!
Regarding the verification of this, the *Mingzong ji* states:
During the time of Chan Master Baizhang, there was an old man who followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma. When the assembly withdrew, only the old man did not leave.
The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am no ordinary person. In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain."

Because a student asked a great practitioner of the Way, "Does one who practices the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect or not? he replied, "One does not fall within cause and effect.
Consequently, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes. Now I beg the Master to provide a substitute phrase on his behalf.
"May you be delivered from this wild fox body. The Master said, "Ask your question. The old man asked, "Does one who practices great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
The Master replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment and was immediately delivered from his wild fox body.
