Corrected by Master Lianchi Zuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
Compiled by Zhuang Guanghuan, a disciple of the Pure Land school from Jili Tongyi:
A Treatise on the Vows for the Pure Land,
stating that those who cultivate the practices of the Pure Land should make vows (the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* contains a precept against not making vows).
The *Direct Pointing to the Return to the Source* states: The Patriarch Cizhao said, "If there is practice without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary.
If there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty. To have neither aspiration nor practice is to dwell in vain within Jambudvīpa. To have both aspiration and practice..."
One enters directly into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is the very foundation for Buddhas and patriarchs to cultivate pure karma (*śukla-karman*).
Why is this so? Practice is guided by wisdom, and action arises from aspiration. When practice and aspiration are brought into equilibrium, wisdom and principle are fully prepared.
Now, aspiration is joy; it is desire. To desire birth in the Pure Land of the West and to delight in beholding Amitābha Buddha, one must necessarily make a vow.

Only then can one attain rebirth. If one lacks the mind of aspiration, one's roots of goodness will sink away. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Without generating the great vow, one is held fast by Māra.
All Buddha-activities arise from the great vow; therefore, if one wishes to accomplish the unsurpassed path, one must obtain the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
This is why Samantabhadra has an infinitely vast ocean of vows, and Amitābha possesses six [vows].
The Eighth Gate of Vows: This is the knowledge that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the ancient sages of antiquity all achieved *bodhi* through the power of their vows.
Examination and verification: The *Āgama Sūtra* states: "To the south of Mount Sumeru is a world named Jambudvīpa."
In that land there is a great tree named Jambu. Beneath this tree is a mass of Jambūnada gold;
because this superior gold emerges from beneath the tree, the tree and the continent are named accordingly. [According to the *Xin suopo lun* (New Sāṃbhava Śāstra), it is also called Jambudvīpa.
That land is narrow in the south and broad in the north. In this land there is a great tree named Jambū.
[The land of] Jambudvīpa. Its leaves are broad at the top and narrow at the bottom; the shape of the earth resembles this, and for that reason it is named Jambudvīpa.
The Sūtra says: "I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṃgha.

I now resolve my mind not for the sake of seeking the blessings and rewards of humans or devas, nor those of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or even the various stages of Bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicles, but solely relying upon the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna)."
I resolve to attain Bodhicitta, vowing that together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, we may simultaneously and equally realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
(Returning to the text: I have carefully examined this sutra; it constitutes the general outline for making vows, while the subsequent vow-texts provide a detailed enumeration of specific items.
The ears establish its substance; the eyes extend its function. To resolve to do so—this is nearly perfect.

The *Kaozheng San gui chumen* (Investigation and Verification of the First Gate of the Three Refuges) states: "Regarding 'taking refuge in the Buddha': 'refuge' (*gui*) takes the meaning of returning.
One turns away from false teachers and returns to serve the true teacher; hence it is called 'refuge' (*gui*). 'Taking' (*yi*) means to rely upon. Thus, one takes refuge in the Buddha."
One shall never again take refuge in other external deities. To take refuge in the Dharma is to turn away from false teachings and return to the cultivation of the True Dharma;
relying on what the Buddha has taught, one attains liberation from the three miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death within the triple world.
To take refuge in the Sangha is to turn away from the followers of the ninety-five kinds of heterodox practices and to take heart in the life of renunciation.
The companions of the right practice of the Three Vehicles, and those who have emerged from the birth-and-death of the triple world... [Fayi’s Commentary states:

According to the *Zhéfú luóhàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Subduing of Arhats), a son of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whose life was ending and who was destined to receive the body of a pig, went to the Buddha seeking salvation.
The Buddha taught him to take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; by diligently practicing the Three Refuges for seven days and seven nights, he attained [liberation].
He was spared from the womb of a sow and became the son of an elder. Furthermore, the *Mukhaṇḍika-sūtra* states that the Buddha told King Virūḍhaka:
"If one pierces mukhaṇḍika seeds while reciting the names of the Triple Gem, one shall sever the karma of fetters and attain the unsurpassed fruit.
Thus, we know that the Triple Gem is the place of refuge for all sentient beings.
The *Scripture on the Meritorious Retribution of Humans and Devas* states: "On the path of humans and devas, the cultivation of merit is primary.
To extensively perform virtuous deeds is called the cultivation of merit; there will certainly be a retribution of merit."
The Ritual for the Four Teachings of the Śrāvaka combined with the *Fayi* (Unfolding the Obscurities) The stages of the Śrāvaka are divided into two:

the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*) and the noble (*ārya*). The ordinary are further divided into two: the outer ordinary and the inner ordinary. Their bodies still abide in the outflows (*āsrava*), and the noble path has not yet arisen.

All are designated as "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). Those who are ordinary beings on the outside have not yet seen the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and still remain outside the realm of principle.

Those who are ordinary beings on the inside gradually see the nature of phenomena, for their minds roam within the realm of principle. Within the category of ordinary beings on the outside, there are three subdivisions.

First is the stage of the five stabilizing mental states (*pañca-vastūni*): those with excessive greed practice the contemplation of impurity; those with excessive anger practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion; those with excessive distraction practice the contemplation of counting the breaths. [Those who are] deluded...
1. Contemplation on the causal conditions of delusion greatly obstructs the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha. 2. The distinct objects of mindfulness are the four foundations of mindfulness:
mindfulness of the body as impure, mindfulness of sensation as suffering, mindfulness of the mind as impermanent, and mindfulness of phenomena as non-self. 3.
The general mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) consist of reflecting that the body is impure, and further reflecting that the body is suffering, impermanent, and non-self;
the same applies to sensation, mind, and phenomena. The three categories above are called the outer ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana). As for the four inner ordinary beings:

These are: Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Regarding "Heat": from the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), the wholesome root of heat arises.

It fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). It gives rise to a concordant understanding, subdues the afflictions and delusions, and attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
It is like the initial heat when drilling wood for fire, or the first signs of warmth before spring; hence it is called "Heat. Regarding "Summits": it employs...
The contemplation is as before, but it becomes increasingly clear and lucid, like looking from a high vantage point over a great distance; this is called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

As for "patience" (*kṣānti*), it means to endure, and also carries the sense of acceptance. It is divided into lower, middle, and upper levels. In the lower patience, one views the eight truths universally and cultivates thirty-two aspects.
In the middle patience, these are gradually reduced until reaching the upper patience, where there is only one aspect for three moments.
This is called "Patience" (kṣānti). Regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma): from the two moments of the preceding Patience, one moment has ended;
while one moment still remains within Patience, when that final moment of mind also ends, one immediately enters the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
"Mundane" (loka) refers to that which is with outflows (sāsrava); being the most excellent within the mundane world, it is called "Supreme" (agra). These four stages constitute...

The inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). These seven stages of skillful means (*upāya*) are the steps for entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*). Beyond these lie the teachings and meanings pertaining to the noble stages.

The noble stages are divided into three: first, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is the first fruit; second, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which comprises the second and third fruits; and third, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), which is the fourth fruit.
First is the *srotāpanna*, here translated as "Stream-enterer. In this stage, one eliminates eighty [afflictions] of the three realms.
The eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are afflictions of view. Because one perceives the ultimate truths (*satya*), it is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Second, the *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner); this is translated as "One who Comes Once. In this stage, among the nine grades of cultivation-delusions (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm, six grades have been completely severed, while the remaining three grades still persist;
therefore, one returns once more. Third, the *Anāgāmin* (Non-returner); this is translated as "One who Does Not Return. In this stage, [the remaining defilements] are severed...

When the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm are exhausted, one proceeds to sever the afflictions of the upper eight stages; these two phases are called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Fourth is the Arhat, here translated as "One Beyond Training" (*aśaikṣa*). In this stage, both the afflictions of views and those of cultivation are completely severed, and the fetters of the "son" [the afflictions] have been cut.

When the fetters of the fruit still remain, it is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is termed the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). Such is the case for the Śrāvaka. The *Yongjia ji* states:
"Because they attain awakening and understanding through the sound of the teachings, they are called Śrāvakas.

Examining what they cultivate, the Four Noble Truths constitute their fundamental practice. Seeing suffering, they constantly harbor weariness and detachment; severing the origin [of suffering], they always stand in fear of it."
Having given rise [to the aspiration for awakening], they realize cessation and alone accord with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). In cultivating the path, they discuss only their own deliverance.

Their great vow has not become universal; the way of establishing transformation is not yet bestowed. The reverence of the six harmonies is empty, and the compassion for the three realms is not exercised.

Because they deviate from the myriad practices, the fruit lacks the perfect and eternal. Since the six perfections have not been cultivated, what category could they belong to other than that of the Lesser Vehicle? Thus it is said:
This is the path of the śrāvaka. Regarding the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), it states:
"Pratyekabuddha" is here translated as "Pratyaya-buddha" (Condition-enlightened) and also as "Viviktaka-buddha" (Solitary-enlightened).

"Solitary" refers to those who awaken by themselves alone; "condition-enlightened" refers to those who awaken based upon the teachings. There are two categories within the Solitary-enlightened: among them, those of sharp faculties...

It is said that the *qilin* (unicorn) serves as a metaphor. This metaphor refers to the *rishi* (solitary realizer) who appears alone in a world without a Buddha; seeing the transformation of phenomena, they personally realize non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Those of duller faculties are called *vargacārin* (group-practitioners); they also appear in a world without a Buddha, traveling in groups and training their disciples and followers.

Those who are *pratyekabuddhas* rely on the Buddha’s teaching to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and effect the cessation of the cycle of transmigration.
Second, those who contemplate phenomena. The *Sìjiàoyí* states: "Pratyekabuddhas encounter a Buddha appearing in the world and receive the teaching of the twelve links of dependent origination;
this differs from the previous [teaching of] the Four Truths only in its expansion and contraction. These are: ignorance, volitional formations, and craving."
Grasping and existence—these five factors combined constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The seven factors constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

A Pratyekabuddha first contemplates the Truth of Origination, namely: "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*)," and so on, up to "conditioned by birth are old age and death."
This is how they arise. As for their cessation: when ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; and so on, until birth ceases, then aging and death cease.
Because they awaken to the principle of the True Truth by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called *pratyekabuddhas*. They are also called *ekabuddhas*;
although these two names differ, there is no distinction between them in terms of their practice or stage. Such a person abandons the three realms [of existence], and as for the Śrāvakas...

The hearing is the same. However, the Pratyekabuddha gives rise to true, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); because the power of his merit is great, he is able to erode and eliminate the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
The Śrāvaka merely cuts off the active afflictions (*kleśa*) but does not erode or eliminate the habit-energies; therefore, the Pratyekabuddha ranks above the Śrāvaka. The *Yongjia ji* states:
"Because conditions disperse and the essence is realized as true, he is called a Pratyekabuddha. If one traces the origin of what he has practiced..."
Taking the twelve links of dependent origination as his fundamental practice, he contemplates ignorance and finds it to be emptiness;

he penetrates the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and realizes they are without volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Since these two causes are not his karma, how could there be any recompense for the five fruits?

With craving, grasping, and becoming free from blemish, what burden can old age and death impose? His mind is solely serene and tranquil; his intellect delights in purity and voidness. He dwells alone.
The solitary peak: observing that conditions disperse and cease, one’s benefit for others is not universal and one’s self-benefit is not yet perfected;
there is a surplus below and a deficiency above, being neither of those two types and situated in the middle. Such is the path of the Pratyekabuddha.
The *Bodhisattva Four Teachings Ritual* states: From the initial generation of the mind, one contemplates the Four Noble Truths and gives rise to the Four Great Vows.
The first section states: Regarding the Four Great Vows: first, "those not yet delivered shall be delivered. This refers to those not yet delivered from the Truth of Suffering;
they are to be delivered from the Truth of Suffering. "Suffering" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). There are two kinds of birth-and-death: first, [partial]...
First, *paricchinna-janma-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death). This refers to sentient beings of the six realms who undergo the formation and destruction of physical bodies in distinct segments.

Second, *pariṇāmi-janma-maraṇa* (transformative birth and death). This refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power who possess the three kinds of *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made bodies).
Although they lack the coarse retribution of segmented existence, they still undergo subtle shifts as causes transform and fruits migrate; thus, it is called transformative.

This is the transition of the realm of birth and death. If there are those who have not yet crossed over the suffering of the two kinds of *saṃsāra*, the Bodhisattva resolves their mind, vowing to enable them to cross over;
this is the vow "to deliver boundless sentient beings. Second, to cause those who do not understand to understand:
this refers to causing those who do not understand the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) to understand it. As for "origination," it is precisely the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The afflictions that moisten karma are capable of summoning and accumulating birth and death (*saṃsāra*); they also comprise two types.

First, the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) moisten the karma of fragmented birth and death (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), which is capable of summoning and accumulating the fruit of suffering within the cycle of afflictive birth and death.

Second, the afflictions of the abode of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) moisten the karma of transformational birth and death (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*), which is capable of summoning and accumulating transformational birth and death.
This is the fruit of suffering. If there are those who have not yet understood these two kinds of origination, the Bodhisattva resolves his mind, vowing to enable them to attain understanding;
this is the vow to sever the inexhaustible afflictions. Third, he vows to bring those who are not at peace to a state of peace.

Regarding those whose speech has not yet settled in the Truth of the Path, causing them to settle in the Truth of the Path is precisely that which serves as the primary and auxiliary paths for penetrating Nirvana.
This also consists of two types: first, to cultivate the primary and auxiliary paths by focusing exclusively on the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*);

this path leads only to the Nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), which is the exhaustion of suffering. Second, to cultivate the primary and auxiliary paths by correctly focusing on the Middle Way of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The Path. This path can lead to the Great Vehicle’s Great Parinirvāṇa.

If there are those who have not yet found peace in these two kinds of paths, the Bodhisattva resolves his mind, vowing to cause them to attain peace; this is the "Infinite Dharma-gates I Vow to Study.
Fourth, regarding those who have not attained Nirvāṇa, he causes them to attain Nirvāṇa; that is to say, he causes those who have not yet attained the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) to attain it.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The Truth of Cessation refers to the cessation of karma and afflictions, and the cessation of the fruit of suffering that is birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

It is also of two kinds: first, the cessation of the karma of fragmented birth and death (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) and the afflictions of the four stages of dwelling (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), whereby the fruit of suffering of fragmented birth and death is extinguished;
this is the Truth of Cessation attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Second, [the cessation of] transformative birth and death (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*).
When the afflictions of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) are extinguished, the fruit of suffering—the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*)—is likewise extinguished.
This is the ultimate Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is unique to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
If there are those who have not yet attained these two kinds of Truth of Cessation, the Bodhisattva resolves to bring about their attainment; this is the Buddha-way.
The above refers to the fulfillment of the vow. Having already resolved the mind (*cittotpāda*), one must practice the deeds to fulfill that vow.

For three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one cultivates the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and plants the seeds for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred eons. The *Yongjia ji* states:

"If the mind has no object of focus, yet is able to benefit sentient beings, its compassion is most great; it is not constrained by views of attachment, and both person and phenomena are [transcended]."
Because they are empty, they are called Bodhisattvas. Examining the source of their practice, the six perfections constitute the direct cause.

In practicing generosity, they exhaust their lives and give away their wealth; in maintaining precepts, they do not commit even a *duṣkṛta* offense; in practicing patience, they deeply realize the absence of self.
What harm is there in cutting [the body]? Through *vīrya* (diligence), one ardently seeks the Ultimate Way without a moment’s interruption.

Through *dhyāna* (meditation), body and mind are tranquil and still, as subtle as *ānāpāna* (breath). Through *prajñā* (wisdom), one thoroughly understands dependent origination and that self-nature is unborn.

One extensively cultivates the myriad practices and impartially contemplates all directions—reaching down to the conditions of the Truths and encompassing upward the Unshared [Buddha-qualities]. Great!

The vow of the mind universally covers all; the path of the four means of integration gathers all within its reach. Compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem; merit and insight provide dual adornment.
Transcending the two vehicles, it stands alone at the summit. Such is the Way of the Mahāyāna.
As for the various stages of the provisional vehicle, those bodhisattvas who are still śrāvakas of the two vehicles and have not yet attained perfect realization are not [true] Mahāyānists.
This refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle.

The *Huangbo Xinyao* (The Essential Teachings of Huangbo) of the Supreme Vehicle states: "If the Tathāgata were to preach the true Dharma of the One Vehicle, sentient beings would not believe it and would sink into the sea of suffering.
If he were to say nothing at all, they would fall into stinginess and greed. [Thus, he does not fail to act for their sake.]
Sentient beings have largely abandoned the wondrous Way; thus, [the Buddha] established skillful means and preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

These vehicles have their great and small, and their attainments have their shallow and deep; yet none of these are the fundamental nature. Therefore, it is said: "There is only the One Vehicle Way; the other two are not the truth.
Nevertheless, they ultimately cannot manifest the Dharma of the One Mind. Thus, he summoned Kāśyapa and separately entrusted to him the One Mind.
The teaching that transcends words: let this single branch stand apart. If one attains realization through it, one shall reach the Buddha-way. *Zongjing Lu* states:
"When the blind touch an elephant, each claims to have seen the whole animal.
He who touches the tusk says the elephant's shape is like a radish; he who touches the ear says the elephant's shape is like a winnowing basket; he who touches the trunk..."
That which touches the trunk is said to have an elephant-like form resembling a pestle; that which touches the feet is said to have an elephant-like form resembling a mortar;
that which touches the belly is said to have an elephant-like form resembling a bed. Apart from these various parts, there is no separate elephant; it is merely not the whole body of the elephant.
One cannot see an elephant merely by speaking of it. If one wishes to see the elephant in its entirety, can it be anyone other than one with clear vision?

Now, although the Four Truths of the Śrāvakas, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Six Perfections of the Bodhisattvas are all aspects of the Buddha-dharma, they are ultimately not the entirety of the Buddha-way; thus, they cannot be called "Buddha."
If one wishes to attain the complete embodiment of a Buddha, it can only be through the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "To arouse the bodhicitta is to arouse the mind of great compassion."
One generates the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) for the sake of universally rescuing all sentient beings.

One generates the mind of peace and happiness for the sake of equally benefiting all the world. One generates the mind of benefit for the sake of causing all sentient beings to extinguish all sufferings.
One generates the mind of compassion for the sake of causing all sentient beings to depart from unwholesome dharmas. For those who are afraid, one protects them all.
One generates the unimpeded mind because one protects [all beings]. One generates the vast mind because one abandons and leaves behind all obstacles.
One generates the boundless mind because it is equal to the realm of empty space, reaching everywhere without exception.
One generates the expansive mind because one perceives all Tathāgatas. One generates the mind of wisdom.
Because it universally enters the ocean of all wisdom. This is called the arousal of the bodhicitta. The *Zongjing lu* says:
"In the ocean there is a treasure named 'Treasury of Jewels' (*ratnanidhi*), which universally manifests all manner of adornments within the sea.
The jewel of bodhicitta is likewise; it universally manifests all the various adornments of the ocean of omniscience."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Commentary of Master Padmasambhava states:
*An* means "without" (*am*); *uttara* means "above" (*upari*); *samyak* means "correctly equal" (*samyak-sama*); and *saṃbodhi* means "perfect awakening" (*saṃbuddha*).
Thus, it refers to "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal Perfect Awakening. The Sub-commentary states: "It is the ultimate, final fruit, as opposed to the lower [stages]."

It is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in contrast to that which is inferior. It is called "right" (*samyak*) in contrast to that which is erroneous, as it correctly contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

It is called "equal" (*sama*) in contrast to that which is partial, as it contemplates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) with equanimity; it is also called "universal. The term "awakened one" (*buddha*) refers to the luminous clarity of one's own mind.
The term "perfectly awakened one" (*samyaksambuddha*) combines the two meanings of "right" and "equal" mentioned above. Thus, he is called an "awakened one."
This is the unexcelled, perfect, and equal enlightenment.

Since all sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, possess Buddha-nature, Bodhi is fundamentally no different from the Buddhas and sentient beings. Obscured by ignorance, they consequently fall into delusion and falsehood;
this is "erroneous awakening" and cannot be called "correct. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas merely destroy [false] views.
Contemplation: Although they have attained Bodhi, their path is not yet centered; this is but a partial awakening and cannot be called "equal.
All Bodhisattvas have exhausted the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*) but have not yet exhausted ignorance (*avidyā*);

although they have attained Right Equal Bodhi, the Buddha-way remains distant, and thus it is not called "unsurpassed. Only the Buddha alone has exhausted delusion and perfected awakening, like the full moon at night.
There is no awakening that surpasses this; it is called Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says: "Awakening cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind;
it is quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Because awakening extinguishes all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it is non-contemplation; because it is free from all conditions (*pratyaya*), it is awakening."
Non-practice is bodhi, because it is free from recollection. Severance is bodhi, because it abandons all views.
Detachment is bodhi, because it is free from all deluded thoughts. Obstruction is bodhi, because it obstructs all vows.
Non-entry is bodhi, because it is free from craving and attachment. Accordance is bodhi, because it accords with the Tathāgata. Abiding is...
Enlightenment is so called because it abides in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). It is the arrival at enlightenment because it reaches the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Non-duality is enlightenment because it is free from the mind and its objects. Equality is enlightenment because it is equal to empty space. Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is enlightenment.
Because it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing, this is known as bodhi. Because it understands the mental activities of sentient beings, it is non-convergence;
because the sense bases do not converge, it is non-convergence. It is non-union, because it is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
It is placeless, because it has no form or color. It is a provisional name, because names are empty. Thus...
Transformation is bodhi, because it is free from grasping and rejecting. Non-existence is bodhi, because it is eternally quiescent.
Perfect stillness is bodhi, because its nature is pure and serene. Non-grasping is bodhi, because it is detached from objective conditions.
Non-duality is bodhi, because all dharmas are equal. Incomparability is bodhi, because there is nothing with which it can be compared. It is subtle and wondrous.
This is bodhi. Because all dharmas are difficult to know... Sengzhao says: That which is the ultimate of the Way is called bodhi;
it is surely the true wisdom of correct awakening that is without marks.
Appendix: The Initial Gate of the Four Noble Truths The term *satya* (truth) takes "thoroughly verifying reality" as its meaning.

This Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths is specifically for the sake of *śrāvakas*, who generate understanding through hearing; therefore, they must rely on the teachings to elucidate the principle.

Now, to clarify that the teaching and the principle are not in vain, it is called "thoroughly verifying reality. 1. The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Suffering takes "oppression and affliction" as its meaning.
I. The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): All conditioned mental formations are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence;
therefore, it is called the Truth of Suffering. II. The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): "Origination" has the meaning of gathering and accumulating.

If the mind is associated with fetters and karma, it will certainly gather and accumulate the suffering of birth and death in the future; therefore, it is called the Truth of Origination. III. Cessation (*nirodha*)...

Regarding the Truths: "Cessation" (nirodha) takes the meaning of extinction through non-being as its definition. Once karmic bonds and activities are exhausted, one is free from the afflictions and entanglements of birth and death;

therefore, it is called cessation. If one gives rise to the untainted, true illumination that perceives and contemplates [the truths] and thereby severs the bonds, then all ninety-eight latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the three realms are extinguished.
Because the afflictions, bonds, and latent tendencies are extinguished, the karma of the three realms [is likewise extinguished].
It is also extinguished. If the karma and afflictions of the three realms are extinguished, this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).
Because the cause is extinguished, the fruit is extinguished; when one relinquishes this retribution-body (*vipākakāya*), future fruits of suffering will never again continue.

This is called entering *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder), the true extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Fourth, regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): the path is that which is able to...
"Penetration" (*prativedha*) is the meaning. The true path (*samyag-mārga*) and the auxiliary path (*pakṣya-mārga*) support one another to enable penetration to *nirvāṇa*;

therefore, they are called "paths. The true path consists of the actual contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and the practice of wisdom that takes principle as its object.
As for the auxiliary path, it refers to the various methods of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) within the context of attaining liberating contemplation.
And all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) serve as aids to the Path; they are thoroughly determined and not false, and are thus the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The *Fourfold Teaching Ritual* (*Sijiaoyi*) states: "Within the Four Truths, there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.

The first two truths constitute mundane cause and effect—namely, suffering as the cause and origination as the effect. The latter two truths constitute supramundane cause and effect—namely, cessation as the effect..."
The Path is the cause. Question: For what reason are there former fruits and later causes regarding the mundane and supramundane? Answer: Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull;

they know suffering and sever the origin [of suffering], and they cultivate the causes out of a longing for the fruit. It is for this reason that it is so. [Combining] seven factors constitutes the thirty-seven wings of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*):

first, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); second, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); third, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); fourth, [the five faculties (*indriya*)].

The five faculties (pañcendriya), the five [powers] (pañca bala), the six [bases], the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga). First, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni):

first, the foundation of mindfulness of the body; second, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; third, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
2. The Four Right Efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*). First: with single-minded diligence and vigor, one strives to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen. Second:

with single-minded diligence and vigor, one strives to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising. Third: with single-minded diligence and vigor, one strives to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
Fourth: with single-minded diligence and vigor, one strives to increase wholesome states that have already arisen.

Progressing to the third and fourth [categories], the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: first, the base of power of desire; second, the base of power of diligence; third, the base of power of mind;

and fourth, the base of power of contemplation. Regarding the subsequent four, five, six, and seven, they are all seen in the *Āmítuó jīng kǎozhèng* (Examination and Verification of the Amitābha Sūtra).
As for the three gates of liberation, see the "Chapter on Cultivating Dhyāna" where the essential doctrine is clarified.
Critical Examination of the Text:
A Vow for the Western Land (Composed by Master Lianchi) I prostrate before the Great Teacher who receives and guides sentient beings To the Land of Peace and Bliss in the West.
I now make this vow, aspiring to be reborn there; may you, out of your compassion, graciously accept me, [Name] and the assembly of disciples.

For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the beings of the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, and in order to seek the unsurpassed Bodhi-path of the One Vehicle of all Buddhas, we single-mindedly hold in mind the vast name of Amitābha Buddha, which embodies his myriad virtues.
I aspire to be born in the Pure Land. Yet, because my karma is heavy and my merit is slight, my obstructions are deep and my wisdom shallow;

defiled thoughts easily flare up, while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish. Now, before the Buddha, I raise my five limbs in diligent prostration, lay bare my single mind, and offer this sincere repentance.
From myself and all sentient beings, throughout kalpas past until the present, we have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind.

We have indulged in greed, anger, and ignorance, defiling the three karmas with immeasurable and boundless sinful stains and immeasurable and boundless karmic debts of enmity. May they all be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, I establish a profound vow to distance myself from unwholesome dharmas and swear never to create them again; I shall apply myself with diligence.
I shall cultivate the Noble Path. I vow not to regress; I vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment; I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Amitābha Buddha, through the power of your compassionate vows, shall bear witness to me, shall have pity on me, and shall bestow your grace upon me.
May I, within the midst of meditative contemplation and during the state of dream, behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha and traverse...
In the land of Amitābha Buddha’s precious adornments, may I receive the consecration of the nectar of immortality from Amitābha Buddha;

may his light shine upon my body, his hand stroke my head, and his robe cover my form. May my karmic obstructions be spontaneously eliminated, my roots of goodness increase, and my afflictions swiftly emptied.
May I suddenly shatter ignorance and fully awaken to the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, opening wide in vast clarity and tranquility.
The true realm of light is constantly manifested before them. When the time of death approaches, they know it in advance;
their bodies are free from all illness, suffering, and calamity, and their minds are free from all attachment and delusion.

Their faculties are joyful and serene, their right mindfulness is clear and distinct, and they cast off their physical existence with composure, as if entering a state of meditative concentration. Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara and [Mahāsthāmaprāpta]...
Upon arriving at the assembly of all the holy sages, they emitted light to welcome us and extended their hands to lead us forth.
With multi-storied pavilions, banners, and streamers, and with extraordinary fragrances and celestial music, the sacred realms of the West were revealed before our very eyes.
All sentient beings who saw or heard this felt joy and moved by wonder, resolving to attain Bodhicitta. At that time, I mounted a vajra pedestal and followed behind the Buddha.

In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, one will be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within a pond of the seven treasures, amidst a sublime lotus flower, as the petals open, one shall behold the Buddha and see all the Bodhisattvas.

Hearing the wondrous sound of the Dharma, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). In a mere moment, one serves the various Buddhas and personally receives their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Having received this prediction, one attains the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). No...
Having fully accomplished hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates and all merits,
they will then not remain in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) but will return to the Sahā world. There, they will manifest countless bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions,
employing various inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers and skillful means to deliver sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement behind and regain purity.
May my mind be reborn together in the Western Land and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
As these great vows are inexhaustible—just as the worlds are inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible, and karma and afflictions are all inexhaustible—may my vows also be inexhaustible.

Now, having paid homage to the Buddha and made this vow, may I cultivate and maintain meritorious virtues and dedicate them to all sentient beings. May the four debts of gratitude be fully repaid and the three realms of existence be equally sustained throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Sentient beings together realize the all-encompassing Buddha-wisdom.

Examining and verifying the four debts of gratitude—toward parents, teachers, sovereigns, and benefactors—one does not forget the causes and effects of the three realms of existence: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Therefore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).
Its five parts are the two elbows, the two knees, and the forehead.
The *Sānchànhuì Tánjīng* (Platform Sutra of Repentance) states: "As for repentance, one repents of former errors; [one repents] of all evils previously committed."
Regarding karma: all transgressions such as delusion, arrogance, deceit, and jealousy are completely confessed and shall never arise again;
this is called "confession" (*chan*). Regarding "repentance" (*hui*): one repents of subsequent faults.

From this day forward, regarding all evil karma and transgressions such as delusion, arrogance, deceit, and jealousy, I have now awakened to them and shall forever sever them, never to commit them again.
To act [in this way] is called "repentance" (huì); thus it is termed *chànhuǐ* (repentance/confession).

Ordinary people, deluded and ignorant, know only to repent for their past transgressions, but do not know to regret their future faults. Because they do not regret them, past transgressions are not extinguished, and future faults arise again.
How can this be called *chànhuǐ*? *Fayin* says: The *Mingxiang ji* records that the śramaṇa Huída...

In the underworld, one beholds Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He says: "Whether you be a śramaṇa or a layperson, recognize the transgressions of your current body as well as the karmic offenses and various evil deeds of your past lives.
If you can fully disclose them before the assembly and repent with diligent sincerity, your offenses will be immediately extinguished.
Observe this, and you will know that the merit of repentance is immeasurable. Thus spoke the Bodhisattva.
Within both the hidden and the manifest realms, Śākyamuni taught people everywhere to repent for their transgressions. The *Zongjing lu* states:
"If one wishes to perform repentance, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, one directly realizes the mind of non-arising and attains liberation in that very place;

this is the great repentance. Therefore, it is said that severing delusions is the repentance of transgressions. Compared to other gradual teachings, it is like [a fine cloth] woven from layered threads."
A thousand catties of flowers are not equal to a single *liang* of pure gold. Regarding the two types of repentance in the *Sijiaoyi lun*:
first, repentance of phenomena (*shisong*); second, repentance of principle (*lisong*). What is discussed here in the *Tanjing fayin* is repentance of phenomena;
what is spoken of in the *Zongjing* is repentance of principle. For those who have not yet awakened to this principle, repentance of phenomena is urgent.
Regarding the method of stroking the head and covering with robes, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, you should know that Śākyamuni Buddha will stroke their heads with his hand and cover them with his robe.
The *Wǎngshēng jí* (Anthology on Rebirth) states: "During a state of meditative concentration, Liu Yimin of the Jin dynasty saw Amitābha Buddha with his hand..."
He stroked his head and drew his *kāṣāya* robe over him to cover him.
Regarding the numerical categories of the three bodies (*trikāya*), it is said: the *dharmakāya* is like the substance of the moon; the *saṃbhogakāya* is like the light of the moon.
The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is like the reflection of the moon. Regarding the three bodies of the Tathāgata:
Vairocana—translated as "Pervading All Places"—is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Rocana—translated as "Pure Fulfillment"—is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Śākyamuni—translated as "Able Sage of Silence"—is the Response-body. Huangbo said: "The Buddha has..."
The three bodies: the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is said to be the dharma of the self-nature’s empty penetration; the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) is said to be all pure dharmas;
the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) is said to be the dharma of the six perfections and myriad practices.
The preaching of the Dharma-body cannot be sought through speech, sound, form, or written characters. There is nothing preached and nothing realized; it is the self-nature’s empty penetration.

Therefore it is said: "There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called teaching the Dharma. Both the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) and the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) manifest according to the karmic responses of sentient beings.
The teachings they deliver likewise respond to specific circumstances in order to gather and transform them; none of these are the true Dharma. Hence it is said:
The retribution and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha.
The *Song of Realizing the Way through the Four Wisdoms* states: "The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence. The commentary explains:

"The four wisdoms are the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*)."

Regarding the grouping of the four wisdoms into the three bodies: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) constitute the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) constitutes the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) constitutes the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
The *Five Eyes Vajra Sūtra* contains the flesh eye, the celestial eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. Regarding the flesh eye:

it illuminates and perceives the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) through birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation. Regarding the celestial eye:
it illuminates and perceives the palaces of the various heavens, clouds, rain, light, and darkness, as well as the revolutions of the five planets and the two luminaries (the sun and moon).
It is also due to conditions. The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) illuminates and perceives the depth and shallowness of the wisdom-nature of sentient beings;
it is the condition for being born in a superior grade in a lower realm, or for taking up a physical form within the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

The dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus) illuminates and perceives that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) pervades the triple world, being formless and signless, exhausting all of empty space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); this is the condition. The Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) illuminates and perceives the Buddha...
Its light shines universally, without obstruction or hindrance, filling the ten directions. By following this light, one perceives its essence and knows that there exists the land of Nirvana.
If a person of superior faculties and superior wisdom can recognize the causal conditions of these five things, [they shall attain it].

Such a person is immediately named a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and the attainment of mastery over the body.
For details, see the "Chapter on the Supreme Fruits of Rebirth" in Volume One. The *Zheng'e ji* states: "The Way (*mārga*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are distinct from one another."
To see through with the eyes and hear through with the ears is *tong* (penetration).
To enter the realm of forms without the eyes being deluded by forms, and to enter the realm of sounds without the ears being deluded by sounds, is *dao* (the Way).

If one considers it merely as *tong*, then spirits possess *tong*, ghosts possess *tong*, and demons also possess *tong*; what connection would these have with the Way? To mistake such penetration for [the Way]...
The Way may thus lead one to fall into the realm of Māra and be born into the lineage of external paths; therefore, one must be cautious in all things.
Huíruì, the Chan Master of Sàpó, said: "If one’s rank is non-retrogressive and one has realized the fruit of non-arising,"

To dwell amidst desire yet remain free from desire, and to transcend the mundane world before one can give rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sahaja-karuṇā*), returning to the realm of afflictions to harmonize with the light amidst the five turbidities—this is the true path.

Yet there are those of shallow learning and limited wisdom who, having attained some minor merit, claim to have forever emerged from the four currents of existence and transcended the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). They disparage the Pure Land and cling to their own attachments.
"Sahā" [world]. With eyes covered, returning empty-handed, one wanders aimlessly as if lost, walking shoulder-to-shoulder with oxen and horses, following in the footsteps of hell-beings.
Not knowing who one truly is, one might compare oneself to a Bodhisattva of Great Power.
Viewed from this perspective, it cannot be said lightly that one has returned to the Sahā world.
Regarding the Dharma-realm that transcends the three realms: it does not undergo the cycle of birth and death. This refers to the four kinds of noble beings:
Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. These four noble ones possess the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*);
within and beyond the three realms, they neither abide nor do they not abide. In summary, there are ten dharma-realms, which function within human experience.
Minds differ; each follows its own karma and is gathered into the various realms of existence.
This is the chart of the ten dharma realms:
the Buddhas (by cultivating the six perfections and myriad practices, and by fully developing the three minds, attain the realization of the Dharma-body).
Bodhisattvas (who cultivate the sequential practice of contemplation and the six perfections to achieve the Great Vehicle Bodhisattva path);
Pratyekabuddhas (who cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas as essence and practice the path of the twelve links of dependent origination to achieve the Pratyekabuddha path);
and Śrāvakas (who cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas as objects and rely on the Four Noble Truths to practice the path and achieve Arhatship).
The various devas (born in the heavenly realms because they practiced the ten wholesome actions of the superior grade while also cultivating meditative concentration);
human beings (born among the human race because they practiced the ten wholesome actions of the middle grade, the five precepts, and the five constant virtues);
and asuras (becoming asuras because they practiced the ten wholesome actions of the inferior grade and the five constant virtues while desiring to prevail over others).
Pretas (due to committing the ten evil acts of the lower grade and being able to repent while performing them);
Animals (due to committing the ten evil acts of the middle grade and being able to repent after having performed them);
and Hell-beings (due to committing the ten evil acts of the upper grade and being unable to repent after having performed them).
The Patriarch Tianru’s Illustrated Explanation of the Ten Dharma Realms. The Patriarch Tianru ascended the seat and said:
"If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
all is created solely by the mind. This single verse encompasses the mundane and supramundane realms, as well as the states of both sages and ordinary beings, without exception.
Regarding what is called the dharma-realm: there are the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings, which together constitute the ten realms.
These ten dharma-realms have originally no self-substance and originally no self-nature;
they have neither seeds of their own nor roots of their own, for they are all created solely by the one mind. What is called "mind" is like the great void: it is fundamentally pure.
For what reason is it said that the dharma-realm is created solely by the mind?
To examine this mind: although it is called "unchanging," it also follows conditions (*pratyaya*). Because it follows conditions, it is said to be "capable of creating. As for following conditions:

it may arise from a single fleeting thought, or it may be triggered by contact with external objects; therefore, these are called causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). As soon as there is a cause...
Through conditions, it becomes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For example, the nature of water is fundamentally pure;
when it encounters the touch of wind, waves arise accordingly. Thus it is said that "water can create waves, and waves exist because of water.
So too, the mind can create the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm exists because of the mind. Such being the case, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) proceeds spontaneously, adorned with myriad virtues.
This is the dharma-realm of all Buddhas. That which perfectly cultivates the six perfections and universally encompasses the myriad practices is the dharma-realm of Bodhisattvas.
That which views causes and conditions with limitation and realizes the principle of partial emptiness is the dharma-realm of Pratyekabuddhas.
That which achieves mastery over the Four Noble Truths and returns to the lesser nirvana is the dharma-realm of Śrāvakas. [The text continues: Cultivating extensively...
The dharma-realm of the heavenly path consists of those who take the precepts and wholesome deeds as causes for outflows (*sāsrava*).

The dharma-realm of the human path consists of those whose defiled attachments do not cease and who are mixed with various wholesome conditions. The dharma-realm of the *asura*s consists of those with dull and stubborn minds who constantly harbor anger and strife.
The [dharma-realm] of the hungry ghosts consists of those for whom craving and views are the root and stinginess and greed are their karma.
This is the dharma-realm of desire. When craving for sensual desires does not cease and deluded thoughts arise recklessly, this is the dharma-realm of animals.
When one creates the ten causes of habitual action and undergoes the sixfold intersecting retributions, this is the dharma-realm of hell.
To speak of it extensively, there are various kinds of dharma-realms, all of which are constructed through transformation according to conditions by this mind. If...
If one can achieve single-minded non-arising and thereby attain clear understanding and realization, then the various dharma-realms will be empty according to that which has been understood.
Therefore, once the ten habitual tendencies are severed, the six mutual interactions do not arise; the mind of hell is thus resolved.
Once desire and greed are severed, deluded thoughts do not arise; the mind of animals is thus resolved. Once attachment and views are...

When stinginess and greed are severed, they do not arise; thus, the mind of a hungry ghost is understood. When the superior [defiled] mind is severed, anger and strife do not arise; thus, the mind of an asura is understood.
When attachment and defilement are severed, right mindfulness manifests before one; thus, the mind of a human being is understood.
By abandoning the causes of outflows (*āsrava*) and cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), the mind of a celestial being is understood. Not...
To grasp the Four Noble Truths without abiding in true emptiness is the fulfillment of the mind of the Śrāvaka.

To transcend the limitations of dependent origination and turn the mind toward the Great Vehicle is the fulfillment of the mind of the Pratyekabuddha. To bring the merit of the Six Perfections to completion and suddenly leap beyond the stages and grounds is the fulfillment of the mind of the Bodhisattva.
To perfect Bodhi and return to the state of non-attainment is the fulfillment of the mind of the Buddha.
Now that I have realized the mind within the six realms of ordinary beings, I must certainly have attained awakening without doubt.
But tell me: within the fourfold realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), in which realm does the mind that has thus been realized reside?
*Hè!* [He] descends from his seat. ○ The *Zuǎnlíng Jì* states: A certain person died and arrived at the gates of hell, where he encountered Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who bestowed upon him a verse.
If one wishes to thoroughly understand it, there are three lines, which are said as follows:

Reciting this verse can destroy the suffering of hell. Therefore, one should know that if one contemplates this mind, not only is the realm of hell destroyed, but even the ten dharma-realms are destroyed all at once.
The *Śīla-śāstra Fa-yin* states: "For one who aspires to reach their goal, the vow (*praṇidhāna*) serves as the precursor;
for one who fortifies that vow so as not to retreat, the oath (*samaya*) serves as the rear guard.
Therefore, the commentary refers to the oath as being within the vow. (Note: The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* contains precepts regarding the necessity of making such vows.)
O you of courageous and fierce resolve! Although I have made this vow, how could it reach its conclusion without a great oath?

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi, and who, before an image of the Tathāgata, burns a single lamp on his body, sears a finger-joint, or consumes a single stick of incense."
"I say that although such a person has not yet clearly realized the path to supreme enlightenment, their mind regarding the Dharma is already resolved.

Master Lianchi said: "Burning the body or the arms is frequently permitted in the Mahayana sutras; these are the deeds of great bodhisattvas who have attained patience (*kṣānti*), and are not within the realm of beginners.
Those who seek rebirth in the Western Paradise should be able to employ the burning of the arm [as a practice]."
If one applies such sincerity, devotion, and vigor to remedy one's evil habits, then those who succeed will surely be many.
As the ancients said, "To learn well from Liu Xiaohui"—is this not precisely the case?
(I humbly) examine that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take their vows as the ultimate ground.
Now, for those born in this defiled age who seek the Supreme Vehicle, they must possess a resolute mind;
and to give rise to a resolute mind, one cannot do so without a vow. Therefore, I have not followed the accounts in various sutras [such as the burning of the arm], but...
Regarding the rules for the vows of training as a Buddha or Bodhisattva: is one who studies the way of Liu Xiaohui thereby studying the Master Padmasambhava?
In verifying this, one should consult the *Āgama Sūtra*, which states: "A bhikṣu who does not make a vow will ultimately..."
One does not achieve the Way of Buddhahood. The merit of one’s vows is beyond measure; it enables one to reach the place of nectar-like extinction (*amṛta-nirvāṇa*).
Therefore, one must certainly make a vow later on. ○ *Fayi* says: Question:

A "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) consists of words of high expectation, while a "pledge" (*samaya*) resembles the language of an oath. Since the fundamental purpose of practice is intended for transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*), why would one [use such terms]?
"Called 'Hell'. Answer: "It refers to the fierce and violent intent within one's vows. 'Dharṣa' (呪呾) refers to the poisonous and harmful intent within an enemy.
How can one take a vow as an enemy, or regard fierce resolve as a poisonous harm?
In the world there are demonic teachers who instruct their demonic followers to close doors and block openings, using perilous speech to fortify their roots of faith. This is evil."
Chewing upon this to shut out external inquiries, one remains sealed and confined for a lifetime, caged and imprisoned through successive kalpas, unable to escape. How tragic!
Consider the virtuous student of Liu Xiahui and the man of Lu who dwelt alone in a room; when the neighbor’s wife was at her window at night—
Defeated by wind and rain, he sought lodging. The man shut his door and would not admit him.
The woman said, "Have you not heard of Liu Xiaohui sheltering the cold woman? The man replied, "It might have been acceptable for Liu Xiaohui, but it is not acceptable for me.

To adopt what was acceptable for Liu Xiaohui while persisting in my own unacceptability—this is why I do not. Thus it is said: "To learn from the acceptability of Liu Xiaohui while remaining in one's own unacceptability."
It is said: "One who studies well under Liu Xiahui [would not lose their integrity even if walking through a thorny forest].

On this day, the month, and the year [of such-and-such], the disciple [Name] respectfully makes a vow to cultivate the pure karma, establishing [this Western Vow Text]. (Compiled by the disciple Guanghuan). The disciple [Name] reverently... on the [day], [month], and [year]. I resolve to practice and maintain the pure karma. I establish [this vow].
I vow before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, saying: "I, disciple [Name], shall cultivate the pure karma. I pray that, relying upon the Mahāyāna, I may give rise to the bodhicitta.
I vow to emulate the act of burning my own arm, to develop a resolute mind, and to uphold the precepts of fasting and purity, practicing them daily."
Lesson: The Dharma of the Perfectly Penetrating School must aim for nothing less than the fulfillment of the Western Paradise vow before it may cease.
Otherwise, one’s emotions will shift with circumstances, ultimately leading to regression. To let this life pass in vain and to wander in saṃsāra for eternal kalpas—is this not truly lamentable?
From this day forward, if you violate your initial vow and fail to apply yourself with diligence, you shall be guilty of deception.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions will surely inflict retribution [upon those who do not practice]. If one attains rebirth there,

one shall see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma, fully realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and accomplish all merits, thereby becoming self-sufficient in one's own benefit.
If I do not universally deliver all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, it shall be as previously vowed.
Only the Buddha is all-illuminating; may He deign to witness this.
Again, he proceeded to...
Before the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, the Honored Deity who responds to the calls of the three continents and protects the Dharma (first the praise, then the vow):
Praise: General Vajrapāṇi, an emanation of a Bodhisattva, eternally guards the Dharma; the vows of the Buddha are vast and profound. With his precious mace, he subdues the demonic armies;
his merit is difficult to describe. I pray that you respond to the sincere devotion of this worldling.
The oath is as stated previously.
Regarding the examination of the three continents, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "To the south of Mount Sumeru is named Jambudvīpa;
it is also called Aparagodānīya. To the east of Mount Sumeru is named Pūrvavideha; it is also called Purvavideha."
Also known as Pūrvavideha; to the west of Mount Sumeru is Aparagoyānī, also known as Aparagodānīya, or Western Go-wealth.
To the north of Mount Sumeru is Uttarakuru, also known as Udyānavatī.
Regarding the four continents, why is it said that there is a response [of the deity] in only three continents? The *Fozu Tongji* states:
"In the northern continent, Buddhas do not appear; therefore, they do not hear the Buddha-dharma. Since the Buddha-dharma does not exist there, Vajrapāṇi does not go."
Therefore, it speaks only of the three continents. Upon examining the sūtras, there are Buddhas in all four directions.

Why, then, is it said that there is no Buddha-dharma in the northern continent? It is said: the statement that there is no Buddha in the north refers only to the Sahā world; it does not speak of the ultimate extent of the four directions.
Because there are immeasurable four-continent worlds, it is said that there are Buddhas.
The Honored Deity Vaiśravaṇa has lived for one hundred and seventeen lifetimes, being a *kumārabhūta* (pure youth) in each and every birth.
The merit he has performed is so vast that it cannot be fully recounted. He attained the Way during the time of the Buddha Ratnakusuma-vaidūryaprabha, and his name was...
The Bodhisattva Universal Eye attained enlightenment during the assembly of Śākyamuni Tathāgata and was named the Bodhisattva True Youth.
He held a vajra-treasure mallet weighing eighty-four thousand *jin*. He made a great vow:
"If this vajra-treasure mallet should break, then may my body as a True Youth be shattered. May I protect the Buddha-dharma whenever a Buddha appears in the world. [He has not been seen.]
Regarding the transgressions of monks and nuns: [the general] wears a helmet with phoenix wings upon his head, black boots upon his feet, and golden chainmail upon his body.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that each of the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings has eight generals who patrol the four continents to protect and assist those who have left the household life.
Among these thirty-two generals, General Wei is the most prominent.
Extensive Protection. When bhikṣus of weak spiritual power are deluded by Māra, General Wei rushes to their aid in agitation and eliminates [the obstacles] according to the occasion.
