General Discourse on the Chapter on Pure Land Precepts and Fasting:
The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states: "When I become a Buddha, may all devas and human beings who give rise to the bodhicitta and uphold..."
If one observes the fasts and precepts, practices the six *pāramitās*, cultivates all manner of meritorious virtues, and makes a sincere vow desiring to be born in my land,
then at the time of their death, I and a great assembly will appear before that person, leading them to their next life as a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression.

The *Longshu Jingtuwen* states: "If one fully observes the precepts and fasts, further worships the Buddha and recites his name, reads and recites Mahāyāna sūtras, and understands the primary meaning [of emptiness], and dedicates these merits toward rebirth in the Western Land, one will certainly attain the highest grade of the highest birth."
What is meant by "fasting" (upavāsa)? It is not eating meat, not drinking alcohol, not engaging in sexual desire, and not eating the five pungent roots.
What is meant by "precepts" (śīla)? Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these constitute the three karmas of the body. False speech...
Frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech constitute the four karmas of the mouth. Covetousness, malice, and wrong views constitute the three karmas of the mind.

Taken together, these form the ten precepts. To maintain them without transgression is the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). If one transgresses and does not maintain them, this constitutes the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*).
To fully observe the ten precepts ensures rebirth in the highest grade of the upper realm. If one merely maintains five...
To observe the precepts while cultivating the Pure Land also constitutes birth in the Upper Grade of the Middle Class.
For verification, see the Chapter on Vows in the third fascicle for *bodhicitta*,
and the Section on Gathering Beings through the Verses of Aspiration in the first fascicle for the six *pāramitās*.
The *Jingtu zhigui* (Guide to the Destination of the Pure Land) states regarding the reading and recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras:
"Mahāyāna sūtras are that which all Buddhas take as their teacher; the Buddha-fruit and Bodhi both emerge from within them.

The three types of pure karma in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, as well as the 'Highest of the High' rebirth, all state that the reading and recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras constitutes the practice for rebirth in the Pure Land. This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The *Avataṃsaka*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Nirvāṇa*, and other Mahāyāna sūtras that exclusively discuss the Pure Land should be upheld, recited, and chanted by those who cultivate pure karma.
Relying on the power of the Mahāyāna Dharma, one will certainly attain rebirth there. *Fayin* says:
"Reciting" means externally relying on the cultivation of hearing and internally supporting it with contemplation of the principle; it is not merely a matter of words, mouth, or ears.

This is what is meant. Some are so exclusively addicted to volumes of scripture that they no longer engage in meditative contemplation; they occupy themselves with them for their entire lives, like one who merely counts the treasures of others.

For this reason, although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra recited the twelve divisions of the sūtras and Tripuṭa recited sixty thousand dharma-aggregates, these two individuals did not cultivate the true Buddha-nature within the path of skillful means, nor did they contemplate the four [noble truths].
Those who harbor thoughts such as these commit a great crime of rebellion and both enter hell; this is what those who recite and chant should know.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "To recite with the mouth and practice with the mind is to turn the sutra; to recite with the mouth while the mind does not practice is not."
Since this scripture was first translated, have those who read and recite it not known this?
[End of] General Discussion on Observing the Fasting Precepts, from the Section on Maintaining the Fast.

(Reply: I have carefully examined the scriptures, which state that the Buddha said: "Observing a single day of fasting provides sixty thousand years of provisions, and furthermore brings five blessings.
Nevertheless, one must fully embody the Way before one may truly observe the fast.
As for the Buddha’s practice of eating only at midday—this is the Way. Is it the Way to eat after midday? As the Chan Master Duanji [Linji] said: [...]
To say that "the food of wisdom" is the Way—does the indulgence of the senses to seek flavors constitute the food of consciousness?
To say that the Great Master Zhiyi’s so-called "pure livelihood" is the Way—does sustaining oneself through improper causes and conditions constitute a wrong livelihood?
One must eliminate what is not the Way to exhaustively realize the Way; furthermore, it is by means of one who is free from desire.
If one maintains this, then is it not in this that the *Shi* (Classic of Poetry) refers to "receiving blessings from Heaven" and "seeking for oneself much fortune"?
Examining the evidence, the five blessings consist of: having little illness, physical ease, little lust, little sleep, and being born in heaven, thereby knowing one's past lives.

Regarding the timing of the meal: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that ten breaths constitute one instant (*kṣaṇa*). If the shadow of the sun has passed by even one instant, it is not the time for the midday meal;
this means one must not eat past noon. Furthermore, it says that if the hour of noon (*madhyāhna*) has passed by even the width of a hair, it is no longer the time for eating.
At that time, furthermore, Zongzhu stated that "time" refers to the hour of *chen* (9–11 a.m.). The *Vinaya-yao-lüe* says: "The various devas eat early;
the Buddha eats at noon; animals eat after midday; and ghosts eat at night. Monks should emulate the Buddha and not eat past noon.
When hungry ghosts hear the sound of bowls and alms-basins, fire erupts from their throats; therefore, they eat at noon.
One should remain in a state of stillness; how much more so after midday?

In the past, there was a high monk who, upon hearing his neighbor in the next room lighting a fire after noon, could not help but weep, grieving for the decline of the Buddha-dharma. People of today are physically frail and prone to illness;
those who wish to eat frequently may be unable to uphold this precept. Therefore, the ancients referred to eating late as "wan-shi" (late meal).
Regarding "medicinal food," this refers to the intent of treating illness. One must certainly recognize that such practices violate the Buddha’s regulations and give rise to great shame and remorse;
by eating little and not eating with a sense of attachment, one may perhaps be saved.
If it were otherwise, the transgression would be even more grave. Alas! How can one not be cautious?
Chan Master Duanjie said: "The body composed of the four elements is afflicted by skin sores and ulcers.
To provide for it in accordance with its needs without giving rise to greedy attachment is called 'food of wisdom' (jishi).

To indulge one's desires in seeking flavors, giving rise to false discrimination and seeking only what suits the palate without developing a sense of weary detachment, is called 'food of consciousness' (shishi)."
Jingming Xiyi said: "First, [eating] wild grasses and fruits in deep mountains; second, constantly practicing begging for food;
third, receiving offerings sent by donors; fourth, eating together with the great assembly. By means of these one sustains life, remaining undefiled."

Therefore, it is called "pure livelihood. First, "mouth-to-mouth" food-gathering, which refers to seeking favors from all four directions. Second, "corner-to-corner" food-gathering, which refers to various arts and calculations.
Third, "upward-facing" food-gathering, which refers to observing the stars and constellations. Fourth, "downward-facing" food-gathering, which refers to planting fields and orchards;
these are all wrong livelihoods by which one sustains oneself. As for what is mentioned in the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* regarding trade and commerce...
To engage in sexual relations with men or women, to assist in evil through incantations, to harm others with drugs, or to hunt with hawks—these constitute grave transgressions;
how could they be considered merely wrong livelihood? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are five types of wrong livelihood, all for the sake of gain and offerings:
first, feigning extraordinary qualities; second, boasting of one's own powers; third, divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy and signs.
Fourth, speaking in a loud voice to manifest an air of authority; fifth, proclaiming the offerings one has received to move the hearts of others.
To sustain one's life through such improper causes and conditions constitutes wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The ode "Jiale" (Joyful) in the Da Ya says: "Manifest and brilliant are his excellent virtues;
he is fit for the people and for men, receiving his mandate from Heaven. Furthermore, the ode "Wenwang" in the Da Ya says: "He forever accords with the Mandate."
"Seek for yourself much blessing.

The *Longshu Jingtuwen* (The Text on the Pure Land of Longshu) concerning the observance of the fast states: "Food, drink, and sexual desire—these are the great cravings that exist within humanity. Of these two..."

These are all places where karma is created. One uses the taking of life to provide for one's mouth and belly; one squanders one's innate truth through lustful desire. How can this not be the commission of sin?
Moreover, these two further assist and incite one another: because of fine food and drink, the blood and qi flourish; when the blood and qi flourish, lustful desire increases;
when lustful desire increases, it conversely damages the blood and qi; and when the blood and qi are damaged, yet again—
One relies on food and drink for nourishment; these two things thus create offenses for one another.
If you wish to restrain your appetite, you must first moderate your lustful desires. If you can moderate your lustful desires, you will then be able to restrain your appetite.
This is the way to secure the body and prolong life. If one truly understands these two matters, how could there be illness or premature death during one's lifetime?
How could there be any possibility of falling into the realms of hell or animals after death? Those who cultivate the Pure Land must not fail to observe this precept.
(Yet) to strictly maintain the fast while claiming not to engage in lust seems inconsistent.
Upon reading the writings of Longshu, I first realized that those who wish to observe the fast must absolutely renounce desire. Alas! As for the ancients—
The establishment of this precept—how could it be in vain?
The *Jieshu fayin* (Unfolding the Obscurities of the Precepts) states: "To speak according to the ultimate principle: when the mind harbors defilement, this is 'eating pungent roots' with the mind.

When speech is foul and evil, this is 'eating pungent roots' with the mouth. When one's conduct is base and vulgar, this is 'eating pungent roots' with the body. A cruel and harsh heart is [eating pungent roots] with the mind..."
To eat meat is to consume it with the mouth; it is the speech of the cruel and violent. To commit acts of poison and harm is to consume it with the body.

To weave delusions in a chaotic tangle, thereby losing one’s spiritual discernment, is to drink wine with the mind. To speak erroneously and perversely, confusing distinctions, is to drink wine with the mouth.
To act blindly and errantly, deviating from righteous principle, is to drink wine with the body. When these reach their extreme—
To speak of it: to relish the foul and miscellaneous flavors of the minor paths and lose the pure fragrance of the Dharma-body of the Great Vehicle—both are the consumption of pungent roots.

To be satiated by the solitary excellence of the Two Vehicles and abandon the flavor of the Dharma-joy of the Great Vehicle that benefits both self and others—this too is the consumption of pungent roots.
All who consume meat eat the flesh of the foolish teachings of the śrāvakas, thereby remaining ignorant of the wisdom of the Mahāyāna’s vast learning and profound penetration;
all who indulge in wine drink the intoxication of such folly. However, a bodhisattva at the initial stage of resolve should first attend to the precepts and only thereafter proceed to the principle.
Why is this? The principle and the precepts are profound and mysterious; were it not for the right person, one might cling to the principle while abandoning the practice, causing widespread harm.
Now, phenomena are identical with principle; the partial is identical with the perfect. The sacrificial vessels are fully arrayed, yet it depends entirely upon the person who employs them.

(Returning to the point: I have carefully examined the discourse on "Unveiling the Hidden" and "Exhausting Principle," which comprehensively addresses the three karmas without being narrowly confined to the trivialities of food and drink.
It speaks to the extreme extent of their deviation from the Way, rather than dwelling on the minutiae of eating and drinking.
End. Regarding Master Tiantai’s attainment of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: how profound and deep it is!

Examining the *Fǎxǐ Āmítuó jīng chāo* (Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* by Fǎxǐ), it says that the *Āgamas*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other texts speak of five supramundane nutriments (*āhāra*):
first, the joy of dhyāna; second, aspiration; third, mindfulness; fourth, liberation; and fifth, the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). That is to say:
Dhyāna-concentration nourishes the spirit; lightness, tranquility, and joy constitute the meaning of "food. The power of aspiration upholds the Dharma;
the growth of the Dharma-body constitutes the meaning of "food. The power of mindfulness maintains clear recollection; the manifestation of the Noble Path constitutes the meaning of "food."
Liberation that removes hindrances and naturally provides sustenance constitutes the meaning of "food.

The internal suffusion of the joy of Dharma, due to its ultimate bliss, likewise constitutes the meaning of "food. Both are the food of the inexhaustible principle of the self-nature of true suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Xingli Tongshu* states: "The *Suipan* (the 'Platter of Grace') is for showing the child.
Nowadays, when a child is born and reaches one year of age, various objects are gathered upon a platter and the child is allowed to take whatever they choose; this is called the *Suipan*."
Regarding the prohibition against eating meat, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat, he shall not eat the flesh of any sentient being.
Indeed, one who eats meat cuts off the seed of the Buddha-nature of great compassion; all sentient beings will see him and depart. For this reason..."
All Bodhisattvas must not eat the flesh of any sentient being; by eating meat, one incurs immeasurable sin.

The *Jieshu fayin* (The Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Precepts) states: "To see [meat] and abandon it is like the seagull departing from the ruse of the old man at sea, or the pigeon fleeing from the shadow of the Arhat.

If such subtlety exists in these instances, how much more so should the gravity [of the offense] be understood! Question: The sutras state that those who eat meat enter [into... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]
In the mountain forests, tigers, wolves, and lions all gather together. Why, then, is it said that all sentient beings see them and depart?
Answer: Those who "depart" do so because they are startled by the [beasts'] murderous intent and distance themselves; those who "gather" [are attracted] by...
They smell their kindred essence and seek one another out; whether they depart or come, it is all due to evil causes and conditions.
All Bodhisattvas, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the fulfillment of their stages, must never eat meat.

Now, there are those who, having acquired a modicum of knowledge and insight, claim that they act without obstruction through "reverse practice" and eat meat as they please; how can the gravity of such a sin be overestimated?
How true! Question: The harm caused by silkworms is also cruel. Why does the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* prohibit the eating of meat but not the wearing of silk?
Answer: This is because the prohibitions are found in different texts. Boiling cocoons involves the severing of life and is thus subsumed under the ten grave precepts against killing.

The cauldron and the silk-reeling wheel are instruments of slaughter and are thus subsumed under the category of lethal implements. Using them for profit to sustain one's body is subsumed under the category of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*...

The sutras also prohibit cotton and silk; thus we know that monks are called "patchwork-robed ones" (nàzǐ) and scholars are termed "plain-clothed ones" (bùyī)—of this there is no need for further discussion.
As for kings and ministers, they detest coarse clothing and prize the embroidered robes and ceremonial caps; herein lies the established teaching of the ancients.
The *Kaizheng Haiweng Jizi Shu* states: There was a man who went to the seashore every day and became intimate with a flock of gulls.
His father heard of this and said to his son, "Tomorrow you may catch a gull to bring back and look at.
The son replied, "Yes. The next day he went to the seashore, but the flock of gulls circled and flew away, refusing to descend.
The Arhat Chāyābuddha stood together with Śāriputra. A hawk pursued a dove; when it entered the shadow of Śāriputra, the hawk did not dare to descend.
Yet the dove continued to tremble without ceasing. When it passed into the shadow of the Buddha, it no longer trembled at all, for such was the Buddha’s great compassion.
The Great Master Zhizhe, whose realization was perfected, stated: "In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), there are fifty-two stages.

First are the external ordinary beings (wailan): the ten levels of faith (shixin). Second are the internal ordinary beings (neilan): the nature of the cultivated seeds (xizhongxing), which comprises the ten abidings (shizhu). Third is the nature of the innate seeds (xingzhongxing)."

The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). Fourth, the Stage of the Seed-nature (*gotra-bhūmi*). The Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Fifth, the Stage of the Noble Nature (*ārya-gotra-bhūmi*). The Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Sixth, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi-bhūmi*), which is adjacent to the ultimate truth and the pinnacle of all that is learned. Seventh, the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-jñāna-bhūmi*).
To clearly perceive one's nature is what is called "wondrous enlightenment" (miao-jue).
Regarding the wearing of coarse clothing, the *Analects* states: "The Master said: 'As for Yu, I have no fault to find with him.
He wore coarse clothing, yet he brought the utmost beauty to his ceremonial robes and caps.'"
Among the ten grave precepts of the Brahmajāla Sūtra, this is the first: the precept against killing. Among the forty-eight minor precepts, it appears as the tenth:

the precept against possessing implements for killing sentient beings; and as the twenty-ninth: the precept against maintaining a wrong livelihood. One should examine these in their respective original sūtras.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Mahāmati Bodhisattva, "There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat.

That is to say, since beginningless time, sentient beings have been related to one another through successive causes and conditions and have constantly been one's own kin. Because they are regarded as kin, one should not eat meat.
Because it grows from the impure elements of the body, one should not eat meat. When sentient beings smell its odor, they all give rise to [fear and aversion]..."
Because it is terrifying, one should not eat meat. Because it prevents the arising of a compassionate mind in practitioners, one should not eat meat.
Because it is the delight of the ignorant and foolish, being foul-smelling, filthy, and impure, and because it lacks a good reputation, one should not eat meat.

Because it causes various mantras and rituals to fail to achieve success, one should not eat meat. Because by seeing the form of a slaughtered creature, consciousness arises and one becomes deeply attached to its flavor, one should not eat meat.
One should not eat meat, for it is abandoned by the devas. One should not eat meat, for it causes the breath to stink.
One should not eat meat, for it results in many evil dreams at night. One should not eat meat, for tigers and wolves can smell its scent. One should not eat meat.

Because it causes people to lose moderation in their eating and drinking, one should not eat meat. Because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of revulsion and detachment, one should not eat meat.
I have always taught that regarding whatever food and drink one consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child or as taking medicine;
therefore, one should not eat meat. The Buddha further spoke in verse, which says in brief: "For profit, they kill sentient beings; for wealth..."
To net various meats—both are evil karmas; after death, one falls into the Hell of Screaming. Therefore, one should not eat them.
Alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path. Eating meat lacks compassion and forever turns one away from true liberation.
Therefore, one should not eat them.
The *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) states: "It is truly excellent if a person can abstain from meat.

If one cannot so abstain, then at least consume the three kinds of pure meat and reduce their intake. If the meal consists of several flavors, eliminate one of them. If both meals consist of meat, then for one meal at least, eat vegetarian food.
Human life has a fixed allotment of sustenance; by acting in this way, one may naturally prolong one's lifespan. Thus it is said.
It is said: "If one wishes for this world to be free from the kalpa of weapons, it must be that sentient beings do not eat meat.

Are these words not to be taken seriously? (Returning to the text: I have carefully examined the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which specifically highlights the gravest offenses, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which addresses other matters as well. Regarding the eating of meat...
The prohibitions were strict; yet, Master Wang [Zhe] instead advocated the doctrine of the "three purities" and the reduction of meat consumption.
Is this not the same as requesting a reduction from one who is plundering daily? He replied: "Not so.
Plundering a chicken is the minor evil of a single individual and can be reformed at once. To speak of 'requesting a reduction' implies an intention to nurture such evil. As for eating meat..."
The accumulated evils of the secular world can be transformed gradually; yet, if one wishes to stop them abruptly, one cannot avoid the fault of encountering resistance.
Therefore, when the people of Lu engaged in competitive hunting, Confucius also engaged in competitive hunting—how could he have helped it otherwise?

The intention of the lay practitioner is likewise such. Nevertheless, observing his discourse on the prolongation of life, one sees that it embodies a subtle power of silent sublimation and imperceptible withdrawal;
as for his remarks on war and weapons, these are an essential technique for stirring fear and inciting self-reflection.
How profound and far-reaching is the lay practitioner’s concern for the world!
An Examination of the Record on Predestined Salaries: When the Tang Duke Jin, Han Hang, was serving in the Secretariat, he summoned a clerk who arrived only after a long delay.
The Duke was angry. The clerk said, "I am unfortunate; I also belong to the Office of the Netherworld.
The Duke asked, "Since you belong to the Office of the Netherworld, what do you preside over? The clerk replied, "That which I preside over is..."
"Regarding the provisions for three grades or higher: if that is so, what food shall I eat tomorrow? The official said, "The opportunity must not be leaked.
I beg you to record this on paper so that it may serve as proof later. The next day, the official was summoned to enter.
He happened to encounter a high official bringing in food: a vessel of sweet rice porridge. The Emperor bestowed half of it upon the Duke of Jin.

Upon returning home, the Duke’s belly swelled; the physician gave him a decoction of tangerine peel, which cured him. When the Duke examined the records kept by the officials, they were all exactly as stated.
The Duke further asked, "Are all the foods consumed by people recorded in registers? The official replied, "For those of the third rank and above, [the daily intake is recorded] every day."
For those of the fifth grade and above who possess official authority, they receive a ten-day ration; if they lack such authority, they receive a monthly ration.

From the sixth grade down to the lowest rank (one-ming), they all receive a three-month ration; those who do not draw a salary receive only an annual ration. Thus, one knows that there are fixed portions for food and drink.
There is no difference between abundance and frugality. Thus, Longshu further said: "The measure of a person's worldly enjoyments is limited;
when that limit is exhausted, one meets an early end. Are these words not indeed true?
Mencius said: "Suppose there is a man who steals his neighbor’s chicken every day.
Someone says to him, ‘This is not the way of a gentleman; you should reduce it. He replies, ‘I shall then steal one chicken a month, and wait until next year before stopping.
What do you think? If he knew it was unrighteous, he should have stopped immediately; why wait for next year?"
"Hunting for the competition" (*lie jiao*) refers to hunters seizing birds and beasts to offer in sacrifice; this was called "hunting for the competition.
It was a non-ritual custom of the state of Lu that could not be abruptly halted. Therefore, Mencius said: "The people of Lu hunted for the competition, and Confucius also hunted for the competition."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, these meats were all produced through my supernatural power;
they originally possessed no life-force. You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the soil is damp and humid, further burdened by sand and stones, such that grasses and weeds do not grow.
Through the application of my great compassion and supernatural power, I have provisionally named these things 'meat' so that you might obtain their flavor. How can this be [otherwise]?"
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings are called "sons of the Śākya.
According to the prophetic words of the former Buddhas, it is clear that the so-called "three pure" and "five pure" meats of the present age should not be eaten.
Alas, how is it that those who find vegetarianism difficult often resort to these "three pure" and "five pure" meats?
To use such an excuse to claim that the Buddha possesses a "gate of expedient means" (upāya-mukha)—how erroneous this is!
Not only this, but in the past, the Sixth Patriarch ate vegetables grown near meat merely because he was concealing his brilliance and hiding his traces.
Those in the present age who are greedily attached to its flavor often eat vegetables grown near meat and say, "This is the established practice of the Patriarchs."
Ah! How laughable this truly is! To examine the proofs for the "threefold purity" and the "fivefold purity":
one does not see the killing, does not hear of the killing, and does not suspect that it was killed for one's sake—this is called the threefold purity.
When these are augmented by the addition of "naturally deceased" and "leftover from birds," it is called the fivefold purity.
"Brahman" refers to the common caste of this Western region. Kumārajīva said:
"One who studies extensively and seeks heterodox paths, relying on his own wisdom to act with arrogance and self-will, is called a Brahman."
The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states: When Huineng arrived at Caoxi, he was again pursued by malicious men.
He consequently took refuge within a band of hunters in Sihui County. Every time it was mealtime, he would have his vegetables cooked together with their meat.
If anyone questioned him about this, he would reply, "I am simply eating the vegetables from the edge of the meat."

Regarding the prohibition against drinking alcohol, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If a child of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol—since alcohol gives rise to immeasurable faults—and if one passes a vessel of alcohol with one's own hand to another to drink, one shall be born without hands for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so if one drinks it oneself? Furthermore, one must not..."
One must not teach any person or any sentient being to drink wine; no kind of wine whatsoever may be drunk.
If one intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The *Jieshu fayin* (Exposition on the Vinaya Commentary: Unveiling the Hidden) states: "As for 'immeasurable faults,' these do not merely consist of the thirty-six faults;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further clarifies thirty-five faults, and the *Vinaya* likewise clarifies ten transgressions. If one investigates them more minutely, their nature as faults is even greater."

They are beyond counting. They possessed the power to subdue dragons, yet they lay prostrate on the ground in ignorance; they practiced the misconduct of treading upon and driving away chickens, whereby all their precepts were utterly lost.
Even the majestic and powerful [King Zhou] was roasted alive on the *pàoluò* machine, while the "ox-drinking" [Shi Chong] brought his clan to extinction.

Although his merit was established at the Shanyuan River, he lost the mission through a leak of his words. How could the arising of such transgressions possibly have a limit? Question: For those who are immersed in the flow of intoxication, it is only logical that...
[The Buddha] said, "He has no hands. How could he have transgressed against a vessel? Thus he incurred this calamity.

Furthermore, when a subject celebrates the longevity of his sovereign or father by raising a cup of wine, how could such a heart of sincerity and reverence instead bring about a retribution of evil and meanness? [The Buddha] replied, "Generally speaking, when one speaks of 'sin' (pāpa),..."

All these statements are made for those who possess the Bodhisattva precepts. Having already received the Great Bodhisattva Precepts, one ought to practice the Great Path of the Bodhisattva, give rise to the Great Mind, and realize the Great Fruit;
this is precisely how one prolongs the life of one’s sovereign and parents. As for the reverence shown with wine and cups, such is but a minor form of respect.
Nevertheless, a response that does not require physical hands is not something felt by those of such [minor] kind; it is felt by them [who possess the Great Precepts].
A "return" (bào) is merely the act of grasping the vessel of delusion, pouring out the medicine of delusion, enticing the deluded person, and thereby bringing about deluded karma.
How can this be compared to presenting a cup to one's sovereign or father? Although it may not be called "great reverence," it does not fail to be an expression of sincere and respectful devotion.
To apply such a "handless return" to these [parents] would surely cause righteous ministers and filial sons to feel indignant.
As for those things that are lamentable yet unjust, I have therefore set them forth here.

Other matters, such as Mallikā drinking wine—possessing the deeds of a man despite being a woman, acting with expedient means upon perceiving the opportune moment—embody the true nature of a Great Being (Mahāsattva).
How can she be constrained by ordinary laws? If one lacks Mallikā’s heart while falsely aspiring to her outward traces, one will incur transgression.
As stated in the Vinaya, there is no greater harm than this; be cautious, be cautious!
Regarding the examination and verification of the "Five Hundred Generations of the Unsheathed Hand" (Wushou fayin), it says: there are five sets of five hundred [lifetimes].
The first five hundred were in the Hell of Saline Dregs; the second five hundred were in the Hell of Boiling Excrement; the third five hundred were in the Hell of Moldy Yeast.

There are four or five hundred [types of] insects; five or six hundred [types] dwell among flies and gnats; and five hundred [types] dwell among the "insects that ripen delusion" (*moha-pācaka-kṛmi*).
These present five hundred may be the final ones, who, by administering the medicine of delusion to humans, are therefore born among the insects that ripen delusion.
As for those "without hands," this does not mean they are exclusively those among humans who lack hands; it refers to species such as snakes, earthworms, leeches, and eels, which have no [limbs].
This is the retribution for [drinking] with the hands.
Furthermore, it is said that there are many kinds of alcohol: first, those made from grains; second, those made from fruits, such as sugarcane, grapes, dates, and so forth;
third, those made from medicinal substances, such as the flowers and leaves of various fragrant trees. Also, [there is that which is] heated milk.
It can also be used to make wine. While all wines intoxicate people, their potency varies in strength or weakness.
There are thirty-six faults in drinking alcohol: being unfilial toward one’s parents; showing contempt for elders and friends; failing to respect the Triple Gem;
lacking faith in the sutras and the Dharma; slandering śramaṇas; exposing the crimes of others; constantly speaking falsehoods; and making false accusations.
People engage in evil deeds: spreading rumors and engaging in double-tongued speech; using harsh words to wound others. This is the root of illness and the foundation of strife.
It causes an evil reputation to spread, leading others to loathe and despise them. They reject the sages and worthies, bringing resentment upon Heaven and Earth.
They neglect their duties and squander their family wealth. Constantly lacking a sense of shame and modesty, they strike others without cause.
They beat their servants; they kill living beings wantonly; they commit adultery with the wives of others; they steal the property of others;

they distance themselves from virtuous people and associate closely with evil friends; they constantly harbor anger and are filled with grief day and night; they are pulled eastward and dragged westward, held south and bound north;
they fall into ditches or lie by the roadside; they tumble from carts or fall from horses; they encounter rivers and fall into the water; they hold lamps and lose them.
Fire: one perishes from the heat in the summer months; one freezes to death in the cold season.
These thirty-five losses are set forth in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. They begin with destitution in the present life and end with folly in future lives.
In the *Daśa-varga-vinaya*, ten faults are further clarified. First, an ugly complexion; and so on, up to the tenth:
after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one falls into the three evil realms.
Even the Venerable Śāgata, who possessed the power to subdue dragons and was skilled at taming wicked nāgas, later drank alcohol.
He was lying on the ground. The Buddha passed by and saw him, and said to his disciples, "Can this man now subdue a frog? [The disciple replied,] "No.

[The Buddha continued,] "He has committed the offense of stealing a chicken; he is not one who observes the five precepts. A woman stole her neighbor’s chicken while intoxicated, killed it, and ate it."
A neighbor questioned him about this, yet he again falsely claimed not to have seen it. With a single drink, all his precepts were utterly destroyed.
King Zhou of Shang was as tyrannical as a bull; he abolished his own lineage through his cruelty, instituting the "burning grid" torture and creating a wine pond and forest of meat.
At a single drum-roll, three thousand men drank like oxen, until he finally met with total destruction.
His merits were established at Shanyuan during the reign of Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty. When the Khitans invaded, Kou Qun earnestly urged the Emperor to lead a personal campaign.
The Emperor followed his advice and traveled north across the river; the six armies all cried out "Ten-thousand-year Emperor!
The Khitans’ morale was shattered, and they returned home after entering into an alliance at Shanyuan. I once heard from my teacher that he had leaked confidential words due to drinking wine.
This was a failure. Such was the habitual character of this Lord Kou (Cui). For instance, when he wished to remove Ding Wei, he was instead cast out by Ding Wei;
this was one instance of his leaking secrets.
Mallikā, the consort of King Prasenajit, had received the Bodhisattva precepts.

When the king intended to execute a kitchen official, she prepared a banquet with wine for the king, encouraging him to drink together to resolve the matter; thus, the kitchen official was spared from death.
The lady then went to the Buddha to confess her transgression. The Buddha said, "For one who has committed such a violation of the precepts, there is no greater benefit. He saw that...
To employ expedient means according to the occasion is the very embodiment of a Great Being (Mahāsattva).
Master Gaofeng said: "Alcohol is the toxic drug that destroys the essence of the precept against killing; it is the cloud of delusion that obstructs right mindfulness;
it is the axe that fells the seeds of goodness; it is the firewood that nourishes the flames of karma. It opens the path to afflictions and closes the gate of merit."
From ancient times to the present, there have been no rulers, ministers, scholars, or commoners who have not met with ruin and disorder because of this.

Even in secular classics, we find the wise maxim of Yu, who loathed fine wine; if this is so even in worldly traditions, how much more so in our Buddhist teaching, where one seeks complete cultivation and sudden enlightenment through the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom?
If the mind does not eliminate the root of ruin and disorder, the path of quiescent extinction will be difficult to attain.
This refers to the five fundamental precepts.

To carefully observe the prohibition against alcohol in order to prevent disorder is indeed appropriate; its foul and corrupting nature is no less than that of the five pungent plants, and thus it must be abandoned.
How could its purpose be limited merely to preventing disorder? Formerly, Tao Yuanming...
When Mingyu was about to join the Lotus Society, he ultimately departed because there was no wine. Alas! If even a man of such wisdom acted thus, how much more so those who are inferior?
A practitioner of the Way should maintain themselves by means of the sutras and the vinaya, taking Yuanming as a model of restraint;
in this way, they will approach the ideal. As for the claim that "wine may be drunk in unlimited measure without reaching disorder," this is merely a prohibition of the Confucian school.
One must be like Wen Zhong, who remained sober throughout his life; or like Siyuan, whose drunkenness surpassed that of the awakened;

or like the Layman Vimalakīrti, who was able to maintain his resolve even when entering a wine shop—it is only after attaining such states that one may speak of this matter. How much less, then, could it be affected by foul and corrupt vapors?
How could this be appropriate for one who cultivates pure karma? To strictly prohibit it is paramount;
be careful not to use this as an excuse. As the Sūtra says: "It would be better to drink molten copper than to dare to violate the precept against alcohol. How can one not be cautious?
Examination and Verification of Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom, Volume Two, by Zheng Qingzhi. Examination and Verification of the Prohibition of Sexual Desire:
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "When such sentient beings enter *samādhi*, they must first maintain their precepts strictly."
Maintain pure precepts, forever sever the mind of lust, and abstain from wine and meat. If one does not sever lust and killing, it is impossible to transcend the three realms.
One should contemplate sexual desire as being like a venomous snake or as seeing a hostile thief.

First, one maintains the four parājikas and eight śaikṣas of the śrāvakas, holding the body so that it does not move. Subsequently, one practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva, holding the mind so that it does not arise.
When the prohibitive precepts are thus perfected, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing in the world;

theft and robbery will not occur, and there will be no mutual debts or burdens. Furthermore, one will not return to the world to repay past karmic debts. This is the cultivation of a person of purity.
Through samādhi, one’s parents’ physical eyes need not be the divine eye;

naturally, they behold the worlds of the ten directions, see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, personally receive the holy instructions, and attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They travel through the worlds of the ten directions with pure past lives and encounter no hardships or perils.
This is called the first stage of progressive advancement in cultivation.
The *Yongjia ji* states: Regarding women’s beauty, the ordinary person has no attachment in their heart;
yet the commoner is inverted, intoxicated by desire, sinking into and deluded by its chaos, unaware of its faults. It is like grasping the stem of a flower without realizing it is a venomous snake.

When the wise observe it, they find that even the mouth of a venomous snake, the paws of a bear or leopard, or a fierce fire of glowing iron are not used as metaphors for it—copper [is but a small part of the comparison].
One is impaled on an iron bed; the back is scorched and the intestines are seared; flesh and blood are crushed and disintegrated, with pain piercing to the heart and marrow.
Contemplate in this way: there is only suffering, no joy.
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* says: The Buddha said, "If there is a person whose lustful passions do not cease, they sit upon the edge of a sharp axe."
He removed his own shroud and said: "Severing the physical aggregates (skandhas) is not as effective as severing the mind. The mind is the chief minister;
if the chief minister is stopped, the followers will all cease. If the deviant mind is not stopped, what benefit is there in severing the aggregates?"
(Reply: I have carefully consulted the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), which states:

"If there are sentient beings who are prone to excessive lust, and they constantly maintain mindfulness of and pay reverence to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from lust. Why is this? It is because their minds abide in reverent devotion.
Thus, the deviant mind will naturally subside; this is simply the law of nature.
Now, as for the two preceding sutras—one speaking of "grasping the mind" and the other of "severing the mind"—are these not the true methods for departing from desire?

The commentary establishes that *samādhi* is synonymous with *samāpatti*. In the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, three types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are distinguished:
first, *śamatha*, which refers to those who attain concentration by taking only extreme stillness as their basis; second, [vipaśyanā]...
Samāpatti refers to those who cultivate meditative concentration by contemplating all illusory transformations.
Third is dhyāna, which refers to those who awaken to the stillness and perfect enlightenment by departing from the two preceding characteristics.
The four *pārājika* offenses for a bhikṣu are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.

The eight *pārājika* offenses for a bhikṣuṇī are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, physical contact with a male body, engaging with a man who has lustful intent, concealing another’s grave offense, and providing robes and food to a monk who has been suspended from the community.

Regarding the verification of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), Yuan’s "Chapter on Dispelling Desire" states:

"When a student wishes to practice the contemplation of impurity, they should first observe the moment a person has just died: their speech is full of lamentation, and their breath is foul and stinking."
The breath departs and does not return; the body grows cold and devoid of sensation. The four great elements have no master; where does the deluded consciousness go?
Contemplating this with intimacy, it is both startling and terrifying. Attachment and desire naturally grow thin, while compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity.

Cultivating from this point onward, there are nine perceptions (*saṃjñā*): first, the perception of bloatedness; second, the perception of disintegration; third, the perception of being smeared with blood;

fourth, the perception of festering pus; fifth, the perception of livid discoloration; sixth, the perception of being devoured by worms; seventh, the perception of fragmentation; eighth, the perception of scattering; and ninth, the perception of skeletal remains.
Eighth, the contemplation of white bones; ninth, the contemplation of burning.

By applying these nine contemplations to those whom I love, one comes to know that speech, laughter, and joyful pleasures all belong to a provisional combination; that purity, warmth, delicacy, and softness ultimately return to emptiness.
Even this body of mine shall likewise become so hereafter. What is there to love or to crave?
Ah! To break desire and eliminate greed, nothing is more supreme than this.
The verses of the Bhikṣu concern impurity prior to life; the chapter on "Dispelling Desire" concerns impurity after death.
Viewing them together, those who indulge in sensual desires may restrain themselves.

Question: Drinking alcohol clouds the spirit, and eating meat harms living beings; their faults are indeed appropriate. As for the five pungent roots, they do not cloud the spirit nor do they harm living beings.

Since the scriptures permit [the consumption of] these five exceptions, is this not a fault? Answer: Although eating the pungent roots does not harm living beings, in the end, they are also capable of clouding the spirit.
It is truly because the energy of filth and turbidity assists in arousing the mind of desire, while pungent and acrid flavors increase the nature of anger.
When desire and anger shroud the mind, one suddenly forgets luminous awareness; how could this be anything other than delusion? Therefore, one ought to exercise restraint.

Someone asked: [The text continues: "If the Four Heavenly Kings can be deceived, how could the two heavenly beings be deceived? Or someone asked: [the text continues].
According to what you have argued, when the ancients established the method of the "short fast" (*duñjāi*), how could they have intended to deceive the people of future generations?

Examining the *Sūtra of the Two Heavenly Physicians*, it states: "There are sentient beings who are beset by various afflictions and calamities;

Reflect further upon its difficulty, yet do not fear that difficulty; then what evil could there be in the three karmas? The *Jingtu zhigui* states:
"The practice of the ten wholesome karmas according to the *Contemplation Sūtra* is a practice of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle; it is the supreme, world-transcending ten wholesome karmas.
It brings about the gathering of all superior and virtuous people in one place and serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood. (As previously stated)
The three types of karma provide the main framework; these ten wholesome karmas elaborate upon its details, yet in essence they are one and the same.

Furthermore, according to the *Zhigui* (Pointing to the Goal), it is said: "Among those who practice the ten wholesome karmas of the superior grade, some achieve the Śrāvaka vehicle, some achieve the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, some achieve the vast practice of a Bodhisattva, and some give rise to the Ten Powers and the Four [Fearlessnesses]."
Regarding the phrase "fearless; all Buddha-dharmas are fully accomplished":
the ten wholesome paths are one and the same, yet they differ because there are differences in the awakening of the mind and its comprehension.

Thus, those who cultivate pure karma should not fail to encourage themselves with the perfect and sudden teachings of the *Contemplation Sutra*, but instead take rebirth in the Pure Land as their own aspiration.
In the commentary on the "Chapter on the Vows Seen by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas," the first gate of the Ten Powers states:
"To clarify the dharma-gates of self-cultivation and the transformation of others attained by all Buddhas."
Therefore, the ten powers are taught: first, the power of the possible and the impossible; second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration;

fourth, the power of the faculties; fifth, the power of aspiration; sixth, the power of disposition; seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives.
The ninth is the power of the divine eye; the tenth is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

These ten are collectively termed "powers" because they constitute the functional application of the Tathāgatas' knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*). They penetrate all things with complete clarity and distinctness;
being indestructible and unsurpassable, they are called "powers."
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which follow the ten powers (*bala*) in this exposition:
because the wisdom of the Buddhas’ ten powers is fully internalized, they possess clear and certain realization; thus, they have no fear in the face of external conditions.
First, the fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, the fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;
and fourth, the fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering. These four are collectively termed "fearlessnesses."
Within the great assembly, he extensively expounds upon his own and others' wisdom and abandonment;
since these are definitively free from error, there is not even the slightest sign of fear. Therefore, they are called the "fearlessnesses" (*vaiśāradya*).
The three physical karmas:
killing and stealing.
Regarding sexual misconduct (and its reversal): examine closely that killing does not consist merely of eating meat; stealing does not consist merely of covetousness;
and sexual misconduct does not consist merely of lustful desire. These are not limited solely to the ten courses of action.
It is the foremost, and indeed the foremost of all precepts; for it is considered a great evil that cannot be evaded.
Thus, should those who uphold the pure precepts not regard this as their most urgent task?
The *Zongjing lu* states: "Observe closely that killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arise from the single mind; they are quiescent in the very place they occur.
Why then need one further sever afflictions? Therefore, by simply realizing the single mind, all myriad objects naturally become like illusions.
Since the mind has no form, how could phenomena possess characteristics?"
(Reply: I have carefully examined this teaching. It is a discourse that probes the root. Does the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* not take all precepts and return them to the single nature?
Is this not the very foundation of the Mirror of the Essence (*Zongjing*)? This applies not only to the three karmas of the body; it applies to all ten karmas.
It applies not only to all ten karmas; it applies to all precepts. If one does not probe their root, [one cannot understand this].
Yet, if one merely attends to its branches, how can one possibly uphold the precepts?

The *Nettippakaraṇa* (The Guide to the Pure Land) states that the cultivation of the ten wholesome karmas according to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* refers precisely to this: the practice of the sudden and perfect vehicle.

Regarding the precept against taking life, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By nature, one is naturally distant from all killing. A bodhisattva does not keep weapons or staves, harbors no resentment, and is fully endowed with benevolence and forgiveness.
Toward all sentient beings who possess life, they constantly contemplate their benefit and maintain thoughts of compassion."
...this mind. These bodhisattvas do not even harbor ill will or afflict sentient beings, let alone intentionally carry out killing with a heavy heart.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra says: The Buddha said, "If a son of the Buddha, whether he kills himself, teaches others to kill, employs the means of killing, or praises [killing]..."
To kill; to rejoice upon seeing [another] kill; even to kill by means of incantations—these are the causes of killing, the conditions for killing, the methods of killing, and the karma of killing.

Regarding all living beings whatsoever, one must not intentionally kill them. This Bodhisattva ought to give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial piety, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
To instead, with a self-indulgent and pleasure-seeking mind, take life oneself—this is [a grave transgression].

Regarding the *pārājika* offenses of a Bodhisattva, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As for the difference between what is permitted (*kai*) and what is prohibited (*zhe*), a Mahāsattva may take life if he perceives the appropriate conditions (*jī*), whereas a Śrāvaka, even if he perceives such conditions, is not permitted to take life.

The *Fayin* (Unfolding the Hidden) explains: "To 'perceive the appropriate conditions for taking life' means that when one sees the presence of a situation where killing is required by the circumstances, one then carries out the act of killing."

It is harmless. Just as one might kill a single person to save many, or sacrifice the physical body to preserve the life of wisdom—this is the grand standard of the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas), beyond the capacity of the Śrāvakas. Therefore, it is permitted for Bodhisattvas but prohibited for Śrāvakas.
Question: "The śramaṇa is dedicated exclusively to the practice of compassion, whereas kings and ministers hold the authority over life and death.

If one does not execute those who have committed crimes, how can they govern the state? Answer: "If there is a crime, then killing is permissible; in such a case, what offense is there in killing? When Yǔ Shùn executed the Four Wicked Ones,"

The Duke of Zhou’s execution of the two rebels was precisely according to this principle. How much more so when one must shed tears before passing a death sentence, and only after three verifications does one carry out the execution?
This is to kill with compassion; since the law is not abandoned, how could such benevolence cause any harm?
State governance and the Buddha-mind are both without obstruction. Question: Humans can be observed for their capacity [for good or evil], whereas things are beyond such judgment.

Thus, the "Great Sacrifice" (tailao) was offered to the Emperor, and the "Grand Feast" (daping) was used to nourish the worthy. Why, then, do kings and ministers regulate the killing of animal species? Answer: Humans commit evils and thus receive the supreme punishment;
but what crime have things truly committed that they must be led to the place of death? Moreover, if the sacrificial offerings are sincere, [the purpose is fulfilled].
It does not hinder the performance of the *yue* sacrifice; even when the offerings are merely bitter vegetables and water, why must there necessarily be sacrificial animals?

To employ livestock for banquets and feasts was merely a provisional teaching (*upāya*) from before the Buddha-dharma had entered China. Is it appropriate to take such provisional teachings as the permanent law?

Thus, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty used flour to fashion sacrificial victims, the rites for sacrificing to his ancestors were already completed, yet the prohibition against killing living beings remained unbroken.
This is a sublime law for ten thousand generations, yet those who are ignorant condemn it. Question: Cattle, sheep, dogs, and pigs may not be killed;
but what shall be done when jackals and wolves block the road, or tigers and leopards devour human beings? Answer:
Fierce beasts cross rivers when they perceive virtue, and crocodiles move far away when moved by sincerity. If one can truly act in this manner, what need is there for killing? Its efficacy is such.
Or it may not be so. Capturing locusts or slaying dragons to eliminate harm for the sake of the people is equivalent to the ordinary penal laws of the state;
thus, such acts should not be prohibited. The *Kaozheng yinyuan faye fayin* states: "A single thought that originally gives rise to the intent to kill is the cause (*hetu*).

The various factors that assist in accomplishing that killing are the conditions (*pratyaya*). The implements and methods employed within the act of killing constitute the *dharma*. [The actual act] is the..."
Its function is the accomplishment of the act of killing as its karma. Other precepts should be inferred by analogy according to their causal conditions, dharmas, and karmas.
Regarding the *pārājika* offenses, see the notes on the two hundred and fifty precepts above.
Regarding the "Four Wicked Ones" (*Sìxiōng*) from the *Zuǒzhuan*: "In ancient times, the Lord of Dihóng had an unworthy son, called Hùndùn.
The Lord of Shǎohào had an unworthy son, called Qióngqí. The Lord of Zhuānxù had an unworthy son, called Tàowù.
These were three clans whose wickedness was perpetuated through generations; even Yáo could not remove them. [There was also] the Lord of Jìnyún..."
There was a man of unseemly talent whom the people of the world ranked among the three villains; he was called Tāotùe.
When Shùn served as minister to Yáo, he banished the clans of these four villains, casting them away to the four remote frontiers to keep off the *chīliǎng* demons.
Consequently, when Yáo passed away, the whole world was of one mind, uniting in heart to honor Shùn as the Son of Heaven.
Second, regarding the reversal [of fate]: after King Wu had executed Shang Zhou, the Duke of Zhou appointed Guan Shu to oversee Yin and Cai Shu to assist him.
Guan Shu rebelled against Yin; the Duke of Zhou executed Guan Shu and banished Cai Shu.
Regarding the *yue* sacrifice, the *Yi* says: "The neighbor to the east slaughters an ox, yet it is not as good as the *yue* sacrifice of the neighbor to the west, which truly receives its blessing.
As for the *yue* sacrifice, it is the most meager of sacrifices.
In the *Shushui Lunyu*, the Master said: "Eating coarse grain and drinking water, resting my arm on my pillow—happiness is indeed found therein.
Regarding the tiger crossing the river during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han: Wang Ba served as the Governor of Yingchuan; a tiger [crossed] to the north.
The crossing of the river was indeed brought about by virtuous governance.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, Han Yu served as the Prefect of Chaozhou.
At that time, crocodiles were causing great harm; the Master composed a text to offer a sacrifice to them, and the crocodiles moved far away and departed.
The *Yongjia Collection* states: "Whether moving in water, on land, or through the air, all sentient beings—regardless of the size of their life—are to be cherished with an impartial mind.
Do not allow any wriggling or flying creature to be harmed. From the beginning, clothing and food have been produced through cultivation and planting;
by tilling the soil, digging the earth, boiling silkworms and moths, and processing them for use, one injures the lives of creatures and causes others to undergo death."

They give [the meat] to themselves, yet they fear only hunger and cold; they do not contemplate the suffering of death. To kill another to sustain oneself—how painful and how lamentable! The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Ānanda, among all the worlds and the sentient beings of the six realms, if their minds do not kill, then they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi in order to transcend worldly toil; if you do not eliminate the mind of killing, you cannot transcend the dust."
[They] emerge. Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not cease killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.
Those of the highest grade become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like;
those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking rākṣasas. These various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed.
"O, after my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma-ending period (*mofa*), many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi.
You should know that these meat-eaters, even if they attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*.
When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha. Thus it was said.
People continue to kill, devour, and eat one another without end. How, then, can such people escape the three realms?
When you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, you must first cause them to sever the taking of life;

this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past (the first being the cessation of sexual desire). If one does not sever killing while cultivating meditative concentration, it is like a person...
They plug their own ears and cry out at the top of their lungs, seeking someone who will not hear them; such acts are said to be "the more one tries to hide, the more it is revealed.
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not even tread upon living grass when walking on a forked path, much less pull it up with their hands.
How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food? If bhikṣus do not wear silken garments from the East...
Cotton, silk, and fine cloth; as well as the boots, shoes, furs, and woolen garments of this land;

and milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—such things, O Bhikṣu, constitute true liberation from the world and the repayment of past debts, such that one no longer wanders through the three realms. Why is this? Because by wearing these parts of their bodies, they all become conditions for those [beings].
It is like a person who eats the various grains produced from the earth; their feet do not leave the ground. One must ensure that both the body and mind are free from...
"Those sentient beings who neither wear [it] nor eat it—I declare such persons to be truly liberated.
Examining the enumerations of the *Mahābala* ghost-dharmas, it is said that there are eight classes of *Mahābala*:
Gandharvas, Piśācas, and Kumbhāṇḍas are led by the Heavenly King of the East; Pretas are led by the Heavenly King of the South.
Those led by the Western Heavenly King are the various nāgas and pūtanas. Those led by the Northern Heavenly King are the yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Furthermore, there are eight other classes: first, devas—this means "heavenly beings" who are naturally and spontaneously superior in pleasure and superior to humans;
these are the twenty-eight heavens of the triple world. Second, nāgas—this...
3. Cloud Dragons (*megha-nāga*). These are dragons that guard celestial palaces, uphold the earth, and pour down rain. 4. Yakṣas.

This is translated as "valiant" or "robust," and they are also called "violent and evil. There are three types: first, those on the earth; second, those who fly through the air; and third, those in heaven.
They guard city walls, gates, towers, and so forth. 5. Gandharvas. This is translated as "fragrance-body" (*gandha-aṅga*). [They do not eat, but subsist on fragrances.]
5. They consume wine and meat; they rely solely on fragrances to sustain their bodies. These are the *nandana* gods who dwell beside the celestial banners. 6. *Asura*.

This is translated as "Not-Ugly" (*wu-nduanzheng*) and also as "Wineless" (*wu-jiu*). During the causal stage, although they practiced the Five Constant Virtues, it was because they desired to surpass others.
See the details in the six realms of the previous fascicle. 7. *Garuḍa*. This is translated as "Golden-Winged."
7. The *Kinnara* (translated as "Doubtful Man"): They are non-humans who resemble humans, yet have horns upon their heads;
they are also celestial musicians and deities. 8. The *Mahoraga* (translated as "Great-Bellied Crawler"): Great... [text continues]
The "Crawlers in the Bellies of Pythons" refers to this. As for the Eight Classes of Deva-Nāgas, there are eight Dragon Kings.
The Gandharvas, Asuras, and Garuḍas each have four kings. The Mahoragas have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of kings as their leaders.
Master Gaofeng said: "To kill a living being is not merely to kill a living being; it is to kill the Buddha, to kill one's father, to kill one's mother, and to kill oneself.
All sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning. Since they are the Buddha, what is there to kill?

As for one's parents, who provide the basis of one's physical form, throughout immeasurable kalpas of saṃsāra, the times I have received a body and inherited vital energy are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The very basis of embodied existence fills the three realms. Whether flying or flitting, crawling or wriggling, whether moving through water, on land, or in the air—there is nothing that is not thus.
How could this be anything other than killing one's own parents? Speaking in terms of karmic retribution: I kill another now, and he will kill me later.
When causes and conditions converge, the retribution is certain and without deviation. How could this be anything other than killing oneself? This applies even to a mosquito.
Even mosquitoes, fleas, lice, and all minute insects possess the Buddha-nature. To kill them intentionally is to sever the seeds of compassion.
The *Longshu Jingtu Wen* states: "Killing living beings is the foremost of the five precepts, and likewise the foremost of the ten precepts."
This is also the foremost of the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus, and the foremost of the fifty-eight precepts for bodhisattvas.
This non-killing is a great good; killing is a great evil.
If one can uphold this precept of non-killing to cultivate the Pure Land, one will certainly not be reborn in the lower grade.
Regarding the verification [of this], the *Candragarbha-sūtra* states that non-killing constitutes ten merits:
first, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings; second, one develops a mind of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward the multitude.
Third, the severing of evil habitual karma; fourth, having little illness; fifth, long life; sixth, being protected by non-human beings;
seventh, having no bad dreams; eighth, being free from resentment; ninth, having no fear of the evil realms; tenth, being reborn in a good realm at the end of life.
Killing is a great evil according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. There are ten evils of killing: first, the mind constantly harbors poison that persists through every lifetime without ceasing;
second, sentient beings loathe and detest one, having no desire even to see one with their eyes; third, one constantly harbors malicious thoughts.
1. One contemplates evil matters. 2. Sentient beings who see one regard them as if seeing snakes or tigers. 3. At all times, the mind is filled with dread.
4. Even when awake, there is no peace. 5. One constantly has nightmares. 6. At the time of death, one is driven to madness by the fear of dying.
8. The causes and conditions for the various karmas that lead to a short life; 9. At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the hells;
10. Even if one obtains human birth, one will always have a short lifespan. Therefore, one must observe the precepts.
Master Lianchi’s “Essay on Prohibiting the Killing of Living Beings” states: When people of the world eat meat, they all claim it is but what reason dictates;
thus they kill living beings at will, extensively accumulating karma of grievance. This has become a habitual custom through mutual imitation, such that they remain unaware of their own condition.
As an ancient said: "There are matters for which one must weep bitterly, shed tears, and sigh deeply"—this is precisely it. To calculate their deluded attachments, there are briefly...
Seven points are set forth as follows; the remainder may be inferred by analogy. First: it is improper to kill living beings on one’s birthday.
One’s parents grieved deeply when they brought me into this world through their arduous toil. The very day of one’s own birth is, in fact, the day upon which one’s parents were closest to death.
On such a day, it is precisely appropriate to abstain from killing, observe the fast, and extensively perform virtuous deeds, so that one’s ancestors—
May our deceased parents attain transcendence and rebirth; may our living parents enjoy increased longevity and blessings.
How can one suddenly forget the hardships endured for their mother’s sake and instead slaughter living beings? This brings misfortune upon one's kin above and harms oneself below.
That this practice is followed by the whole world without anyone realizing its error is the first cause for which we must weep bitterly, shed tears, and sigh deeply in lamentation.
The second point is: when giving birth to a child, one should not kill living beings. Generally, people grieve when they have no children and rejoice when they do.

One should consider that all birds and beasts likewise cherish their own offspring; to celebrate the birth of one's own child while causing the death of another's child—is this truly at peace with the mind?
Furthermore, a newborn infant has not yet accumulated merit, yet instead of doing so, one would rather kill living beings and create karma. This too is improper.
How utterly foolish! This is something practiced by the whole world without anyone realizing its error; it is a matter for "tears of bitter lamentation" and long sighs—this is the second point.
The third says: one should not take life in sacrifices to the ancestors.

On the anniversary of a death, as well as during the spring and autumn ancestral rites, one should strictly refrain from killing to provide merit for the deceased in the afterlife. To sacrifice by taking life merely increases one's karmic burden. Indeed...
Even if the eight delicacies were spread before one, how could they raise the remains of bones from the nine springs to cause them to eat?
It is without benefit and even harmful; the wise do not do such things. Yet this is practiced by the whole world, and people fail to perceive its error.
This is the third point for which one may weep bitterly, shed tears, and heave long sighs. The fourth is that wedding ceremonies should not involve the slaughter of living beings.
From the inquiries regarding the bride's name and the formal betrothal, up until the consummation of the marriage, the number of creatures slaughtered in worldly weddings is beyond counting.
Now, marriage is the beginning of human life; to practice slaughter at the very beginning of life is contrary to reason.
Furthermore, wedding ceremonies are auspicious rites. To employ such inauspicious matters on an auspicious day—is this not tragic?
This is a practice universally followed by the world yet remains unperceived as wrong; it is the fourth matter for which one may weep bitterly, shed tears, and sigh deeply.

The fifth point: When entertaining guests, one should not kill living beings. On a fine day and in a beautiful setting, with a worthy host and distinguished guests, a vegetarian meal of greens and broth is perfectly suited to a refined atmosphere.
Why must one extensively slaughter living creatures to exhaustively indulge in rich delicacies?

While the music of flutes and songs fills the cups and plates to satiety, the cries of the slaughtered resound upon the chopping blocks. Alas! Does anyone possessing a human heart not feel sorrow at this?
This is the fifth matter for which one may weep bitterly, shed tears, and sigh deeply: that this practice is followed by the whole world without anyone realizing its error.

The sixth point is: it is improper to kill living beings in the performance of propitiatory rites. When people of the world fall ill, they slaughter living creatures to sacrifice to the gods in order to pray for blessings and protection;
yet they fail to reflect that in sacrificing to the gods, their own desire is to avoid death and seek life. To kill—
To prolong my own life by taking the life of another is nothing short of defying Heaven and violating the principles of reason. Indeed, the upright are the gods;
how could the gods have any private interests? Since life cannot be prolonged, yet the karma of killing remains fully present, it is the same with all manner of licentious sacrifices.
That this is practiced throughout the world as a matter of custom, while people remain unaware of its error, is truly a cause for bitter lamentation.
Sixth, shedding tears and heaving long sighs. Seventh: One should not take life for the sake of sustaining one's livelihood.
For the sake of food and clothing, people of the world either hunt, or fish, or slaughter oxen, sheep, pigs, dogs, and so forth, to support their means of living.
Yet, in my observation, those who do not engage in such occupations likewise possess clothing and food; it is not necessarily the case that they will suffer from cold or hunger.

To die. To cultivate one's livelihood through killing living beings is to be struck down by the principles of the divine spirit (*shenli*). Among those who prosper through killing, there is not one in a hundred.
To plant the profound causes for the hells and receive the evil retribution of future lives—nothing is more extreme than this.
That this is practiced as a habitual custom throughout the world without anyone realizing its wrongness is the seventh matter for which we may weep bitterly, shed tears, and sigh deeply.
(He replied: "I have carefully examined how Master Jia [Jia Yi] wept and shed tears for his sovereign; this was indeed the natural course of righteousness.
Yet, as for what Master Lian taught—being a man of Yue—he did not speak of it with smiles or jests, but likewise wept and shed tears for him.
Why was this? It was because his heart of deep compassion and loving-kindness was sincere within and manifested outwardly."
Regarding those outside oneself, one views another’s killing as if one were the one killing;
thus, what is manifested in these words is one of profound sorrow and intense passion, such that one cannot remain so indifferent.
If people today read this essay and yet cannot refrain from killing, they not only lose their own innate goodness, but also betray the fervent exhortation of our Master.
Are these exhortations not too many?
Examining the evidence, we find that during the time of Emperor Wen of Han, the young man from Luoyang, Jia Yi, submitted his "Memorial on the Security of the Realm," stating:
"There is one matter for which one may weep with bitter grief; two matters for which one may shed tears; and [three matters] for which one may sigh deeply."
There are six sighs.
Mencius of Yue said: "Suppose there were a person here, and a man from Yue drew his bow and shot at him;
he would speak of it with a smile and in jest. There is no other reason than that he is distant from him. But if it were his own elder brother who drew his bow and shot at him..."
He then shed tears and spoke of it with grief. There was no other reason than that he felt a sense of kinship toward them. Zhen said:
"To refrain from killing does not merely mean that one's own person does not wield a blade, nor that one's fingers do not prepare a lamb.

It means that upon encountering any creature, one does not give rise to even a single desire to kill; or, upon hearing of a killing, one feels compassion and alarm; or, upon seeing a killing, one offers protection."

In all these cases, the mechanism of killing has not been severed. If one traces this mechanism of killing, it is like thorns and brambles tangled in the breast, with spears and halberds harbored within one's nature.
It kills oneself in the near term and kills the world at large. Thus, by bestowing beauty and surrendering the soul, one empties the very marrow;
this is killing with flower-arrows. By plucking bees and gathering dust, one unleashes their rhetoric; this is killing with the blade of the tongue.
Furthermore, one with a defiled head bared his arm to unleash his venom; this is killing by the fire of anger. Another openly plundered and stole until he exhausted the contents of the other's bag;
this is killing by the blade of greed. The harm wrought by the mechanism of these killings is truly great.
The practitioner who cultivates purity severs the mind of contrivance with the sword of wisdom. Exhausting my compassionate vows, I shall deliver them from the limits of suffering.
While in this world, they shall share in heaven and earth; when their retribution is fulfilled, they shall be born together in the Pure Land.
Is this not joyful?

Dedication Text (seen in the *Yuan Min Gong Ke Lu*. However, while that text dedicates merit to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time during the recitation of the Cundī Dhāraṇī, this text instead takes single-minded refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The following three texts are identical).
I prostrate to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. I prostrate to the Responsive Protector of the Three Continents.
Venerable Dharma-Vaiśravaṇa Deva: I humbly reflect that the sages cherish all things and Heaven and Earth favor life.
To nurture this heart of unbearable [at the suffering of others] is the very root of benevolence. I, the disciple [Name], follow the Buddha’s clear instructions and do not dare to kill living beings.
Yet all that stirs and breathes is the life-force of sentient beings. The karma of the ignorant and foolish is heavy; they constantly harm one another.
Even if one refrains from killing a single living being from this day forward, it is difficult to repay the debt of ten thousand lives from the past.
