Therefore, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha several times and rely upon the power of this Buddha, so that I, your disciple, may from now on exercise both compassion and wisdom, and observe the prohibitive precepts.
May the Sole Venerable One deliver all sentient beings who have suffered harm in the past. May the sins of sentient beings’ craving for slaughter be entirely eliminated.

May every household observe the fast, so that in this present life the horrors of war and weapons are severed; may every person refrain from killing, so that the gates of the hells and the realm of karmic retribution are emptied.
We pray that the Buddha, in his compassion, will take pity upon us and accept us. We pray that Weituo will look upon us with mercy.
I act as a witness to this, causing adverse conditions to dissipate and virtuous deeds to reach completion. May pure causes increase daily, and may rebirth be attained according to one's wishes.
(The final two phrases are newly added.)
The verification is entirely based on the *Longshu jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land of Longshu), which includes the following prayer:

"I, disciple [Name], respectfully recite 'Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western [Quarter]' one hundred and twenty times for the sake of all sentient beings currently being killed and eaten here in this Jambudvīpa. I humbly entreat the Tathāgata..."

Come, O Great Compassionate One! By my recitation of the names of the Tathāgatas—each single name of a Tathāgata delivering one sentient being—may it be so for every instance up to the total number of recitations.
May all beings be delivered and born in the world of Sukhāvatī. Homage.
Regarding the saying about the calamity of war: "If one wishes for the world to be free from the kalpa of weapons, there is no way except for sentient beings to refrain from eating meat.
Master Foyin’s Text on Prohibiting Killing states: "One knows only how to indulge one's nature and give rein to ignorance."

One does not fear that the underworld officials will record even a hair’s breadth of one's deeds. As soon as life ends, karmic creditors arrive; facing King Yama in person, how could one dare to deny anything?
One must report everything from beginning to end without error. Where can one escape the glowing furnaces and boiling cauldrons?
(Reply) I respectfully examine the matter of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It does not consist merely in prostrating and reciting before the Buddha;
rather, one must maintain this mindfulness at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and in every location, so that no transgression occurs. Only then is it true dedication.
If it were limited to prostrating and reciting before the Buddha, then while one might be granted progress, one would not be granted retreat. Dedication...
What more need be said? Let those who uphold the precepts strive for this.
Regarding the examination of evidence and the discourse on their progress, the *Analects* states: "The Master said, 'I favor their advancing, not their retreating.
The commentary says: 'I favor their advancing so that they may be seen to do good; I do not favor their retreating so that they may do evil.'"
"Excellent.

It is appended to the *Record of the Merit of Compassionate Liberation of Living Beings* (*Fangsheng Cixin Gongde Lu*), which states: Someone asked, "Is observing the fast and abstaining from meat superior to the practice of liberating living beings? He replied:
Those who do not eat meat can merely sever the conditions for killing and avoid their own transgressions, yet they lack the merit of benefiting sentient beings.

This is precisely why the Buddha taught people to observe the fast (*upavāsa*): he intended for them to increase their heart of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-citta*). As for those who observe the fast today—
Though one may abstain from eating meat, if one is unwilling to release captive creatures, such a person is called one devoid of compassion. Alas!
To eat vegetarian food for a lifetime achieves no merit in saving living beings; yet to give away wealth even once immediately brings the virtue of releasing life.
In the past, our Buddha even cut flesh from his own body to ransom a pigeon;
as a disciple, if one cannot relinquish illusory wealth to save a life, how can there be the cause for attaining Buddhahood?
Master Lianchi’s Text on Releasing Living Creatures states: "I have heard that among all things in this world, life is most precious;
and among all things in the world, slaughter and injury are most cruel. Therefore, when confronted by capture, even lice and nits flee as if to avoid death;
when rain is imminent, even ants migrate, still craving life. Why then do you set nets upon the mountains and snares in the depths, employing every means to ensnare them?"
They are captured—curved like hooks and straight as arrows. Employing every stratagem to hunt them down, they are made to lose heart and flee in terror;
mothers are separated from their young and scattered. Some are imprisoned in cages, as if confined within a dungeon; others are placed upon the blade and the block, as if facing execution by slicing.
The doe, pitying her fawn, licks its wound until her tender entrails break in pieces; the monkey, fearing death, gazes toward the bow.
Their shadows cast double as they shed tears of sorrow. To rely on one's own strength to oppress the weak is, in principle, deemed inappropriate;

to consume the flesh of others to nourish one’s own body—how could the mind find such conduct endurable? It is for this reason that the High Heavens bestowed compassion and the ancient sages practiced benevolence.
King Tang of Yin released the nets; Zi Chan of Zheng promoted the raising of fish. How sagely was the flowing water, moistening the withered and parched with its spring-like bounty!
How tragic was Śākyamuni, who cut his own flesh to save those facing peril and death! Zhiyi of Tiantai excavated ponds for the release of living beings;
the Immortal of the Great Tree protected the crows that nested within it. By redeeming fish and shrimp, they attained liberation and long life.
The lingering affection of the Zen Master remains; he saved the dragon’s offspring and transmitted the methods [of healing].
The compassionate influence of the Real Man Sun has not faded; he once revived an ant. A novice monk transformed a short life into longevity;
a scholar changed his humble name to that of a high-ranking graduate. Mao Bao escaped peril by facing danger; Kong Yu, by means of a small...
By performing meritorious service, one may be enfeoffed as a marquis. Qiu Shi released carp at Yuancun, and his longevity increased by a full decade.

Marquis Sui rescued a snake in the fields of Qi, and was rewarded with pearls worth a thousand pieces of gold. By saving a fly that had already fallen into a liquid, the wine-maker’s death sentence was commuted.
The turtle about to be slaughtered was released, and the chronic illness of the kitchen maid was cured; one exchanged his life for that of a butcher’s family;
Zhang, the Judicial Commissioner, had his soul ascend to the celestial realm; Li Jingwen traded his remaining life on a fishing boat; and Li Jingwen’s poison was neutralized by cinnabar.

Sun Liangsi released [birds] from the peril of the hunting net; when he divined the site for burial, feathered creatures gathered to assist him. County Magistrate Pan established prohibitions against fishing and hunting in the rivers and lakes;
upon his departure from office, the aquatic life wailed in grief. Sengxin spared the sacrificial victims of the ignorant masses, and sweet rain fell in Xiangfu.
Huichao prevented hunters from casting their nets at Caoxi, and the Way spread throughout the land of China; even sparrows brought pearls in gratitude.

How kind! The fox was able to approach the well and bestow its arts, whereby even this wretched body obtained life. It hung a white jade tablet to hear the sutras; in a land of hardship, it sought to live.
It appeared in yellow robes and entered a dream. Every act of giving has its retribution; such matters are not without evidence.

They are recorded in the annals and clearly manifest to our ears and eyes. May all universally vow that, upon seeing any object, they shall give rise to a heart of compassion and relinquish what is unnecessary.

One who possesses steadfast wealth and practices skillful means may bestow kindness upon many lives, thereby accumulating great hidden merit. Even if the benefit extends to but a single insect, how could it not be a virtuous act?
If one increases such deeds daily and accumulates them monthly, one's own practice will expand and one's blessings will become sublime.
Compassion fills the human realm, and their fame reaches the celestial courts. Hostile obstacles are swept away and empty; manifold blessings converge in this present life.

The roots of goodness are nurtured and moistened, so that remaining prosperity extends to future lives. Should you further assist them by reciting the Buddha’s name and chanting the sutra texts, [the merit will be even greater].

If one dedicates these merits toward rebirth in the Western Paradise, causing them to be forever free from the evil realms, then one’s resolve becomes even greater and the planting of virtue becomes all the more profound.
Through this support, the work of the Path will be swiftly accomplished, and one will be born as a superior class of being upon a lotus throne.
Examination and Verification: Xu Zhenjun was fond of hunting during his youth. One day, he shot and struck a deer.
The mother deer licked the wound for a long time, yet the fawn did not revive; the mother deer also died.
Zhenjun cut open her belly to examine it and found that her intestines were broken inch by inch. This was because she had grieved excessively over the death of her offspring.

When his entrails were nearly broken with grief, the True Lord felt great resentment and regretted his transgressions. He broke his bow and arrows, entered the mountains to cultivate the Way, and attained immortality.
While King Chu and Yang Youji were out hunting, they encountered a monkey; the King ordered Youji to shoot it. The monkey looked toward—
When Jianyou saw Ji, tears fell from his eyes; he wept in grief, knowing that Ji was certain to die.
When King Tang, the Great Shao of the Shang dynasty, encountered a hunter who had spread nets on all four sides, the King untied three sides and left only one.
He made this prayer: "Only those who do not obey their mandate shall enter my net."
Regarding the keeping of fish: someone sent a gift of live fish to Zichan of Zheng, but he did not eat them; instead, he kept them in a pond.

The *Nengquan Jinguangming Jing* (The Sutra of the Golden Light of the Flowing Spring) states that the Elder’s Son Shuishiliu saw ten thousand fish swimming in shallow water, on the verge of death from exhaustion.
He used an elephant-hide water bag to pour in water, saving their lives, and then preached the Dharma for them.
The Dharma. When the fish passed away, they were all reborn in the heavens.
Regarding the cutting of flesh: in the past, when Śākyamuni Buddha was a bodhisattva, he encountered a hawk pursuing a dove.
To escape the danger, the dove threw itself into the bodhisattva’s lap for refuge. The hawk said to the bodhisattva, "You wish to save the dove, but how can you allow me to die of hunger?"
The Bodhisattva asked the hawk, "What food do you require? It replied, "I eat meat. The Bodhisattva cut flesh from his own arm to compensate it.

When the hawk desired that the flesh be equal in weight to the pigeon, the Bodhisattva continued to cut his flesh; yet the more he cut, the lighter it became. This continued until his flesh was nearly exhausted.
The flesh could not equal that of the pigeon. The hawk asked whether he felt any regret. The Bodhisattva replied, "I have no regret.
If these words of mine are not false, may my flesh grow back as it was before. Having made this vow, his flesh grew back as it was.
The hawk transformed into the body of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and prostrated and offered praise from mid-air.
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai once excavated a pond and exhorted all people to release living beings.
Regarding the protection of birds, there was once an immortal who sat beneath a great tree, contemplating dhyāna and entering meditative absorption. There was...

A bird perched within his lap; fearing that it might be startled, he remained in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) without moving. He waited until the bird had settled elsewhere before emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
As for Chan Master Yongming Shou, who ransomed fish and shrimp: initially, he served as a storehouse clerk in Yuhang. Repeatedly, because of the storehouse...
He used money to purchase fish, shrimp, and other creatures to release them. Later, he was convicted of embezzlement while on duty and was sentenced to execution by public dismemberment.
The King of Wuyue, who was well aware of his practice of releasing living beings, instructed the executioners to observe his facial expression and demeanor before reporting back to him.
The Master’s face showed no sign of distress. People marveled at this, and the Master said, "I have used temple funds to purchase the release of living beings;
their number is beyond reckoning. That they shall die and go directly to the Western Paradise—is that not a joy? When the King heard this, he released him.
He subsequently left the household life to become a monk. After his master entered *nirvāṇa*, a monk entered the underworld and saw King Yama paying homage to a statue of a monk.
When he inquired about it, [he learned that] Master Yongming had already been reborn in the Western Pure Land at the highest grade;
because King Yama revered his virtue, he paid homage to this image from time to time.
When the Realized Man Jiulongsizun was not yet an immortal, he encountered a village boy who had caught a snake; the creature was exhausted and on the verge of death.
The Realized Man purchased it and released it into the water. Later, while sitting in silence, a person in blue robes came to invite him.
Following them, he went to a palace and court, where a sovereign extended him a seat of honor and said, "The child [who caught the snake] yesterday..."
He went out on a journey; had it not been for the Master, he would have died. He brought forth various kinds of rare treasures as a token of gratitude, but the Real Man would not accept them.
The King then retrieved the thirty-six formulas from the Jade Casket. From this time forward, the Real Man’s medical arts became even more refined.
Regarding the "Living Ants": Formerly, there was a śrāmaṇera who attended upon an elder.
The elder, knowing that his life had reached its end, ordered him to return home to visit his mother, instructing him, "You must return in seven days," desiring that he should pass away at home.

When he returned after seven days, the master marveled at this. He entered samādhi to investigate the matter; it turned out that when the boy had been at home, he had seen a swarm of ants in distress.
In the midst of the water, he built a bridge to ferry them across. The ants were thus saved from death. Because of this, he lived a long life.
○ Song Jiao and Song Qi were brothers. Both were candidates for the imperial examination. Jiao once saw a swarm of ants being submerged by water;

he wove a bridge of bamboo to ferry them across, so that the ants were not killed. At that time, a foreign monk beheld his face and said in astonishment: "Your countenance resembles [that of a great man]."
Jiao once saved millions of lives; he countered this by citing his own act of saving ants. The monk said, "That is sufficient.

Your younger brother shall be the preeminent leader among the many scholars, yet you yourself shall not fall behind him. Later, when the names were called, Jiao prayed that he would indeed be the first choice.
The court, however, deemed it improper for the younger brother to precede the elder, so they changed Qi’s rank to tenth and made Jiao the first.
First: When Fang Guimao was young, he encountered a man on the road carrying a tortoise; he purchased it and released it.
Later, while serving as a general, he was defeated in battle and leaped into the water. He felt something beneath him in the water supporting his feet, and thus managed not to drown. Upon reaching...

They disembarked. As for those who witnessed the tortoise's legs, it was the very same tortoise they had previously released. ○ Kōnyū was originally a low-ranking official; he too once released a tortoise.
As the tortoise floated upon the water, it repeatedly turned its head back to look at Nyū before finally departing.

Later, when Nyū was entitled to the rank of Marquis for his meritorious service and was having a seal cast, the head of the tortoise-shaped seal-stone (nyū) looked back as it was being forged. He had it recast.
It was as before. The founder was greatly astonished and informed Liu Yu. Suddenly, Liu Yu recalled the time he had released the tortoise;
as it turned its head back to look at him, he realized with sudden clarity that the one who would become a marquis was the reward for releasing the tortoise.
While Zongli was serving as a teacher in Yuancun, he encountered a red carp. He purchased it and released it.

Later, he dreamed that the Dragon King invited him into his palace and said to him, "Your natural lifespan has come to an end; because you saved a dragon, your life shall be extended by one *jì* (twelve years)."
When Ji She was about to travel to the state of Qi, he saw a snake on the road by a sandy desert. It was distressed, with blood flowing from its head.
He prodded it with his staff into the water and departed. Later, when he returned to the place where the snake had been, the snake presented him with a pearl.
Ji She did not dare to take it. That night, he dreamed that he was treading upon a snake; he woke up in a startle. Then...
He obtained a pair of pearls.
Once, while saving a fly for a wine-maker, he saw a fly fall into a wine jar; he took it out and released it onto dry ground, covering it with ash so that the fly could survive.
After doing this for many days, he released a great many flies. Later, when he was pursued by bandits, he was unable [to escape].
He confessed. As the prison was about to be completed and the executioner took up his brush, intending to pass judgment, flies kept gathering on the tip of the brush;
he brushed them away, yet they gathered again. Unable to reach a verdict, the official suspected the man’s innocence. Upon interrogating him closely, it was found that he had been falsely accused.
He summoned the thief and, after a single interrogation, the man confessed; he was subsequently released and allowed to return home.
Later, the Cheng family couple, who were fond of turtles, instructed their maidservant to prepare one for them. The master had briefly gone outside.
The maidservant thought she would release him, saying, "I am willing to endure the beating. She then placed him in the pond. When the mistress returned and sought the turtle, she was severely beaten.
Later, the maidservant contracted an epidemic and was on the verge of death; her family carried her to the water pavilion.
At night, a creature suddenly emerged from the pond and smeared wet mud over the maidservant's body. Her illness then subsided and she recovered. The mistress...
He found it strange that it had not died and questioned him. The man related the matter exactly as it happened. The host did not believe him;
he went out at night to observe secretly and saw that it was indeed the very turtle he had lost. The entire household was struck with amazement and never ate turtles again.
Zhang, the Judicial Intendant, frequently visited slaughterhouses to redeem animals with money and release them.
Later, when he was nearing death, he said to his family, "Because I have practiced the release of living beings, the celestial palace has come to welcome me;
I shall be reborn in the heavens. He passed away peacefully.
Li Jingwen habitually purchased cinnabar from fishermen and would release it back into the water.
Jingwen had long been taking cinnabar; the accumulated heat had formed a carbuncle that no medicine could cure.
He fell into a stupor, as if a school of fish were moistening each other with their breath, yet his poison was cooled and refreshed, and he subsequently recovered from his illness.
Sun Liangs encountered birds caught in hunting nets and arrows; whenever he saw them, he would purchase their release.
Later, when he was dying and wished to be buried, he was so poor that he had no means to provide for it. Several hundred birds gathered, carrying mud in their beaks to build a mound over him.
Onlookers were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, attributing this to the power of his compassionate influence.
While serving as County Magistrate, Lord Pan established prohibitions for the rivers and lakes, forbidding the common people from entering them to fish.
Later, when he left his post, a great sound of wailing arose from within the waters, as if they were mourning the loss of a parent.
Everyone who heard it could not help but marvel at this extraordinary event.
During a severe drought, the people slaughtered livestock as offerings to pray for rain.
The Master, pitying their ignorance, said to them, "If you can refrain from using livestock, I shall pray for you. The people agreed.
The Master then offered prayers with utmost sincerity, and a refreshing rain fell suddenly. Many people near and far were moved and converted.
Shouwang, the Sixth Patriarch, having already received the heart-seal of Huangmei, concealed himself among hunters in lay attire and was ordered to guard the nets.
Observing when they were absent, he would release any deer, rabbits, or similar creatures that could be set free.
Thus sixteen years passed. Subsequently, he sat at the Caoxi Daochang, extensively delivering all classes of beings.
His lamp was divided into five schools, and his bounty descended for ten thousand generations.
When Yang Bao was young, he saw a yellow sparrow being struck by an owl and falling to the ground.
Furthermore, he was once trapped by ants. He took them and kept them in a basket, providing them with yellow flowers until they were healed, at which point he released them.
That night, he dreamed of a youth dressed in yellow who bowed in thanks and presented him with four jade rings, saying, "I am a messenger of the Queen Mother of the West.
Grateful for your saving my life, I wish that your descendants shall remain pure and virtuous, and that you shall rank among the Three Ducal Ministers, just as I have been."
This was the end of that lineage. For four subsequent generations, they were prominent and illustrious.
Once, a monk named Hu Lin heard that yellow essence (huangjing) could arrest the aging process and wished to test it for himself.
He placed the yellow essence in a dry well, lured a man into the well, and covered the opening with a grinding stone. The man inside the well was terrified and distressed beyond measure.
As he was calculating, a fox suddenly appeared at the well and said to the man, "Do not worry;

I shall teach you a technique. I am a fox who has attained communion with the heavens. Dig a hole in a burial mound and lie beneath it, fixing your gaze into the hole. After a long while, you will fly out.
This is what the *Shenjing* (Scripture on the Divine) calls 'the spirit being able to make the form fly. You must fix your gaze upon it."
"Is this not the hole of a millstone? In the past, I was captured by a hunter; it was thanks to you that my life was ransomed.
Therefore, I have come to repay your kindness. Please do not neglect this. The man followed his advice, and after more than ten days, the bird flew out. The monk was greatly delighted.

Taking this to be proof of the efficacy of yellow essence (huangjing), he then separated himself from the group. Carrying the yellow essence, he entered a well and agreed that it should be opened after about a month.
When the time arrived and he opened it to look inside, [the man] was dead.
When Pai-pi heard this account of the Lotus Master, he said, "I once stayed in a hermitage.
Someone had caught several centipedes and was pinning their heads and tails with a bamboo bow. I ransomed them and released them;
the rest were half-dead, but one alone survived entirely and fled away in haste. Later, while sitting at night with a friend, there was a centipede on the wall."
I took a wooden ruler and struck it forcefully against its side to shake it and drive it away, yet it would not leave.
I said, "Was this not the one you released in the past? Are you now coming to apologize to me?
If that is indeed so, I shall preach the Dharma for you; listen attentively and do not move. Then I addressed it, saying: "All sentient beings are but the mind."
He replied, "It is so. Those with cruel hearts transform into tigers and wolves; those with venomous hearts transform into snakes and scorpions.
If you eliminate your poisonous heart, this form may be cast off. Having finished speaking, he told him to leave; thus, without waiting for him to be driven out, he slowly stepped outside the window.
A friend who was sitting there marveled at this rare occurrence. This took place in the fourth year of the Longqing era.
In a dream, a woman of the Gan family from Hushu in Hangzhou saw ten people dressed in yellow robes and wearing pointed hats enter her chamber.
A neighbor’s house had been robbed; the woman had sent ten live carp to her mother as a gift of comfort, which she had kept in a jar, but they had vanished.

One night, she dreamed of those ten figures in yellow robes and pointed hats kneeling before her and begging for their lives. Upon waking, she was filled with suspicion and consulted various diviners.
A person said, "There must be living creatures seeking release. He searched throughout the room and found ten large eels inside a jar.
Greatly startled, he released them. This event took place in the ninth year of the Wanli era.
Non-solid wealth refers to that which may be swept away by water, consumed by fire, seized by officials, or plundered by thieves;
because it is precarious, fragile, impermanent, and not a solid substance, it is also called "illusory wealth."
It is said that the Heavenly Treasury is vast and the celestial vault is remote; how, then, can they be interconnected?
One does not know that the Heavenly King, on the six days of fasting, tours the human realm, where there is no good he does not know and no evil he does not observe.
Furthermore, when humans practice the ten wholesome deeds, the heavens prevail; when humans commit the ten unwholesome deeds, the asuras prevail.
Therefore, the Heavenly Emperor frequently desires that humans do good. When even a single person performs a virtuous deed, the Celestial King of the Flying Devas reports it to the celestial capital.
The sutras contain explicit texts; this is not a mere speculative assertion.

Once the release of living beings has been performed and the prayers for their liberation have been offered, one should perform wholehearted prostrations before an image of the Buddha and address him, saying: "I, the disciple [Name], take refuge with single-minded devotion."
I address Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss: In accordance with the clear instructions of the Buddhas of the past, I now practice the release of living beings;
I have already released a certain number. By this merit, may my karmic offenses be eliminated and my grievances resolved;
may the roots of goodness I cultivate increase day by day; and at the moment of death, may my body and mind be peaceful and secure, and my right mindfulness be clear and distinct.
May I be received by the Buddha and born within a lotus flower in the seven-jeweled pond of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Upon the opening of the flower, may I behold the Buddha, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and become fully endowed with the wisdom of a Buddha.

By means of great supernormal powers, may all living beings whom I have released, as well as all infinite sentient beings throughout the ten directions, be completely liberated and achieve the Unsurpassed Way. May it be so!

The Buddha is compassionate; may he take pity on me and accept me. Having made this vow, one should recite the Buddha’s name either a hundred times, a thousand times, ten thousand times, or as many times as one desires.
Regarding the mantra for releasing living beings, the Buddha said: "In the waters there are minute insects that the ordinary eye cannot see;
therefore, the Vinaya teaches people to filter water with a cloth strainer before drinking. If one can write this *dhāraṇī* for protecting life and submerge it in a river..."
In wells and in water vessels, one should likewise recite the mantra seven times while calling upon the name of the Buddha;
all the insects will then be reborn in the happy realms. I shall now write the dhāraṇī below.
Oṃ vaśiparamaṇi svāhā huṃ traṃ khaṃ jaḥ hūṃ bhrūṃ aḥ namo pramuditavyūharājendrabuddhāya.
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin.
Reflecting carefully upon the reach of the Buddha’s compassion, it is evident that it extends not merely to tiny insects within water.
The Buddha further stated that upon the flames of lamps and candles there are certain minute sentient beings who swallow the light as their sustenance.
If one blows on it, they die immediately. Therefore, Buddhism teaches people not to blow out lamps or candles, fearing that it might harm their lives.
Inferring from this, how could there be any sentient being in the world who is not cherished and protected? Thus, Master Sengsong said:
"As for the most minute sentient beings whom humans cannot see, only the Buddha’s compassion can reach them. This...
This is why the Buddha’s compassion pervades the ten directions without interval.
Regarding non-stealing, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By nature, one does not steal. A bodhisattva always knows contentment with his own resources, and toward those of others..."

Being compassionate and forgiving, they do not wish to encroach upon or harm others. If an object belongs to another, they perceive it as belonging to another and never give rise to a mind of theft toward it.
Even regarding a blade of grass or a leaf, they do not take what is not given; how much less so other articles for the necessities of life?
The Commentary states: "Ultimately, there is no intention to steal" should rather be expressed as "taking with the intention to steal.

If there is no intention to steal, even if one knows it is another's property, whether one takes it for temporary use, takes it with the consent [of the owner], or intends to let the owner know [of its presence], none of these constitute stealing.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple steals themselves, teaches others to steal, employs means to steal, or uses incantations to steal;

whether through the causes of stealing, the conditions of stealing, the methods of stealing, or the karma of stealing—even down to the property of spirits and deities, the goods of thieves, or any material wealth, down to a single needle or a blade of grass—one must not intentionally steal.
A Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filiality toward the Buddha-nature, a mind of compassion, and should always assist [others]."
For one who, while all people seek to produce merit and happiness, instead steals another’s wealth and property— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
This includes the investigation of preparatory means, such as stealing by means of incantations, the preliminary acts of theft, breaking through walls, or picking locks.
It is of this nature. Regarding "stealing by means of incantations": there are malevolent sorcerers who can take another's property through the power of incantatory arts.
Regarding "lacking sympathetic joy and praise": the plotting of theft must be conducted in secret consultation; thus, instances of praising or sympathizing with such acts are rare.
Therefore, these are omitted.
Regarding the phrase "even down to ghosts and spirits" (*naitai guishen*): this indicates a progression from the more serious to the lighter offenses. First, objects belonging to ghosts and spirits;
second, objects that merely have an owner; third, objects belonging to bandits; and fourth, all other objects.
Master Gaofeng said: "Among all things, there is neither noble nor base, neither large nor small. To take what others have not given because one gives rise to the thought of doing so is theft.
From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity who sought the work of the Way, they clearly observed that all phenomena are empty and still;
thus they were willing to give away even their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains. How much more so, then, external wealth and possessions, which are but floating illusions?"
One regards [objects] as mere motes of dust floating in the air. Even if one were forcibly compelled to take them, one would neither take them nor find them worth taking;

how much less so if one takes them voluntarily? Or, while walking along a road, if one encounters objects left behind by others, one does not even look at them with the eyes, let alone grasp them with the hands.
This extends to money, wealth, and goods; to conceal official taxes and fail to pay them is likewise termed theft, for it is born of greed.
One is bound by that which one is driven by. Once the greedy mind is not extinguished, one abandons the seeds of worldly merit.
(Returning to the main point: I have carefully examined the account of Guan Ning and Hua Xin as friends. Once, while they were together weeding vegetables in a garden, they saw gold on the ground.
Ning waved his hoe away without a second glance, while Xin seized it and threw it aside; by this, people came to know their relative merits.
In the world today, there are many who conceal taxes and fail to pay them; yet one cannot even find a person like Hua Xin, let alone one like Guan Ning.
Alas! It is truly lamentable that it is so difficult to cultivate pure karma. How regrettable!

Investigation and Verification: Regarding Ning Xin’s Superiority or Inferiority during the Later Han Dynasty. During the time of Gongsun Du, whose authority extended across the seas, Guan Ning fled the chaos and sought refuge with him.
He then lived in a thatched hut in the mountains and valleys; whenever he saw Du, his speech was limited solely to the classics and never touched upon worldly affairs.
Consequently, Du respected his worthiness and the people were transformed by his virtue. Ning remained in non-official status for the rest of his life.
He died. Xìn served under Cáo Cão and participated in the acts of regicide. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Ānanda, furthermore, if the minds of sentient beings within the six realms do not steal, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi in order to fundamentally escape from worldly toil; if the mind of stealing is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust."
Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever their thievery, they will inevitably fall into deviant paths.
They will be possessed by superior spirits, middling demons, or inferior wicked persons—various maras. These various devils also have their own followers.
Each and every one of them claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world.
Concealing their wickedness and deceit, they shall call themselves "Good Knowledge" (kalyāṇamitra).

Each will claim for himself that he has already attained the dharmas of a Superior Man (uttaramanuṣyadharma), deluding the ignorant and causing them to lose their minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit will suffer depletion and dissipation. My teaching [is as follows]...
I, Kiu, wander from place to place begging for food in order to cause them to abandon greed and achieve the path to Bodhi.

How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit and create all manner of karmic deeds, all while claiming they are the Buddha-dharma? Because of this, they delude and mislead immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell.
(You must teach: When people of the world practice *samādhi*, they should subsequently sever the act of stealing; this is called being a Tathāgata.

The World-Honored Buddhas of the past have given this third definitive and pure instruction: if one does not sever stealing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup;
though they may seek to fill it, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.
Investigation and Verification: Regarding the superior grade of spiritual beings, the *Zongjing lu* states:

"What is spirit? It is that which is refined to the extreme and thus becomes intelligent. The *Chunqiu zhuan* says: "The application of its resources was vast; the refinement it took up was abundant."
To use objects on a grand scale and extract their essence in great abundance is likewise a form of theft.
Is there anything that can become spiritual without reaching the utmost refinement? When the essence is utterly exhausted and the spirit is depleted, one will inevitably fall into the evil realms.
Dedication Text (from the Yuan Family Daily Recitation Record):
I prostrate to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. I prostrate to the Honored Deity Vajrapāṇi, who responds to the three continents and protects the Dharma.
I humbly reflect that among the hundred deeds of human life, integrity and purity come first; the wise have always stood in awe of this.

Regarding the four things to be known, the sages of old have always treated even a single instance with the utmost gravity. I, [Name], disciple, follow the Buddha’s clear instructions and dare not engage in theft;

yet, while striving to fulfill the ultimate essence of righteousness, I find it difficult to fully examine my own conduct. To momentarily neglect a minor precept would immediately bring error upon my entire life.
What has been gained does not equal a hair’s breadth; what has been lost already exceeds mountains and peaks.

I specially call upon the name of Amitābha Buddha several times, relying on this power of the Buddha to cause my disciples from this day forward to feel a more intense sense of shame, for their pure virtue to become ever loftier, for their acceptance and refusal of things to be in harmony with propriety, and for them to exert themselves with the austerity of ice and gall. May those who behold my face find their own baseness transformed.

Upon hearing my name, may those who are greedy be inspired to cultivate integrity; may the eight quarters of the world all observe pure precepts, and for ten thousand generations, may they forever take me as a teacher of yielding virtue.
I pray that the Buddha, in his great compassion, will pity and accept me; I pray that Vajrapāṇi will look upon me with mercy and act as my witness.
May all adverse conditions be dispelled and all wholesome deeds be brought to fulfillment; may pure causes increase daily, and may I be reborn according to my wish.
Verification of the "Four Knowledges": When Yang Zhen served as Grand Marshal during the Later Han dynasty, someone attempted to bribe him with gold.
Yang Zhen declined it. The man said, "At this hour of night, there is no one who knows. Yang Zhen replied, "Heaven knows, Earth knows, you know, and I know.
How can you say there is no one who knows? Ultimately, he would not accept it.
Mencius said: "If it is not righteous, and if it is not the Way, I shall not give even a single grain to another, nor shall I take even a single grain from another."
Regarding the fulfillment of righteousness, Mencius said: "This is the fulfillment of the category [of righteousness] to its ultimate limit.
Regarding the base person, the Master of the *Lunyu* said: "Can a base person be employed to serve his ruler?

When he has not yet attained [his position], he is anxious to obtain it; once he has obtained it, he is anxious to avoid losing it. If he is anxious to avoid losing it, there is nothing he will not do."
"It is the ultimate.
Xinglian said, "I have heard that those who encounter the influence of Boyi become incorruptible even if they were formerly greedy.
"The eight *yan* (boundaries) refer to the eight directions of the world."
Appendix: A Chapter on Refraining from Theft (Composed by Master Lianchi) On the full moon of the ninth month, the assembly of monks recited the precepts.
One person rose from the assembly and knelt upright, confessing his transgression, saying:
"I, so-and-so, have committed theft. Looking at him, it was the Layman Hanxu. I said to him: "The Layman has always been circumspect and observant in your conduct."
"In the Dharma, how could such a thing exist? The layman replied, "It is not so. The eye steals forms; the ear steals sounds;
the nose steals fragrances; the tongue steals flavors; and even so, the mind steals dharmas. All of these take what is not their own. Can this be called 'not stealing'?
He continued, "I only pray that you will show me compassion and repent for my transgressions on my behalf. I said, "Among the sayings of the world..."
There are two kinds of thieves: one who goes to another's place and takes what belongs to them is a "stealer by theft";
one who takes what comes to them of its own accord is a "stealer by seizure. Layman, consider this:
when the eye steals forms, does the eye go to the forms to take them and bring them back to the eye? He replied: "The eye has never gone to the forms. How so?
It is said that form reaches the eye, and the eye follows it to grasp it. But [the Master] says: "Form has never reached the eye.
If this is so, then it is neither theft nor robbery. Why then is it called stealing? The Layman replied: "The eye does not reach the form, nor does the form reach the eye;
that which acts as the intermediary between them is consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is like when blue, yellow, and other colors encounter the eye, and consciousness seizes them."
...into the field of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṣetra*). Therefore, consciousness is the thief. I said: "This is indeed so. However, one who proves a theft must produce the stolen goods.
These are the colors blue, yellow, and so forth; let us now take them out. The lay practitioner said:

"Although blue and yellow cannot be physically grasped, yet when I reflect upon them in stillness, they appear vividly as if present within my mind and eyes. Therefore, it is said that consciousness is [the thief]."
“Thief! I said. “This is indeed so. Once the stolen goods have been recovered, one must punish the thief.
As for the colors—blue and yellow—are they the thief of color, or are they blue and yellow themselves? The layman replied, “Color is originally non-existent; it exists only through conditions.”
"The essential nature is empty and quiescent; who then perceives blue or yellow? I said, "Since the consciousness that could steal does not exist, how can the color stolen from exist?
Both are unreal; how can one be called a thief? Examining this thoroughly from every angle, no thief can be found.
What, then, will you repent for? The layman sighed and said, "How wonderful is this discourse! This is the repentance of non-repentance."
This is true repentance. It is appropriate that those of superior capacity practice it. But as for those of middling or inferior capacity, how may they proceed? I said:
"When a thief enters a person's room, he must wait for them to be asleep; when an object of perception enters a person's mind, it must take advantage of their mental obscurity.
Never has a thief been able to carry out his will while the master of the house remains wide awake."
When the mind-king is vividly present, yet the sensory objects find their opportunity, it is said: "A great thief has arrived; he plunders and seizes them.

How then can one say that [the mind] is not asleep? I have therefore composed a verse for this: "The ruler is enlightened and the ministers are virtuous; the main ropes are raised and the secondary nets are spread wide.
He tempers his fierce warriors and strengthens his golden walls and moats. When hostile states begin to plot and foreign tribes come to submit as kings."

"Even with such great thieves, how could they not perish? The lay practitioner bowed his head to the ground and said, "I pray that you will grant me these words so that I may take them as an excellent remedy for quelling banditry."
(Reply: I have carefully examined that theft is not uniform. There is theft with form and theft without form.
That which was discussed in the previous three sutras refers to theft with form; that which was discussed by Master Padmasambhava refers to theft without form.
Theft with form has a limited degree of culpability, whereas theft without form brings about inexhaustible calamity.
How much more so for the theft of form, which is easy to prohibit; yet the theft of the formless is difficult to suppress.
Now, even if people could prohibit crimes of form, who could suppress these inexhaustible calamities?
Alas! Not only are they unable to suppress them, but everyone mistakes the thief for their own son.
It is all thus. This is truly lamentable.
The verification verse says: "The mind is the sovereign of the single body, like a ruler.
The ears, eyes, and other faculties each have their respective duties, like ministers. When the mind is not obscured by desire, the ruler is enlightened. The ruler—
When one is thus enlightened, how could there be any among the hundred officials who would not listen with deference?
Consequently, the eyes are not deluded by forms, and the ears are not deluded by sounds; the six thieves are all thereby extinguished. Who then could plunder and seize this treasure of my house?
When such a person serves as the ruler of a state or as a virtuous minister, the administration will be equitable and affairs will be settled.
In principle, when military strength is formidable and defenses are secure, even great bandits cannot take advantage of the situation;
is this not because the method differs while the underlying principle is the same? Therefore it is said: "The confession that is not a confession is the true confession."
"When the main ropes are raised, the subsidiary cords are stretched" refers to how all matters of state, both great and small, are carried out without neglect or decline.
"Boars and wolves" refers to the strength of the military.
"Golden walls and moats" refers to the firmness of the defense.

Regarding non-incestuous conduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By nature, he practices non-incestuous conduct. The Bodhisattva is content with his own wife and does not seek the wives of others.

Toward the wives or concubines of others, daughters protected by their kin, those betrothed through family mediation, and those protected by the Dharma, he does not even give rise to [unwholesome thoughts]."
This applies even to a mind of lustful defilement; how much more so for engaging in the act, and especially through improper means?
The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "If a disciple of the Buddha indulges in sexual misconduct himself, or teaches others to do so—even with any woman—he must not intentionally engage in lust.
This includes the causes of lust, the conditions for lust, the methods of lust, and the karma of lust—even with female animals, or the daughters of devas and ghosts."

Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva engages in sexual misconduct through improper means— when he ought to give rise to a heart of filial piety and obedience, rescue and deliver all sentient beings, and bestow the pure Dharma upon others—
yet instead gives rise to sexual desire for all manner of people, without distinction even toward animals, or even committing incest with his mother,
daughter, sister, or other close relatives, lacking any heart of compassion, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

The *Jieshu fayin* (Exegesis on the Precepts: Unveiling the Hidden) states: Regarding the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the precepts do not begin with a vow against killing; rather, they first take a vow against sexual desire.

This is because the human body is born of desire, and desire is fulfilled through women. To fathomlessly deepen the ocean of affectionate attachment and to firmly entrench the roots of birth-and-death, nothing surpasses the color of women.
Therefore, this is what is vowed against at the outset. It is better to subject this body to the suffering of being burned within fierce flames than [to succumb to such desires]. Great...
I would rather endure the suffering of being submerged in pits and traps, or the agony of being pierced and cut by swords and blades upon mountain peaks—
with myriad sufferings crowding together— than ever bear to transgress the sacred scriptures by engaging in impure conduct with women.
Truly, the red furnace and white blades destroy the physical body in a single moment, while the flower-arrows and honeyed blades sink the life of wisdom for ten thousand kalpas.
When comparing sufferings within suffering, there are degrees of severity; how could one endure this rather than that?
These are words of a vow to reach the ultimate point of severance. In the past, there was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation, and he may have been able to escape this.
When the student recites the precepts reaching this point, they should feel a chill to their heart and a piercing cold to the very marrow of their bones, yet persevere in upholding them.

(Returning to the text,) I have carefully examined the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states: "Vimalakīrti appeared to have a wife and children, yet he constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*)."
Thus, even regarding sexual misconduct, one would naturally refrain from it without being constrained by a formal precept; how much more so for illicit sexual conduct!
For a lay practitioner, merely restraining oneself from illicit sexual conduct is already considered the very least; yet, even that is something they are often unable to avoid.

Alas! The *Kaozheng xieyin jie shu* (Commentary on the Precept Against Sexual Misconduct) states: "The five assemblies [of monastics] are governed by both the prohibitions against sexual misconduct and improper conduct; the two assemblies [of lay followers] are governed only by the prohibition against sexual misconduct.

Nevertheless, regarding one's own wife, it is forbidden to engage in intercourse through non-natural orifices or at improper places, as well as during periods such as lactation, pregnancy, or immediately after childbirth."

Regarding sexual misconduct: the five groups who have left the household life are the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, and śikṣamāṇā—the latter being women who have left the household life but have not yet shaved their heads. The two groups who remain at home are...
Upāsakas and upāsikās who give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience think: "I regard all sentient beings as my own parents.
By extinguishing all deviant thoughts, this is called the mind of filial piety and obedience.
Regarding the phrase "Pure Dharma and the Person," Kumārajīva said: "In a foreign land, there was a woman whose body was golden in color.
There was an elder’s son named Dhamudhara who, for a price of a thousand taels of gold, entered the Bamboo Grove with her, traveling together in a carriage.
On the way, Mañjuśrī transformed himself into a layman (white-robed) and appeared wearing [garments]..."
There was a precious robe, most magnificent and beautiful. When the woman saw it, a covetous mind arose within her.
Mañjuśrī said, "If you wish to obtain this robe, you must generate the bodhicitta. The woman asked, "What is the bodhicitta? He replied:
"It is your own body. The girl asked, "In what way is it so? He replied, "The nature of bodhi is empty;
your body is also empty. For this reason, it is so. This girl had previously planted roots of goodness under Kāśyapa Buddha and fundamentally cultivated wisdom.
Upon hearing this teaching, she immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). She then returned with the son of the elder.
In the Bamboo Grove, after his body had died, it became bloated, putrid, and rotten. Upon seeing this, the elder’s son was struck with great terror and went to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he too attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
From this perspective, those who bestow pure dharmas upon others are of this same category.
A bhikṣu practicing seated meditation revealed a hidden incident, saying: "In the past, there was a bhikṣu practicing seated meditation.
A māra transformed himself into a beautiful woman and spoke a verse to entice him. The bhikṣu replied: 'You shameless and depraved person, you speak such impure words!'"
"Washed away by water or consumed by fire, I would rather not see or hear of you. Māra sighed and said, "The waters of the ocean may be exhausted, and Mount Sumeru may be toppled;
yet that Superior Person maintains a firm and steadfast resolve. To be steadfast and firm is to be courageous and resolute."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, if the minds of sentient beings in the six realms of existence were free from lust, they would not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi to fundamentally transcend worldly toil; yet if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of demons—becoming a high-ranking demon-king in the superior grade, or..."

As for the classes of Māra’s followers, there are those of the lowest grade who are Māra-maidens; these various Māras also have their own retinues, each of whom claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such Māra-followers will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
They cause sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views, leading them to lose the path to Bodhi. You must instruct [them].

When people of the world cultivate *samādhi*, they must first sever the mind of lust. This is the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
If one who has not severed lust is called a practitioner of dhyāna-concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would still be known only as hot sand. Why is this? Because it is not the source of rice; it is composed of sand and gravel.
If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?
You must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind; even the nature of this severance must be non-existent. Only then may you hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
(Reply: I have carefully examined the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which speaks only of "the mind of lust" (*yīn xīn*) and does not mention "sexual misconduct" (*xié yín*). Why is this?
It is because the mind of lust is the root of sexual misconduct. While the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* strike down its branches, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* uproots the very foundation.
If the foundation is not uprooted, then sprouts will soon grow again, even if one applies the axe daily.
What benefit could there possibly be in that?
The *Kaozheng Aijian Keng Chumen* (Examination and Verification of the First Gate of the Pit of Attachment and Views) states:

"When examining the root of afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not go beyond views (*dṛṣṭi*) and attachment (*rāga*). ○ First, regarding the affliction of views: to contemplate reality with a distorted mind is termed 'view. If, regarding the conventional..."
Regarding the principle of reality: when the mind is deluded, it gives rise to inverted thoughts and seeks erroneously; through false views and partial principles, one falsely clings to them as real.

This is collectively termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). As for the afflictions of view, these refer to the five sharp-facultied proclivities (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*), the eighty-eight proclivities abandoned through the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya-prahātavya*), the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth.
Second, the afflictions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the mind of greedy attachment.

This is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). If one is deluded regarding the two types of phenomena—the provisional and the real—and becomes stained by attachment and entangled in all objects and circumstances encountered by the mind, this is collectively termed "craving.
As for the affliction of craving, it refers to the five dull underlying tendencies (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*).

The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through contemplation, as well as the fetters (*saṃyojana*), floods (*ogha*), bonds (*yoga*), cravings (*tṛṣṇā*), yokes (*yuga*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) that are to be abandoned [therein].
Regarding the eighty-eight proclivities—the sharp and dull varieties of the ten proclivities—both are discussed in the lower fascicle, in the "Recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*) section.
The first pure and clear instruction concerns the precept against sexual misconduct. *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) says: "Sexual desire is the source of birth and death.
Śrāvakas do not give rise to great compassion; they only fear birth and death, and therefore sexual misconduct is mentioned first.
Killing is the enemy of compassion. Mahāsattvas do not fear birth and death; they universally deliver others through great compassion, and therefore killing is mentioned first. [End of citation] I—
He asked the Master, "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is a Mahāyāna scripture; why does it begin its instruction with the subject of sound?
The Master Padmasambhava replied, "The Buddha was merely responding to the circumstances of the Mātangī incident; that is why he took lust as the starting point."
Although both sexual misconduct and killing are grave precepts, it is not necessary to concern oneself with their chronological order.
Dedication Text (from the Yuan Family’s *Record of Daily Devotions*):
I prostrate to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. I prostrate to the Responsive Protectors of the Three Continents.
Dharma-Vaiśravaṇa Deva, I humbly reflect that the loss of virtue and reputation both stem from form; that the depletion of merit and lifespan is nothing more than the result of lust.
Therefore, to preserve the body, one must sever the dust of passion, and the precepts regarding sexual conduct are especially strict.
I, your disciple [Name], follow the Buddha’s clear instructions and dare not engage in illicit lust; yet the waves of desire are easily defiling, and whenever I face—
The sensory realm tends toward stagnation and sinking; though one has previously observed the precepts against desire, one may fall at the crossroads of circumstance.

A single thought of transgression can nearly pierce the heart with thorns. Therefore, I specially call upon the name of Amitābha Buddha several times, relying on this power of the Buddha to cause my disciple, from this day forward, to stabilize their nature like the moon in a clear pool and to respond to forms like the wind passing through trees.
One contemplates the foul and impure as being within a leather bag; one no longer accepts the deceptive heat of the skull.

One awakens to the poisonous snake within the flower-stalk and forever casts off the deep entanglements of affection and love. This transformation began within the domestic gate and its rites spread across the vast seas.

Men remain outside and women remain inside, such that every household established a custom of distinction. The husband leads and the wife follows, such that for generation after generation, the world maintained a path free from depravity.

I pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will take pity on me and accept me. I pray that Vajrapāṇi will show mercy and act as my witness, causing adverse conditions to dissipate and virtuous deeds to be fulfilled.
May pure causes increase daily, and may I be reborn according to my wish.
The Diagram of the Four Karmas of Speech (Return):
I have carefully examined that although there are four types of karmic action of speech, their essential point lies in being cautious with one’s words.

If one can exercise such caution, one will not utter them recklessly, and thus the mouth will remain free from the four transgressions. Otherwise, if one does not err in the easy cases, one will surely err in the difficult ones.

Amidst these afflictions, it is difficult to avoid the four karmas; therefore, the *Book of Changes* uses few words, the *Analects* advises reticence, and Laozi speaks of "guarding the center"—there is indeed good reason for this.
The examination of these proofs reveals that excessive simplicity leads to extravagance, while excessive prolixity leads to digression.
Regarding the scarcity of words, the *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) says: "The words of the auspicious person are few; the words of the restless person are many."
Regarding the desire for speech to be circumspect: The Master said, "The gentleman desires to be circumspect in speech and quick in action.
Regarding the preservation of the center: Laozi said, "Excessive talk frequently leads to exhaustion; it is better to preserve the center."
Regarding the precept against false speech, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By nature, one does not speak falsely. A bodhisattva always utters truthful words, words of reality, and timely words;
even in dreams, they cannot bear to utter words of concealment. They have no intention to do so, let alone intentionally commit such an offense."
The Commentary (*Shu*) states: "To act in opposition to one's conceptions and contrary to one's mind is called 'delusion' (*wang*). The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) says:
"Even if one acts in opposition to the object, if it accords with the mind, it is not termed 'delusion.'"

The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "If a son of the Buddha speaks falsely himself, teaches others to speak falsely, employs the means for speaking falsely, or [engages in] the causes of false speech, the conditions for false speech, the methods of false speech, or the karma of false speech—even to the point of saying one has seen what one has not seen, or saying one has not seen what one has seen."
To speak falsehoods with body and mind, while the Bodhisattva himself constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and causes all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view,
yet conversely incites all sentient beings to engage in wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions—
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the Bodhisattva.

The *Jieshu fayin* (Unveiling the Obscurities of the Precepts Commentary) states: "Externally, there is right speech; internally, there is right view. When these are combined with the aforementioned [right] body and mind, this constitutes not daring to speak of what is non-righteous.
Generally, not daring to speak of what is non-sacred is precisely right speech and right view."
The *Jiayan bujian fayin* (Examination and Verification: On What Is Seen and Not Seen) states: Question:
When the Buddha saw the rabbit enter [the mouth] yet said he did not see it, was this a false speech? Answer: It was for the sake of saving the rabbit;

this is what is meant in the preceding section on the precept against killing, where it is said that there is no transgression and much merit is generated. That he saw the rabbit enter yet said he did not see it—this is...
To act contrary to the external object for the sake of saving a rabbit is to accord with the mind.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this world, although the beings of the six realms may have no killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct in their bodies and minds..."
The three practices are already perfected. If one utters a great falsehood, then samādhi will not attain purity; one will become a demon of craving and views and lose the lineage of the Tathāgata.
This refers to claiming to have attained what has not been attained, or declaring to have realized what has not been realized, or seeking to be honored, superior, and foremost.

This refers to speaking to others, saying, "I have now already attained [realization]," and thus seeking their prostrations and repentance out of greed for their offerings, thereby deluding and confusing sentient beings and committing a great falsehood.
You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* and must further eliminate such great falsehoods;
this is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past. If one does not eliminate these great [falsehoods]...
As for those who speak falsely: it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood and hoping to find its fragrance; such a thing is impossible.
If bhikṣus have minds as straight as a bowstring and are entirely truthful, they will enter samādhi and never encounter demonic interference.
I certify that such persons shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), it refers to asserting that which is right as wrong, or that which is wrong as right;

to say one has seen what was not seen, or to say one has not seen what was seen; and all such forms of empty and unreal discourse. If an ordinary person claims for themselves the realization of the state of an *arhat*, this is called a "great lie" (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*), and its transgression is extremely grave.
Except for expedient or provisional speech used to rescue others from urgent distress, in all other cases, [such speech] is not permitted.
It is so. Master Gaofeng said: "Since immeasurable kalpas past, we have instead been ignorant of our own selves. Deluded, we pursue external objects, giving rise to false imaginings.
Internally, we falsely identify the four elements as ourselves; because of this false identification, there arise false conditions. (2)
Deluded appearances give rise to false speech. Because of the falsehood of my single word, I lead others into a hundred kinds of error;

Zhen said: "Among the four karmas of speech, it is only false speech that arises easily but is difficult to eliminate. Why is this?
The people of the world become habituated to delusion, and their discursive thoughts fly about in confusion, giving rise to various forms of false speech.
These manifest in all manner of ways—in poetry and song, in rhapsodies and eulogies, and in inscriptions, prefaces, and records—wherein they resort to forced interpretations and manipulations."
To turn one's back on principle and deviate from the truth is delusion. To take pride in one’s own schemes and exhaust oneself with them;
to take pride in one’s own resolute judgments and provoke anger in others—these are delusions. To speak forcefully and deceive before gaining trust;
to use sweet words as a hook before achieving harmony—these are delusions. All are practiced merely for the sake of immediate victory.

To use craftiness and flattery to seek favor is delusion. To use the extraordinary and beautiful to adorn what one hears, and to use jesting and frivolity to harmonize with circumstances, is delusion.
To hear a single secret discourse and be unable to contain it, yet recklessly divulging it before others, is delusion.
To hear of another’s minor transgression and fail to conceal or protect them, instead embellishing it into a great crime, is delusion.

To speak of external matters while inside the boundary, or internal matters while outside the boundary; to conceal and distort matters internally and externally so that they are biased and unjust—these are delusions.
To discuss one matter when another is at hand, or to speak of one thing when another is present;

to speak of what precedes or follows an event rather than hitting the mark of the immediate situation—these are delusions. To hastily establish a doctrine when one's见闻 (knowledge and experience) has not yet been broadened—this is delusion.

To employ praise and censure to judge the ancients and the present, before one has deeply experienced the ways of the world yet delights in following worldly conventions to weigh right and wrong, is delusion.
To be free from delusion is to attain sincerity. When sincerity is attained, delusive thoughts naturally vanish and delusive conditions spontaneously sever.
Within, there was no hidden sentiment; without, there were no words of shame. It could pierce metal and stone, and it could move even the gods and spirits.

(Reply: I have carefully examined the various precepts. Why is it that there is only the prohibition against false speech?
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "There are four kinds of false speech: frivolous talk, slander, and harsh speech; these all belong to the category of false speech.

It is indeed true that for one who upholds the precepts of verbal action, the prohibition against false speech must be the primary concern. What is called "the mouth being free from the four faults" does not lie outside of this.
This is how it is attained.
Examining the evidence, the *Bai Gui Yi Dian* (The White Jade and the Flaw) from the *Shi Jing* says in its chapter on "Bai Gui":
"A flaw in white jade may still be polished away; but a flaw in these words cannot be remedied."
The *Lunyu* states that it is difficult to overtake a fine team of horses; Zigong said, "A team of four horses cannot catch up with the tongue.
The *Jia Yu* records that when Confucius visited the Grand Ancestral Temple in Zhou, he saw three golden figures with their mouths bound by triple seals.
And on its back, he inscribed: "The person of ancient times who was cautious with speech—be warned! Do not speak much;
much speaking leads to many failures.
It is said that even half a word, if it is not spoken with care, exhausts one's merit from a lifetime.
In *Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden), it says: "One who is about to exhaust their residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) is a Bodhisattva;
this is called 'Nirvana with remainder. One who has already eliminated and exhausted the habit-energies is a Tathāgata; this is called 'Nirvana without remainder.'"
Regarding the "untainted pure land," some may ask: Because one contemplates the true reality (dharmatā) and gives rise to the genuine untainted state, it is called "real" (shi).
As for "real," it means the "realized sage" (shisheng).
"Refining one's words and establishing sincerity. The *Appended Phrases* of the *I Ching* says: "The gentleman refines his words and establishes his sincerity;

It is like a fish [out of water].
